courses.title: AI Foundations for Everyone
courses.subtitle: For any professional with no technical background who wants to understand what today's AI tools are, how they work, where they fail, and how to start using them safely at work.
courses.summary: A plain-language grounding in artificial intelligence: what AI, machine learning and generative AI actually are, how chat assistants produce text, why they sometimes get things confidently wrong, and how to use them safely for real work.
courses.description:
AI tools are now on most work laptops, but few people were ever shown how they actually work. This course fills that gap without math or code. You will learn what separates AI, machine learning and generative AI; how a large language model turns your request into tokens and predicts a reply one piece at a time; and what the difference between training a model and using it means for you.

From there the course turns practical. You will learn the predictable ways these systems fail (hallucination, knowledge cutoffs, bias, overconfidence), get an overview of the main vendors and the difference between closed and open-weight models, adopt a simple rule set for what data you may share, build verification habits, and finish with a set of first workflows you can use the same day. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Professionals in any role with no technical background
Managers deciding where AI fits in their team's work
Staff whose organization has just rolled out an AI assistant
outcomes: Explain the difference between AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI using everyday examples
Describe in plain language how a large language model produces text from tokens and next-token prediction, and how training differs from inference
Identify the common failure modes of AI assistants, including hallucination, knowledge cutoffs and bias, and predict when each is likely
Compare the major AI vendors and the difference between closed and open-weight models at an overview level
Apply a data-classification rule to decide what information is safe to share with a given AI tool
Verify AI-generated output using a proportionate checking routine before relying on it
Write clear, structured requests and run at least three practical everyday workflows with an AI assistant
prerequisites: None. Comfort using email and a web browser is enough.

courses.title: How Large Language Models Work, Without the Math
courses.subtitle: For non-engineers who use AI assistants daily and want an accurate mental model of what happens inside one, so they can predict its behavior instead of being surprised by it.
courses.summary: A guided tour of the machinery inside a large language model, told in diagrams and analogies rather than equations: tokenizers, embeddings, attention, pretraining, instruction tuning, reasoning models, context windows and sampling. You leave able to explain why models behave the way they do.
courses.description:
Most explanations of large language models stop at "it predicts the next word". That is true but not enough to explain why a model can follow instructions, why it forgets the middle of a long document, why the same question gets different answers, or why newer "reasoning" models pause to think. This course opens the box one layer at a time, using worked examples you can try in any chat assistant and the free tokenizer and playground tools vendors publish.

You will follow a piece of text from tokenizer to embedding vectors, through the attention layers of a transformer, and back out as a probability distribution over the next token. You will see how pretraining on internet-scale text differs from the instruction tuning and preference training that turn a raw model into an assistant, how reasoning models spend extra computation before answering, and how context windows, tools and retrieval extend what a model can do. The course closes by tying each mechanism to a behavior you have seen at work. It ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Professionals who use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot and want to understand them properly
Managers and analysts who evaluate AI products and vendor claims
Anyone who finished an introductory AI course and wants the next level of depth without equations
outcomes: Trace how a sentence is split into tokens and explain why token counts drive cost, limits and some odd mistakes such as miscounting letters
Describe embeddings and attention in plain language and use them to explain how a model relates words across a passage
Distinguish pretraining, supervised instruction tuning and preference training, and explain what each contributes to an assistant's behavior
Explain what reasoning models do differently at answer time and when the extra cost and latency are worth it
Explain how temperature and sampling produce varied answers, and when to expect consistency
Describe context windows, tool use and retrieval, and predict where a model will struggle with long or unfamiliar material
Map common surprising behaviors, such as hallucination, sycophancy and knowledge cutoffs, to the mechanism that causes them

courses.title: Generative AI for Images, Audio and Video
courses.subtitle: For professionals who want to understand how AI creates pictures, voices, music and video, use it responsibly at work, and recognize synthetic media when they meet it.
courses.summary: How diffusion and related models generate images, speech, music and video; what today's tools from OpenAI, Google, Adobe, Midjourney, Runway and ElevenLabs can and cannot do; and the provenance, consent, copyright and labelling rules that govern synthetic media as of October 2026.
courses.description:
Generative media moved from curiosity to everyday tool in a few years. This course explains, without math, how diffusion models turn noise into an image, how the same idea extends to video frames, and how speech and music models generate audio. You will see why these systems are good at style and texture but can fumble text, hands, counting and continuity, and how editing features such as inpainting, reference images and voice cloning work.

The second half is about using media generation responsibly. You will compare the main tool families at a conceptual level, learn the provenance technologies in play (C2PA Content Credentials and invisible watermarks such as Google SynthID) and their limits, understand consent rules for likeness and voice, the copyright position on AI-generated works, and the deepfake labelling and machine-readable marking duties in Article 50 of the EU AI Act, including the transitional period added by the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI. You finish with a practical checklist for spotting synthetic media and a team policy template. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Marketing, communications and design staff starting to use AI media tools
Managers setting rules for AI-generated images, voice and video
Anyone who needs to judge whether a picture, clip or recording is synthetic
outcomes: Explain in plain language how diffusion models generate and edit images, and how the approach extends to video
Describe how text-to-speech, voice cloning and music generation models work and where they fail
Choose an appropriate tool category for a given image, audio or video task and write an effective media prompt

courses.title: AI Literacy for Teams
courses.subtitle: For team leads, L&D staff and managers who need to build practical, role-appropriate AI literacy across a whole team and show that they have done it.
courses.summary: Turn AI literacy from a slide deck into a team habit: assess where people start, define role-based competencies, agree shared norms for tool use, run hands-on practice, and keep simple records of what you did, including what Article 4 of the EU AI Act, as amended in 2026, expects of providers and deployers.
courses.description:
Rolling out an AI assistant is easy; getting a team to use it well, safely and consistently is not. This course gives team leads a practical method. You will learn what AI literacy means in practice, how to assess where each role starts, and how to define the competencies different roles actually need, from occasional users to people who configure AI workflows for others.

You will then build the team-level pieces: shared norms for what data goes into which tool, review rules for AI-assisted work, a prompt and workflow library, and practice sessions built on the team's own tasks. The course covers the AI literacy obligation in Article 4 of the EU AI Act, which has applied since 2 February 2025 and was amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI: providers and deployers must now take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff, without having to guarantee a specific level for any individual. It is a useful reference point even for teams outside the EU. You leave with a 90-day literacy plan for your team. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Team leads and department managers rolling out AI tools
Learning and development and HR staff designing AI training
Compliance and operations staff responsible for AI literacy measures
outcomes: Define AI literacy for your organization in terms of knowledge, skills and judgment appropriate to each role
Assess a team's starting point with a short skills and usage survey and identify the highest-value gaps
Design a role-based competency map distinguishing everyday users, power users and workflow owners
Set shared team norms for data handling, disclosure and human review of AI-assisted work
Run hands-on practice sessions built around the team's real tasks and build a shared prompt and workflow library
Explain what Article 4 of the EU AI Act, as amended in 2026, asks of providers and deployers, and document proportionate literacy measures for a team
Produce a 90-day AI literacy plan with simple measures of adoption and quality

courses.title: Python for AI Work
courses.subtitle: For analysts, researchers and technical professionals with little or no programming experience who want enough Python to clean data, automate small tasks and make their first AI API calls.
courses.summary: A beginner's path from installing Python to a working script that reads a CSV, cleans it with pandas, sends text to an AI model through an official SDK, and saves the results. Uses current tooling as of October 2026: Python 3.14 or newer, uv for environments, Jupyter and VS Code.
courses.description:
Almost every AI tutorial, notebook and API example is written in Python, and a modest amount of the language goes a long way. This course teaches the parts you actually need for AI work and skips the rest. You start by setting up a clean environment with uv, working in both Jupyter notebooks and VS Code, and learning the core language: values, lists, dictionaries, loops, functions and error messages.

You then work with real data: reading and writing CSV and JSON, cleaning and summarizing tables with pandas, and making simple charts. The final modules connect to AI services: keeping API keys out of code, making a first call with an official OpenAI, Anthropic or Google SDK, processing a batch of rows safely with retries, and using an AI assistant to help write and explain code without trusting it blindly. You finish with a small end-to-end project. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.

Technical professionals who need to read and adapt Python examples from AI documentation
Anyone preparing for hands-on AI courses that assume basic Python

courses.title: Machine Learning Concepts for Practitioners
courses.subtitle: For analysts, engineers and technical managers who need to frame, evaluate and discuss machine learning projects competently, with hands-on scikit-learn examples rather than theory for its own sake.
courses.summary: The working concepts of machine learning: framing a problem, preparing features, splitting data honestly, choosing and tuning models, reading evaluation metrics, avoiding leakage, and knowing when deep learning or a foundation model is the better tool. Every concept is grounded in a scikit-learn notebook.
courses.description:
Generative AI gets the headlines, but most production predictions — churn, fraud, demand, risk scores — still come from classical machine learning, and the same concepts underpin how large models are trained and evaluated. This course gives practitioners the vocabulary and judgment to frame an ML problem, build a sound baseline and tell a trustworthy model from a misleading one.

You will work through the full loop in scikit-learn: turning a business question into a supervised or unsupervised task, preparing features with pipelines, splitting data with cross-validation and time-aware splits, training linear models, decision trees and gradient-boosted ensembles (XGBoost and LightGBM), and evaluating them with the right metric for the cost of errors. You will learn to spot overfitting, data leakage and class imbalance, interpret models with permutation importance and SHAP values, and decide when a neural network, a pretrained embedding model or an LLM is the better choice. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Data and business analysts moving into predictive modeling
Software engineers who work alongside data scientists
Technical product and project managers who scope and review ML work
outcomes: Frame a business question as a supervised, unsupervised or ranking problem with a clear target, unit of prediction and success metric
Build reproducible preprocessing and modeling pipelines in scikit-learn
Split data correctly with holdout sets, k-fold cross-validation and time-based splits, and detect data leakage
Train and compare linear models, decision trees and gradient-boosted ensembles against a simple baseline
Select and interpret evaluation metrics, including precision, recall, ROC AUC, PR AUC, calibration and regression errors, based on the cost of mistakes
Diagnose overfitting and underfitting and tune hyperparameters without contaminating the test set
Explain model behavior with permutation importance and SHAP, and recognize when deep learning or a foundation model is the better tool

courses.title: Math for Machine Learning
courses.subtitle: For practitioners who can code but feel lost when a paper or framework doc turns to vectors, gradients and probability, and want the specific math that modern ML and LLMs rely on.
courses.summary: The linear algebra, calculus, probability, statistics and optimization behind machine learning, taught through NumPy and PyTorch code so every formula has a running example. Ends by assembling the pieces into the math of attention and of a training step.
courses.description:
You do not need a math degree to work in machine learning, but you do need a specific toolkit: vectors and matrices for representing data and model weights, derivatives and the chain rule for gradients, probability for model outputs and losses, and optimization for training. This course teaches exactly that toolkit, each idea paired with a short NumPy or PyTorch example so you can check your understanding by running code.

You will work through matrix multiplication and its shapes, dot products and cosine similarity for embeddings, eigenvectors and SVD for dimensionality reduction and low-rank adaptation, derivatives, gradients and backpropagation with PyTorch autograd, probability distributions, softmax, cross-entropy and maximum likelihood, and gradient descent with momentum and Adam. A final module combines these into scaled dot-product attention and a complete training step, and reads the numerical-precision concerns (floating-point formats, overflow, log-sum-exp) that matter on real hardware. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Engineers and analysts preparing for deep learning, fine-tuning or model-training courses
Data practitioners who want to read ML papers and documentation with confidence
Technical leads who review model training and evaluation work
outcomes: Manipulate vectors and matrices, predict the shape of matrix products, and implement them with NumPy broadcasting
Use dot products, norms and cosine similarity to reason about embeddings and nearest-neighbor search
Explain eigen-decomposition and singular value decomposition and their use in PCA and low-rank methods such as LoRA
Compute derivatives and gradients with the chain rule and verify them with PyTorch autograd

courses.title: AI Safety and Alignment Concepts
courses.subtitle: For non-specialists who need to follow the AI safety conversation: understand what alignment means, how labs try to achieve it, where it fails, and how frontier risk is governed today.
courses.summary: A plain-language tour of AI safety and alignment: why getting a model to do what we intend is hard, the training methods labs use, the failure modes researchers study, and the frontier safety frameworks, institutes and laws that now govern the most capable models.
courses.description:
AI safety discussions mix very different concerns: a chatbot that flatters users, a model that games its training signal, misuse for cyber or biological harm, and long-term questions about systems more capable than people. This course gives each a precise name. You learn the alignment problem through concrete examples of specification gaming and reward hacking, how RLHF, Constitutional AI and model specifications shape assistant behavior, and why behaviors such as sycophancy, deceptive alignment and evaluation awareness worry researchers.

The second half covers how safety is checked and governed: interpretability research, dangerous-capability evaluations and red teaming; the published frontier safety frameworks of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind; the International AI Safety Report; national AI safety and security institutes; and laws such as the EU AI Act's general-purpose AI obligations and California's SB 53. Facts are stated as of October 2026, and the course separates what is established from what is contested. It ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Professionals who read about AI safety and want to judge the claims
Managers and policy staff who need a working vocabulary for frontier AI risk
Engineers new to AI who want the safety concepts behind model behavior
outcomes: Define alignment, outer and inner alignment, and distinguish safety, security and misuse risks
Explain specification gaming and reward hacking using concrete examples
Describe how RLHF, Constitutional AI and published model specifications shape assistant behavior, and their known limits
Recognize failure modes such as sycophancy, deceptive alignment and evaluation awareness and explain why they are hard to detect
Explain what interpretability, dangerous-capability evaluations and red teaming can and cannot establish
Compare the structure of the Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind frontier safety frameworks

courses.title: AI Image Generation Tools Compared
courses.subtitle: For marketers, designers and communicators who need to pick the right image generator for a job, get usable results from it, and publish without rights or disclosure surprises.

Learn how they differ, run a fair comparison on your own briefs, prompt and edit across tools, fit them into real design workflows, and handle licensing, provenance and disclosure correctly.
courses.description:
There is no single best image generator. Some tools lead on photorealism and conversational editing, others on aesthetic style, legible text inside images, open weights you can run yourself, or commercial-safety terms backed by indemnity. This course gives you a working map of the major tools, explains in plain language why they behave differently, and teaches a repeatable way to compare them on your own briefs, scoring prompt adherence, text rendering, consistency across a series, artifacts and cost per usable image rather than relying on someone else's leaderboard.

You will practice prompting and editing in ways that transfer between tools, use reference images to keep a character or product consistent, and see how Midjourney, Adobe Firefly inside Photoshop and Express, Canva and text-focused generators fit into an actual production workflow. The final module covers what you are allowed to do with the output: each vendor's commercial-use terms and indemnity position, Content Credentials (C2PA) and Google's SynthID, disclosure expectations, and a pre-publication checklist for likeness, trademarks and sensitive content. Product details are stated as of the review month and linked to official documentation. Completion and a passing exam score earn a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification and is not endorsed by any vendor named.

courses.title: Meta Llama and Open-Weight Models
courses.subtitle: For engineers, architects and technical leads who want to deploy Meta's open-weight models with a clear understanding of the license, the hardware they need, and how Meta's model line has changed.
courses.summary: A practitioner course on Meta's open-weight models: how the Llama line evolved to Llama 4 Scout and Maverick, where the Muse family and Muse Spark Open now fit, what the Llama community license and acceptable use policy actually require, how to size hardware for mixture-of-experts models, and how to run, safeguard, evaluate and maintain Llama deployments.
courses.description:
Llama made open-weight models a mainstream enterprise option, and many production systems still run Llama 3.x or Llama 4 checkpoints. By 2026 Meta's public model line has changed shape: Meta's developer site now leads with the Muse family, including Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model released in October 2026 under Meta's separate Muse Model License, and models offered through the Meta Model API, while the Llama 4 models remain available under their community license. This course gives technical teams a clear, current picture of what Meta publishes, under what terms, and what it takes to run it well.

You will read the Llama 4 Community License and Acceptable Use Policy clause by clause (attribution and naming rules, the large-platform user threshold, geographic restrictions on multimodal use) and see why 'open weight' is not the same as open source under the OSI definition. You will size GPU memory for total versus active mixture-of-experts parameters, download gated checkpoints from Hugging Face, serve a model with vLLM and llama.cpp, use the correct chat template and tool-calling format, add Llama Guard 4 and Prompt Guard 2 as safety classifiers, and evaluate a model on your own tasks before committing. The final module covers when to fine-tune, managed Llama on the major clouds, and how to pin versions and plan for roadmap changes. Facts are stated as of the review month with links to Meta's official documentation. Completion and a passing exam score earn a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a Meta certification and is not endorsed by Meta.

Solution architects
Technical leads evaluating self-hosted models
IT and legal reviewers of open-weight adoption

courses.title: Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek and the Open Model Landscape
courses.subtitle: For technical leads and architects who need to understand the open-weight models beyond Llama, what each publisher offers, and how jurisdiction, license and hardware shape the right choice.
courses.summary: A publisher-by-publisher guide to the open-weight field in 2026: Mistral's Apache 2.0 and premier lines, the Qwen family, DeepSeek V4 and its reasoning lineage, GLM and Kimi, and smaller Western open models such as Gemma, gpt-oss and Nemotron, followed by the license, jurisdiction and hardware questions that decide which one you can actually deploy.
courses.description:
The strongest open-weight models no longer come from one company. European, Chinese and US labs now publish models that compete with closed systems on many tasks, under licenses ranging from Apache 2.0 and MIT to modified-MIT and custom community terms, and with very different implications for data jurisdiction depending on whether you use the publisher's hosted app or run the weights yourself. This course teaches you to read that landscape with the discipline of an architect rather than a leaderboard follower.

You will learn to read a model card (total versus active parameters, context length, modalities, training disclosures), then work through each major publisher: Mistral's Apache 2.0 models such as Mistral Large 3 and Mistral Small 4 alongside its premier and specialist models; the Qwen family's dense, mixture-of-experts, vision-language and coder variants and thinking modes; DeepSeek V4 and the reinforcement-learning reasoning approach popularized by R1; GLM and Kimi for long-context and agentic coding work; and Gemma, gpt-oss and Nemotron for deployment-sized models. The final modules cover matching model size to hardware, license fine print by publisher, government and procurement restrictions on certain models, and a worked selection for a hypothetical on-premises assistant. Facts are stated as of the review month and linked to official model cards. Completion and a passing exam score earn a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment; it is not endorsed by any vendor named.

courses.subtitle: For software engineers and engineering leads who want to get real productivity from AI coding assistants and agents without shipping unreviewed, insecure or unmaintainable code.

Covers completions, agent modes and cloud agents in each, how to configure them with instruction files, permissions and MCP servers, how to work with agents through tests and review, and how to roll them out securely across a team.
courses.description:
AI coding tools have converged on a similar feature set (inline completions, chat, agents that edit many files and run commands, cloud agents that turn issues into pull requests, automated code review and MCP integrations), yet they differ sharply in where they live and how they fit a team: an extension across many IDEs, a terminal-first agent, an AI-native editor, or a CLI and cloud service tied to a chat subscription. This course teaches each tool hands-on and then teaches the durable skill underneath all of them: giving an agent the right context, constraining what it may do, and verifying what it produces.

You will configure GitHub Copilot agent mode, Copilot cloud agent (formerly the Copilot coding agent) and Copilot code review; Claude Code's CLAUDE.md, permission modes, plan mode, hooks, skills, subagents and MCP servers; Codex's AGENTS.md, sandboxing and approval modes across CLI, IDE and cloud tasks; and Cursor's Agent, Tab, rules, cloud agents and Bugbot. The later modules cover test-first loops, reviewing AI-written diffs for hallucinated APIs and silent behavior changes, secrets and prompt injection through repositories and issues, licensing and data-retention settings, and measuring impact honestly. Product details are stated as of the review month with links to each vendor's documentation. Completion and a passing exam score earn a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification and is not endorsed by any vendor named.

courses.title: Choosing AI Models and Vendors
courses.subtitle: For technical leads, architects and product owners who must pick, justify and revisit LLM choices across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, the hyperscalers and open-weight models.

courses.description:
Model choice is now an ongoing engineering and commercial decision, not a one-off pick. New models ship monthly, the same model is sold through several channels with different terms, and published leaderboards rarely predict how a model will behave on your documents, your tools and your latency budget.

This course gives you a repeatable process. You will learn how the market is structured (frontier closed models, open-weight models, and the hyperscaler platforms that resell both), which capability dimensions actually separate models, how to read benchmarks critically, and how to build and run a task-specific evaluation. You will model cost per completed task, including prompt caching, batch discounts, reasoning tokens and the total cost of self-hosting. You will check data residency, retention and enterprise terms, read open-weight licenses for the clauses that matter, and design for portability and multi-model routing. The course ends with a weighted selection scorecard and a full worked example you can adapt. Specific prices and product facts are stated as of October 2026 or clearly labeled as illustrative.

courses.description:
The OpenAI platform has consolidated around the Responses API, with the Assistants API now listed as legacy and scheduled for shutdown in August 2026, and a growing set of built-in tools (web search, file search, code interpreter, remote MCP servers, computer use, shell and apply-patch) plus the Agents SDK for orchestration. This course takes a developer from a working call to a production-grade integration: choosing among GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna and setting reasoning effort, managing conversation state, getting schema-valid JSON with structured outputs, designing function tools and handling parallel calls, and choosing built-in tools versus your own.

Later modules cover agents with handoffs, guardrails and tracing; long-running work with background mode, webhooks and compaction; sandboxing computer-use and shell actions; migrating from the Assistants API and Chat Completions; image generation with the GPT Image models; voice agents over the Realtime API via WebRTC, WebSocket and SIP; and the operational side: prompt caching, the Batch API and flex processing, retries and rate-limit handling, embeddings and moderation, evals and graders, the fine-tuning methods (supervised, vision, DPO and reinforcement), and data-retention and admin controls. Code examples use the official Python and TypeScript SDKs. Model and feature names are stated as of the review month with links to OpenAI's API documentation. courses.title: Anthropic Claude API: Tools, Caching and Agents
courses.subtitle: For developers who have called an LLM API and now need to build production tool-using applications and agents on the Claude Developer Platform.
courses.summary: A hands-on tour of the Claude Messages API as of October 2026: content blocks, thinking and effort, client and server tools, prompt caching, batches, the Files API, context management, MCP, Agent Skills and the Claude Agent SDK.
courses.description:
The Claude API has grown from a single chat endpoint into a platform for building agents: client tools you execute, server tools Anthropic executes (web search, web fetch, code execution), tool search for large toolsets, prompt caching and batches for cost, context editing, compaction and a memory tool for long-running work, a connector for remote MCP servers, Agent Skills, and the Claude Agent SDK that packages the same agent loop used by Claude Code.

This course works through each layer in the order you need it in a real build. You start with the Messages API request and response shape, streaming and token accounting; move to the tool-use loop and its failure modes; then cut cost and latency with cache breakpoints, the Message Batches API and file uploads. The second half covers long-running agents: managing the context window, connecting MCP servers, packaging procedures as Skills, building with the Agent SDK's subagents, hooks and permissions, and deciding when Anthropic's hosted Claude Managed Agents harness (in beta as of October 2026) is the better fit. It closes with what changes when you call Claude through Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry instead of the direct API, and how to evaluate an agent before launch. Product facts are stated as of October 2026; beta features are labeled as such and checked against platform.claude.com documentation.

Platform engineers responsible for cost and reliability of LLM features
Solution architects designing agentic workflows on Claude

Implement a robust tool-use loop with strict JSON Schema tools, parallel calls, tool errors and server tools such as web search and code execution
Place prompt-caching breakpoints correctly and verify savings from cache read and write token counts
Choose between synchronous calls, the Message Batches API and the Files API for a given workload and estimate the cost difference
Design context management for long-running agents using context editing, compaction and the memory tool
Build an agent with the Claude Agent SDK that uses subagents, hooks, MCP servers and scoped permissions
Decide whether a workload should run its own agent loop with the Agent SDK or use Claude Managed Agents, given data-retention and control requirements

courses.title: Google Vertex AI and the Gemini API
courses.subtitle: For developers and cloud architects who need to build on Gemini through the Gemini Developer API and Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI).
courses.summary: Build on Gemini through both of Google's doors: the Gemini Developer API and the enterprise platform Google renamed from Vertex AI to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform in April 2026. Covers the Gen AI SDK, the Interactions API, grounding, caching, batch, ADK agents, the Live API and enterprise controls.
courses.description:
Google sells Gemini through two front doors that share a model family but differ in authentication, quotas, data terms and surrounding services. The Gemini Developer API (keys from Google AI Studio) is the fastest path to a prototype; Google Cloud's enterprise platform, called Vertex AI until Google Cloud Next in April 2026 and now Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, adds IAM, VPC Service Controls, regional data residency, Model Garden, provisioned throughput and managed agent hosting. Many docs, SDK parameters and console labels still say Vertex AI, so this course teaches both names.

You will use the Google Gen AI SDK against both endpoints, compare the legacy generateContent interface with the Interactions API that Google made generally available in June 2026 and now recommends for new projects (and the features, such as batch and explicit caching, that still require generateContent), and control thinking, multimodal inputs and structured output. You will ground answers in Google Search, URL context and your own data, lower cost with implicit and explicit context caching and batch jobs, and size quotas and provisioned throughput. The agent modules cover the Agent Development Kit, deployment to Agent Runtime (formerly Agent Engine) and the Live API for real-time voice. The course ends with Model Garden partner and open models, Gen AI evals, and the security controls regulated organizations ask about first. Facts are as of October 2026.

courses.description:
Azure AI Foundry was renamed Microsoft Foundry in late 2025, and Azure OpenAI now lives inside it as one family of Foundry Models alongside models sold directly by Azure and partner models such as Anthropic's Claude. The portal, resource types, SDKs and API surface have all shifted: the v1 API lets you use the standard OpenAI SDK without dated api-version parameters, and Microsoft Agent Framework has replaced Semantic Kernel and AutoGen as the recommended agent SDK. This course uses the current names and points out the old ones you will still meet in tutorials and Terraform modules.

You will choose deployment types (Global, Data Zone or geography-based processing, each billed as Standard pay-per-token, Provisioned or Batch) against residency and throughput needs, call models with the Responses API using Microsoft Entra ID instead of keys, and configure content filters, Prompt Shields and groundedness detection. You will connect Azure AI Search for retrieval, decide when fine-tuning is justified, and build agents with Foundry Agent Service and Microsoft Agent Framework, including MCP tools. The final module covers TPM quotas and PTU sizing, private networking, Azure API Management as an AI gateway, and tracing and evaluations. Product facts are as of October 2026 and checked against Microsoft Learn.

courses.title: Amazon Bedrock: Multi-Model AI on AWS
courses.subtitle: For developers and AWS architects who need to build, govern and scale applications and agents across the many model providers available in Amazon Bedrock.
courses.summary: Use Amazon Bedrock as a multi-model platform as of October 2026: model access and IAM, the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, the Converse API, cross-Region inference, service tiers, caching and batch, Knowledge Bases, Guardrails, Bedrock Agents vs AgentCore, and production operations.
courses.description:
Bedrock's value is breadth behind one AWS control plane: Amazon's Nova models alongside Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Mistral, Cohere, DeepSeek, Qwen and others, all governed by IAM, logged to CloudWatch and billed to your AWS account. That breadth comes with choices that trip teams up: two inference endpoints (bedrock-runtime for Converse and InvokeModel, and bedrock-mantle for OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic Messages APIs, with AWS guidance on which to use for new applications having shifted during 2026), model-specific feature support, cross-Region inference profiles, and four service tiers (Reserved, Priority, Standard and Flex) that trade latency against price.

This course teaches you to make those choices deliberately. You will call models with the Converse API so one request shape works across providers, add tool use and streaming, and plan throughput with inference profiles and tiers. You will cut cost with prompt caching, batch inference, Intelligent Prompt Routing and distillation. You will build retrieval on Knowledge Bases, enforce policy with Guardrails, and evaluate both models and RAG pipelines. The agent module compares classic Bedrock Agents with AgentCore's Runtime, Gateway, Memory, Identity and Policy services. The course closes with custom model import, logging and cost allocation, and a hypothetical reference architecture for a governed internal assistant. Facts are as of October 2026 and checked against the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

courses.title: NVIDIA NIM and AI Enterprise
courses.subtitle: For platform and MLOps engineers who need to deploy, license and operate NVIDIA NIM inference microservices and the NVIDIA AI Enterprise software stack on their own GPUs.
courses.summary: Learn what NVIDIA AI Enterprise actually includes and how it is licensed, then deploy NIM microservices with Docker and the NIM Operator, scale with Dynamo, add NeMo Retriever and NeMo Guardrails, customize with NeMo microservices, and benchmark and monitor the result. courses.description:
NVIDIA AI Enterprise is a per-GPU software subscription that bundles supported drivers, operators, frameworks and the NIM inference microservices. NIM packages a model with an optimized serving backend behind an OpenAI-compatible API, so a team can stand up a production endpoint in minutes, but the details matter: model profiles, engine selection, cache volumes, NGC credentials, release branches, and the difference between Developer Program access and a production entitlement.

This course starts with licensing and lifecycle so you know what you are buying and supporting. You will run an LLM NIM with Docker, select profiles for your GPUs, and call it with standard OpenAI clients. On Kubernetes you will layer the GPU Operator, Network Operator and NIM Operator, cache models with NIMCache, deploy NIMService resources, and see where NVIDIA Dynamo adds disaggregated prefill and decode and KV-cache-aware routing. You will assemble retrieval with NeMo Retriever embedding and reranking NIMs, enforce policies with NeMo Guardrails, use AI Blueprints as reference architectures, and fine-tune or serve LoRA adapters. The last module covers benchmarking (TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput under concurrency), Prometheus and DCGM monitoring, and an honest build-versus-buy comparison with self-managed vLLM or SGLang.

courses.title: Hugging Face: Hub, Transformers and Endpoints
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers and developers who need to find, evaluate, run, fine-tune and deploy open models using the Hugging Face Hub, its libraries and its hosted inference options.
courses.summary: Work fluently across the Hugging Face stack as of October 2026: Hub repos, licenses and gating, the hf CLI and Xet storage, Transformers v5, Datasets, TRL and PEFT fine-tuning, Inference Providers, Inference Endpoints, Spaces, smolagents, and the supply-chain and organization controls enterprises need.
courses.description:
Hugging Face is where most open models, datasets and demos are published, and its libraries are the default way to load and fine-tune them. The stack changed substantially over the past year: the huggingface_hub 1.x release made hf the command-line tool and Xet the default storage backend, Transformers v5 went PyTorch-only and reworked quantization and loading, Inference Providers became an OpenAI-compatible router across third-party inference companies, and the ggml team behind llama.cpp joined Hugging Face in February 2026.

This course takes you from reading a model card critically to shipping an endpoint. You will manage downloads, caching and revision pinning; load models efficiently with dtype, device_map and quantization configs; serve with transformers serve or hand off to vLLM and SGLang; prepare data with Datasets and fine-tune with TRL and PEFT on one or many GPUs with Accelerate. You will compare Inference Providers, dedicated Inference Endpoints and Spaces with ZeroGPU for demos, build a small agent with smolagents and MCP, and run Hub models locally as GGUF. The final module covers organization plans, access tokens, SSO and audit, plus supply-chain hygiene: safetensors versus pickle, malware scanning and trust_remote_code. Version-specific facts are as of October 2026.

courses.title: Running Models Locally: Ollama, LM Studio and llama.cpp
courses.subtitle: For developers, analysts and IT teams who want to run open-weight models on laptops, workstations and small servers, and to do it securely enough for real work.
courses.summary: Size hardware, pick quantizations and run open models locally with llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio as of October 2026, then connect them to coding tools, RAG and MCP clients and lock down the local server before a team depends on it.
courses.description:
Local inference has become practical for everyday work: a recent laptop or a single workstation GPU can run capable open-weight models at interactive speeds, with no per-token bill and no data leaving the device. The three tools most people use sit on a shared foundation. llama.cpp (whose ggml team joined Hugging Face in February 2026) provides the GGUF format and the inference engine; Ollama wraps a model library, a Modelfile format and an API around it; LM Studio adds a desktop app, an MLX engine on Apple silicon and a headless daemon called llmster.

This course teaches you to choose models and quantizations that fit your hardware, build and tune llama.cpp and llama-server, manage models and Modelfiles in Ollama, and run LM Studio both on the desktop and headless. You will connect local models to coding assistants, RAG and MCP clients through OpenAI-compatible APIs, get reliable tool calls and structured output from smaller models, and run embeddings locally. The final module covers what can still leave your machine (cloud model options, telemetry, remote access), securing a model server that others can reach, license obligations, and when to move from a desktop tool to a shared server such as vLLM. Tool versions and features are as of October 2026.

Analysts and researchers handling data that cannot leave their machine
IT and security teams supporting local AI tools on managed devices

Build and run llama.cpp and llama-server with appropriate GPU offload, context and parallel-slot settings

courses.title: Multi-Vendor AI Architecture: Routing, Fallback and Cost Control
courses.subtitle: For senior engineers and architects who must run LLM workloads across several model providers with predictable availability, quality and spend.
courses.summary: Design and operate a multi-provider LLM platform: a canonical request layer, policy-aware routing and cascades, failure-specific fallback with behavioral parity checks, capacity and cost controls across PTU, provisioned and priority tiers, gateway selection, OpenTelemetry observability, and outage game days.
courses.description:
Most organizations that depend on LLMs now use more than one provider, whether for availability, capability, price, data residency or negotiating leverage. Doing that well is an architecture problem. APIs differ in message formats, tool-call schemas, structured-output guarantees, caching semantics and rate-limit behavior; a fallback model that is technically available can still break downstream parsers or change answers users rely on; and cost controls only work if every call is attributed to a tenant, feature and budget.

This expert course builds a reference architecture layer by layer. You will design a canonical request schema and adapters, then routing strategies from static rules through classifier routing and cost-quality cascades, constrained by residency, tenant policy and context length. You will build a failure taxonomy and map each failure to the right response (retry, hedge, circuit-break, fail over or degrade), including mid-stream and mid-tool-call failures, and gate every fallback model on regression evals. You will plan capacity across committed options such as Azure provisioned throughput, Bedrock reserved and priority tiers and Google provisioned throughput, and enforce budgets, quotas, caching and batch offload. You will compare gateways (LiteLLM, Portkey, OpenRouter, cloud-native gateways and build-your-own), instrument with the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (still marked Development rather than Stable as of October 2026, so attribute names can change), and finish with contracts and exit plans, outage game days and a hypothetical capstone design for a regulated enterprise. Product facts are as of October 2026.
audience: Staff and principal engineers owning shared LLM platforms
Solution and enterprise architects designing AI platforms
SRE and platform teams on call for LLM-dependent services
FinOps leads responsible for AI spend
vendors: Google (Gemini API, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform)
outcomes: Design a canonical request and response schema with provider adapters that preserves tool calls, structured output and usage data
Select and justify a routing strategy (rules, classifier, cascade or learned router) under residency, tenant and context-length constraints
Map each class of provider failure to an appropriate retry, hedging, circuit-breaking, failover or degradation response
Gate fallback models on regression evaluations that measure behavioral parity, not just availability
Plan committed and on-demand capacity across providers and enforce per-tenant budgets, quotas, caching and batch offload

courses.description:
Most disappointing AI answers come from prompts that leave the model guessing about the audience, the goal, the source material or what a good answer looks like. This course teaches a small set of techniques that fix most of those problems in any mainstream assistant. You will practice writing prompts with clear context and constraints, using examples to show rather than tell, asking for specific formats such as tables and checklists, and assigning a perspective without relying on empty "act as" tricks.

You will then learn to work in conversation: refining a draft over several turns, asking the model to critique and revise, breaking big tasks into steps, and knowing when to start a fresh chat. Further modules cover prompting with attached files, spreadsheets and images, using reasoning modes and web search sensibly, and checking answers before relying on them. You finish by building a personal library of reusable prompts. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.

courses.description:
Prompting in production is engineering: a prompt is a component with inputs, outputs, failure modes and a release process. This course starts with the anatomy of a production prompt and the core techniques that still matter — few-shot examples, decomposition and chaining — and then covers how reasoning models change the rules, how to get reliable structured output with JSON schemas, and where OpenAI, Anthropic and Google genuinely differ in their published guidance.

The second half is context engineering and operations: treating the context window as a budget, placing retrieved and long documents where models use them best, managing tool results and long conversations with compaction, building a prompt test set, grading outputs with code checks, rubrics and model judges, iterating one change at a time, recognising prompt injection risk, and versioning prompts like code. A capstone walks a ticket-triage prompt from first draft to a tested, versioned release.

courses.description:
Schema-constrained decoding has largely solved the problem of malformed JSON, but it has not solved the harder one: getting the right values into the fields. This course treats extraction as an engineering discipline. You start with schema design — field types, enums, nullable fields, nesting, descriptions that act as instructions, and evidence fields that make answers checkable — and then use each major vendor's structured-output feature: OpenAI Structured Outputs with strict JSON Schema, Anthropic's JSON outputs and strict tool use, and the Gemini API's JSON Schema response mode, with Pydantic models and the Instructor library as a portable layer.

You then apply them to real inputs: native and scanned PDFs, tables, invoices and contracts, email threads and chat logs, with chunking strategies for long documents and entity normalization. The second half covers validation and quality: business-rule checks after parsing, handling refusals and truncation, confidence and abstention, building a gold set, field-level precision and recall, and running batch extraction pipelines with cost control and human review queues. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.

courses.description:
Reasoning models and million-token-class context windows reward different habits from the ones prompt engineers learned on earlier models. Step-by-step instructions that once helped can now waste tokens or constrain a model that plans better on its own; dumping an entire corpus into context is possible but not free, and recall across very long inputs is uneven. This course teaches the practices that hold up, grounded in each vendor's published guidance as of October 2026.

The first half covers reasoning models: how hidden or summarized reasoning works, the controls each API exposes (OpenAI reasoning effort, Anthropic adaptive thinking and effort, Gemini thinking levels), how to write goal-and-constraint prompts instead of procedures, how to preserve reasoning across tool calls in agent loops, and how to verify outputs with self-consistency, checkers and graders. The second half covers long context: how attention and position affect recall, placement and query-at-the-end patterns, building your own needle and multi-hop recall tests, prompt caching economics, compaction and memory for long-running agents, and the decision between long context and retrieval. A capstone tunes a long-document analysis pipeline for accuracy, latency and cost. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.

courses.summary: AI across the employee lifecycle with the legal guardrails built in: drafting and screening in recruiting, NYC Local Law 144, Illinois HB 3773 and the EU AI Act's employment rules, handbook assistants, performance writing, and employee privacy.
courses.description:
HR is the function where a convenient AI feature most easily becomes a legal exposure, because tools that rank, screen or evaluate people can be automated employment decision tools under several laws. This course separates the low-risk uses of generative assistants (job descriptions, interview guides, policy Q&A, learning content) from decision-influencing tools such as screening and matching in Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and Eightfold, and teaches what each requires. It also covers the other side of recruiting AI: candidates using AI to mass-apply, complete assessments and, in some cases, misrepresent identity in remote interviews.

A full module covers employment AI law as of October 2026: NYC Local Law 144 bias audits and notice, Illinois HB 3773 amendments to the Human Rights Act effective January 1, 2026, Colorado's repealed-and-rewritten AI statute and its revised effective date, the EU AI Act's treatment of employment as high-risk under Annex III (whose deadline was moved by the 2026 Digital Omnibus), disparate impact and the four-fifths rule, and the issues raised in Mobley v. Workday. The course ends with employee data rights, workplace monitoring limits and how to communicate AI use to staff and works councils. The course is educational and is not legal advice. Completion and a passing exam score earn a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification or endorsement.

Customer support is where AI agents are most widely deployed in front of customers, and where the gap between a demo and a working operation is widest. courses.title: AI for Researchers and Academics

courses.summary: AI across the research workflow: literature discovery with Semantic Scholar, Elicit, Consensus and Scite, deep research agents and their failure modes, grounded paper Q&A, systematic-review extraction, qualitative coding, writing within ICMJE and publisher rules, and funder policies such as NIH NOT-OD-25-132.
courses.description:
Researchers face two pressures at once: AI tools that genuinely speed up reading, coding and drafting, and integrity rules that are tightening as fabricated references and AI-written submissions appear. This course covers both. It compares academic search tools (Semantic Scholar, Elicit, Consensus, Scite) by what they index and how they rank, examines deep research agents for scoping work and how they fail, and builds the habit of verifying every reference, including against retraction data. It covers grounded reading in NotebookLM and Claude Projects, extraction tables for systematic reviews compatible with PRISMA reporting, and keeping a Zotero library in step with AI notes.

Later modules cover analysis code in R and Python, qualitative coding with LLMs using codebooks and inter-rater checks, and writing within the rules: ICMJE and COPE positions that AI tools cannot be authors, publisher disclosure policies, AI-generated images, and why confidential manuscripts and grant applications stay out of AI tools during peer review. The final module covers NIH NOT-OD-25-132 (applications substantially developed by AI and the per-PI application limit), human subjects data and IRBs, and research integrity cases. Policies are stated as of October 2026 and should be checked against each journal and funder. Completion and a passing exam score earn a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification or endorsement.

The last module asks you to measure your own productivity honestly and manage cost, rate limits and model choice. courses.description:
An assistant that writes a plausible query in seconds is valuable only if the query is right, and analytical errors are quiet: a fan-out join or a time-zone mistake produces a confident wrong number. This course teaches analysts to use AI for speed while building in the checks that catch those errors. It covers code-executing assistants (ChatGPT data analysis, Claude's analysis tools, Gemini in Colab), notebook assistants in Jupyter, Hex and Databricks, and what data should never be uploaded.

The SQL module covers text-to-SQL with schema context and semantic layers, warehouse-native assistants such as Snowflake Cortex Analyst, Databricks Genie and Gemini in BigQuery, and a review checklist for joins, NULLs and time. Later modules cover pandas and Polars cleaning pipelines, classifying free text with an LLM at row level with sampling and agreement checks, choosing statistical tests with effect sizes and power, spotting leakage, p-hacking and Simpson's paradox in AI-proposed analyses, baseline-first forecasting, and reproducibility. BI dashboards and spreadsheet AI are covered in wrk-202. Product details are as of October 2026. Completion and a passing exam score earn a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification or endorsement.

courses.subtitle: For operations staff, analysts and technically minded business users who want to build reliable AI-powered automations on Zapier, Make, n8n and Power Automate.
courses.summary: Building AI into business automations that hold up in production: deterministic versus LLM steps, Zapier Agents and MCP, Make AI Agents, the n8n AI Agent node and self-hosting, Power Automate with AI Builder and Copilot Studio agent flows, then approvals, error handling, cost and governance.
courses.description:
Workflow platforms now let anyone put a language model in the middle of a business process, which makes it easy to build an automation that works on the demo input and fails quietly on the hundredth. This course teaches the design discipline first: triggers, actions, branching and data mapping that are common to every platform, and a clear rule for which decisions belong to deterministic steps and which to a model. It then works through four platforms on their own terms: Zapier AI steps, Zapier Agents and Zapier MCP; Make scenarios, Make AI Agents and the Make MCP server; the n8n AI Agent node with tools and memory, self-hosting in queue mode and the Sustainable Use License, and retrieval inside a workflow; and Microsoft Power Automate with AI Builder prompts, Copilot Studio agent flows and desktop flows for legacy applications.

The production module covers human-in-the-loop approvals, retries, idempotency and rate limits, structured outputs, and how each platform bills (tasks, operations or credits, executions, flow actions) on top of model tokens. The governance module covers prompt injection through emails, forms and documents that automations read, secrets and connector permissions, data loss prevention policies, and an inventory and change-control process for citizen-built automations. Platform capabilities and billing units are as of October 2026. Completion and a passing exam score earn a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification or endorsement.
audience: Operations and business process owners
Automation builders and citizen developers
IT and RevOps staff supporting automation platforms
Consultants implementing workflow automation
outcomes: Decompose a business process into deterministic steps and LLM steps, and justify each model decision point
Build an equivalent AI-assisted workflow on at least two of Zapier, Make, n8n and Power Automate and compare their trade-offs
Constrain LLM steps with structured output schemas and validate the results before downstream actions
Implement approvals, retries, idempotency and error notification for an automation that writes to business systems
Estimate the monthly cost of an automation from platform billing units and model token usage
Identify prompt-injection paths in an automation and apply connector permissions, DLP policies and change control
prerequisites: Comfort with JSON, spreadsheets and the idea of an API

courses.title: No-Code AI Assistants: Custom GPTs, Projects, Gems and Copilot Studio
courses.subtitle: For non-developers who want to turn a repeatable task into a shared AI assistant: build, test, share and govern one in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Microsoft 365 without writing code.
courses.summary: A hands-on course on building no-code assistants with the builders already in your workplace tools: ChatGPT projects, custom GPTs and their successor plugins, Claude Projects and Skills, Gemini Gems, and Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder and Copilot Studio. You leave with a tested, documented assistant and a plan to share it safely.
courses.description:
Most teams already have a no-code assistant builder in a tool they pay for. This course shows how each one works and what it is good for: instructions and knowledge files in ChatGPT projects, plus how to audit an existing custom GPT and migrate it to a plugin, since OpenAI has stopped new custom GPT creation and announced their retirement in favour of plugins that bundle skills, apps and reference files; Claude Projects and Skills; Gemini Gems and sharing in Google Workspace; and Microsoft 365 Copilot's Agent Builder alongside Copilot Studio for agents that need connectors, topics and governance.

You will write instructions that hold up, pick and prepare knowledge sources, test an assistant against a small set of real cases, and decide when a no-code build has reached its limit. The final module covers sharing permissions, data exposure through knowledge files and connectors, admin controls, and documenting an assistant so someone else can own it. Product details are stated as of October 2026 and change often; the course teaches you how to check them. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment, not a vendor certification.

Team leads who want a shared assistant for their team's playbook
IT and Microsoft 365 administrators approving no-code assistants and agents
outcomes: Choose the right no-code builder (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Microsoft 365 Copilot) for a task based on where the users, data and licences already are

Prepare knowledge files and connected sources so the assistant retrieves the right material and does not expose what it should not
Build a working assistant in at least two platforms, including a Copilot Studio or Agent Builder agent grounded in SharePoint content
Test an assistant against a written set of representative and edge-case requests and record pass or fail before sharing it

courses.title: Building with LLM APIs Across Vendors
courses.subtitle: For developers who want to call OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini models from Python and TypeScript, and ship code that survives a vendor switch.
courses.summary: A hands-on, code-first course on the three major LLM APIs side by side: messages, streaming, structured outputs, tool calling, vision, cost, caching, batch, retries, abstraction layers, cloud routes and testing. You finish by building and hardening a small multi-vendor service.
courses.description:
Most teams start with one vendor's quickstart and discover the hard parts later: leaked keys, streams that drop, JSON that does not parse, tool loops that never end, a surprise invoice, a 429 storm, and a rewrite when the business wants a second vendor. This course teaches the OpenAI Responses API, the Anthropic Messages API and the Google Gemini Interactions API side by side in Python and TypeScript, with the official SDKs as of October 2026, so you learn the shared concepts and the real differences at the same time.

You will build every capability twice or three times, then learn to put a thin, honest abstraction around them, when OpenAI-compatible endpoints help and when they quietly drop features, and how the same models are reached through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry. The course closes with testing strategies that do not burn tokens and a capstone ticket-triage service with structured output, tools, retries, cost reporting and a one-line vendor switch.
audience: Software engineers adding LLM features to products
Backend and platform developers building internal AI services
Data and ML engineers moving from notebooks to production API calls
Technical leads who must keep an application portable across model vendors
outcomes: Configure API keys and cloud credentials for three vendors without committing, logging or shipping secrets to clients
Write equivalent text, streaming, structured-output and tool-calling requests against the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini SDKs in Python and TypeScript
Estimate and measure per-request cost from token usage, and cut it with prompt caching and batch processing
Implement error handling that distinguishes retryable from non-retryable failures, with backoff, jitter and Retry-After support
Design a thin provider abstraction and decide when OpenAI-compatible endpoints or gateways are appropriate
Choose between direct vendor APIs and cloud routes (Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry) based on identity, data and feature requirements

courses.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
courses.subtitle: For engineers who can call an LLM API and now need to ground it in their organization's documents: design, build, evaluate and operate a RAG system that holds up in production.
courses.summary: A practitioner's course on retrieval-augmented generation: when to use it, how to ingest, chunk, embed and index documents, how to combine BM25 and vector search with reranking, and how to measure, debug and operate the result. Every module includes working Python sketches.
courses.description:
Most RAG prototypes work on the demo questions and fail quietly on everything else. This course teaches the full pipeline as an engineering system with measurable parts: parsing and chunking that preserve structure, embedding model selection, approximate nearest-neighbour indexes such as HNSW, hybrid lexical and dense retrieval fused with reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoder reranking, query rewriting, and prompt assembly that produces verifiable citations.

The second half covers what separates a prototype from a system people rely on: enforcing document permissions at retrieval time, building an evaluation set and tracking recall@k, MRR and faithfulness, a stage-by-stage debugging method, agentic retrieval loops, and the operations work of re-indexing, freshness and cost control. Code is vendor-neutral Python with notes on pgvector, FAISS, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and Claude's search-result citations where they apply. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Software and ML engineers building LLM features over internal content
Platform and data engineers who will own ingestion, indexes and pipelines
Technical leads deciding between RAG, fine-tuning and long-context designs
outcomes: Decide between RAG, fine-tuning and long-context prompting for a given use case and justify the choice on freshness, scale, access control and cost
Build an ingestion pipeline that parses, cleans and chunks documents while preserving structure and metadata needed for citations and permissions
Select an embedding model and configure a vector index such as HNSW, explaining the recall, latency and memory trade-offs of its parameters
Implement hybrid retrieval with BM25 and dense vectors fused by reciprocal rank fusion, followed by cross-encoder reranking and query rewriting
Assemble grounded prompts that produce checkable citations and enforce document-level permissions before any content reaches the model
Build a labelled evaluation set and measure recall@k, MRR and faithfulness to compare pipeline changes objectively
Diagnose RAG failures by isolating the failing stage, and operate the system through re-indexing, freshness monitoring and cost control

courses.title: Embeddings and Vector Databases
courses.subtitle: For engineers who need semantic search, deduplication, clustering or recommendation at scale: choose an embedding model, size and tune a vector index, and run a vector database in production.
courses.summary: A deep dive into the two layers under every semantic search system: embedding models and vector databases. Covers how embeddings are trained and benchmarked, Matryoshka truncation and quantization, ANN index internals (HNSW, IVF-PQ, DiskANN), filtering, multi-tenancy and the operational work of re-embedding and capacity planning.
courses.description:
Embeddings turn text, images and other data into vectors whose distances mean something; vector databases make finding the nearest ones fast. This course treats both as engineering components with measurable trade-offs. You will learn how contrastive training shapes an embedding space, how to read MTEB results without over-trusting them, how to evaluate candidate models on your own data, and how to cut storage with Matryoshka dimensions and scalar or binary quantization. Hosted models from OpenAI, Google (including the multimodal Gemini Embedding 2), Cohere and Voyage AI are compared with open models run through Sentence Transformers.

The second half is about the database: exact versus approximate search, HNSW and IVF-PQ parameters, disk-based indexes such as DiskANN, metadata filtering and why it breaks recall, sparse and multi-vector representations, and a structured comparison of pgvector, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and LanceDB. It closes with operations: capacity and memory sizing, recall monitoring, multi-tenant isolation and migrating to a new embedding model without downtime. RAG pipeline design is covered in bld-210; this course goes deeper on the vector layer itself. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Backend and ML engineers adding semantic search or similarity features
Platform engineers choosing and operating a vector database
Data engineers responsible for embedding pipelines and re-embedding
outcomes: Explain how contrastive training, pooling and normalization determine what an embedding space captures and which distance metric to use
Evaluate candidate embedding models on a domain test set and justify a choice beyond leaderboard rank
Reduce vector storage with Matryoshka truncation and scalar, product or binary quantization while measuring the recall cost
Configure HNSW and IVF-PQ indexes and tune their parameters against a recall, latency and memory budget
Design filtered, hybrid and multi-tenant queries that keep recall acceptable
Compare pgvector, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and LanceDB on deployment model, filtering, scale and cost for a given workload
Plan and execute a zero-downtime migration to a new embedding model, including dual-writing and validation
prerequisites: Comfort with Python, NumPy and basic SQL

courses.title: Evaluating LLM Applications
courses.subtitle: For engineers and product owners who need to know whether an LLM feature is good enough to ship and whether a change made it better: build eval sets, graders and an eval pipeline that gates releases.
courses.summary: A practical course on application-level LLM evaluation: turning product requirements into test cases, choosing between code checks, human review and LLM-as-judge, calibrating judges against people, running evals in CI with tools such as Promptfoo and Inspect, and closing the loop with production traces and online experiments.
courses.description:
An LLM feature that passes a demo can still fail a meaningful share of real requests, and every prompt or model change can silently move that number. This course teaches evaluation as an engineering discipline. You start with error analysis on real outputs, derive failure categories, and build a dataset that represents both typical traffic and the edge cases that matter. You then build graders: deterministic assertions, reference-based metrics, rubric-based LLM judges, and pairwise comparisons, and you measure each judge's agreement with human labels before trusting it.

The second half puts evals to work. You will wire an eval suite into CI with Promptfoo or Inspect AI, compare open-source frameworks (DeepEval, Ragas) with hosted platforms (LangSmith, Braintrust, Arize Phoenix, Langfuse), noting that OpenAI is shutting down its hosted Evals platform on 30 November 2026 and points users to Promptfoo, which it acquired and which remains open source, handle non-determinism with repeated trials and confidence intervals, and connect offline results to online signals such as user feedback and A/B tests. Retrieval-specific metrics are covered in bld-210 and agent trajectory evals in bld-320; this course is the general foundation both build on. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Software and ML engineers shipping LLM features
Product managers and QA leads defining acceptance criteria for AI features
Teams replacing ad-hoc 'vibe checks' with repeatable evaluation
outcomes: Run an error analysis on real model outputs and turn the observed failures into named, testable categories
Build an evaluation dataset that covers typical traffic, known failures and adversarial cases, with a documented sampling rationale
Choose between code assertions, reference metrics, human review and LLM-as-judge for each quality criterion
Write a rubric-based LLM judge and measure its agreement with human labels using precision, recall and Cohen's kappa
Quantify run-to-run variance and decide whether a score change is real using repeated trials and confidence intervals
Integrate an eval suite into CI so prompt, model and retrieval changes are gated on regression thresholds
Connect offline eval results to production traces, user feedback and online experiments
prerequisites: Comfort reading Python or TypeScript and YAML configuration

courses.title: Conversational and Voice Agents
courses.subtitle: For engineers building chat and phone agents that talk to customers in real time: design the conversation, choose between speech-to-speech and cascaded pipelines, and ship a voice agent that handles interruptions, telephony and handoff.
courses.summary: Build real-time conversational agents for chat and voice. Covers conversation design, dialogue state, speech-to-speech models such as OpenAI's Realtime API and the Gemini Live API, cascaded STT-LLM-TTS pipelines, turn detection and barge-in, WebRTC and SIP telephony with LiveKit, Pipecat and Twilio, latency budgets, and testing voice agents.
courses.description:
Voice is the least forgiving interface for an LLM: users interrupt, talk over the agent, mumble account numbers and hang up after a long pause. This course starts with conversation design that works in both chat and voice, including dialogue state, slot filling with tool calls, confirmation strategies and escalation to a human. It then covers the two main voice architectures: native speech-to-speech models (OpenAI's Realtime API with the gpt-realtime-2.1 models, Google's Gemini Live API, Amazon Nova 2 Sonic on Bedrock) and cascaded pipelines that combine speech-to-text such as Deepgram, an LLM, and text-to-speech such as ElevenLabs or Cartesia.

You will learn voice activity detection and semantic turn detection, barge-in handling, a millisecond latency budget from microphone to first audio, transport over WebSockets, WebRTC and SIP, and how open-source frameworks such as LiveKit Agents and Pipecat orchestrate it all. The final modules cover telephony integration with Twilio and SIP trunks, call-recording and AI-disclosure obligations, simulated-caller testing and production monitoring. Regulatory notes are educational, not legal advice. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.

Contact-centre technology teams adding AI agents to phone lines
Product and conversation designers working with engineering on voice experiences

Choose between a speech-to-speech model and a cascaded STT-LLM-TTS pipeline for a use case, justifying latency, control, cost and voice quality
Implement turn detection and barge-in so the agent stops speaking and recovers context when interrupted
Build a voice agent with LiveKit Agents or Pipecat that calls tools during a live conversation
Connect a voice agent to the phone network over SIP or Twilio and transfer calls to a human with context
Construct and measure a latency budget from end of user speech to first agent audio
Test voice agents with scripted simulated callers and monitor production calls for failure patterns
prerequisites: Comfort with Python or TypeScript and asynchronous code
