courses.title: Multimodal Applications: Vision, Documents and Audio
courses.subtitle: For engineers building features that read images, screenshots, PDFs, audio and video: send the right input to the right model, get structured results back, and know where multimodal models still fail.
courses.summary: Build application features on multimodal models: image understanding and visual question answering, PDF and scanned-document extraction, chart and screenshot reading, speech-to-text and audio understanding, and video analysis. Compares frontier APIs with open-weight vision-language models and teaches cost control, evaluation and the failure modes specific to non-text inputs.
courses.description:
Frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google now accept images, PDFs and, in some cases, audio and video in the same request as text, and open-weight vision-language models such as Qwen-VL and Llama 4 can run on your own hardware. This course teaches how to use that capability in applications rather than demos. You will learn how each API tokenizes and prices images and pages, how resolution and cropping affect accuracy, how to extract structured data from photos, receipts and screenshots with a JSON schema, and how to ground answers in a region of an image.

Later modules cover document-level work (native PDF input, page images versus extracted text, tables and charts), audio (transcription with models such as OpenAI's gpt-transcribe, which replaces the deprecated gpt-4o-transcribe and whisper-1 API models, and open-weight Whisper run locally, diarization, and audio-native understanding in Gemini), and video (frame sampling versus native video input). The final module is about shipping: building a multimodal eval set, the characteristic failures (counting, small text, spatial reasoning, hallucinated reading of illegible content), privacy for images of people and documents, and cost control. Large-scale document ingestion pipelines are covered in dat-210. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Application engineers adding image, document or audio understanding to a product
Automation teams processing forms, receipts, screenshots or recordings
Technical product managers scoping multimodal features
outcomes: Estimate token cost and latency for image, PDF, audio and video inputs across major APIs and choose resolution or sampling accordingly
Extract validated structured data from photos, screenshots, receipts and forms using JSON schemas and confidence checks
Choose between native PDF input, page images and text extraction for a given document type and justify the choice
Build a transcription and audio-understanding pipeline with diarization and timestamped output
Analyse video by frame sampling or native video input and tie answers to timestamps
Compare frontier multimodal APIs with self-hosted open-weight vision-language models on accuracy, cost and data control
Build a multimodal evaluation set that targets known failure modes such as counting, small text and spatial reasoning
prerequisites: Comfort with Python and calling REST APIs

courses.title: Agent Frameworks Compared: LangChain, LlamaIndex and Others
courses.subtitle: For engineers choosing an LLM application framework: understand what LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, Pydantic AI, DSPy, Haystack, CrewAI and Microsoft Agent Framework actually do, build the same app in several, and decide which to adopt, or none.
courses.summary: A side-by-side, code-first comparison of the main LLM application frameworks. You build one reference application (a document-grounded assistant with tools) in LangChain 1.x with LangGraph, LlamaIndex, Pydantic AI and Microsoft Agent Framework, then examine DSPy, Haystack, CrewAI and Mastra, and finish with a framework decision record and a migration plan.
courses.description:
Framework choice shapes an LLM codebase for years, yet most comparisons are feature checklists. This course compares frameworks by building with them. Each module looks at a framework's core abstractions and runtime model: LangChain 1.x's create_agent and middleware on the LangGraph runtime, LangGraph's state graphs, checkpointers and interrupts; LlamaIndex's data connectors, indexes, query engines and event-driven Workflows; Pydantic AI's typed agents and dependency injection; Microsoft Agent Framework, the successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen; DSPy's signatures and optimizers; Haystack pipelines; CrewAI's crews and flows; and Mastra for TypeScript teams.

The last module turns comparison into a decision: lock-in and abstraction cost, observability and debugging, upgrade churn, and when a thin in-house layer over vendor SDKs is the better answer. Agent architecture and MCP are covered in bld-320, which compares vendor agent SDKs; this course concentrates on general-purpose application frameworks and their trade-offs. Version details are stated as of October 2026. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.

Teams maintaining an existing LangChain or LlamaIndex codebase
Architects setting framework standards across several AI projects

courses.title: AI Agents: Tool Use, MCP and Multi-Agent Orchestration
courses.subtitle: For engineers shipping LLM agents to production: design tools, build and secure MCP servers, choose an SDK, orchestrate multiple agents, and prove it works with evals.
courses.summary: An engineering course on building agents that call tools reliably, speak the Model Context Protocol, coordinate with other agents and stay safe, measurable and affordable. Every module pairs concepts with working code across the major vendor SDKs.
courses.description:
Agents fail in production for predictable reasons: vague tool interfaces, runaway context, unbounded permissions, multi-agent designs that multiply cost without improving results, and no way to tell whether a change helped. This course works through each of those failure points with code you can run.

You start with the agent loop itself and the wire formats for tool calling at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, then design tool interfaces that models use correctly. You build and secure an MCP server against the current (2026-07-28) specification, including Streamable HTTP and OAuth 2.1. You compare the OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Google ADK and LangGraph on the same problems, and learn when a plain loop beats all of them. Later modules cover context and memory for long tasks, planning, orchestrator-worker and handoff patterns, parallel fan-out and when not to use it, computer and browser use, human approvals, prompt injection through tools, sandboxing, trajectory and outcome evaluation, and cost and latency control. Product facts are current as of October 2026.
audience: Software and ML engineers building agentic features
Platform engineers who own tool, MCP and credential infrastructure
Technical leads deciding between agent frameworks
Security engineers reviewing agent deployments
outcomes: Implement a tool-calling agent loop and translate tool definitions between the Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini wire formats
Design tool interfaces with clear contracts, bounded outputs and actionable errors that reduce model misuse
Build an MCP server exposing tools, resources and prompts, and secure its Streamable HTTP endpoint with OAuth 2.1 audience-bound tokens
Select an agent SDK or a plain loop for a given workload using explicit criteria such as durability, approvals, tracing and model portability
Manage context and memory for long-running tasks using trimming, compaction, external memory files and explicit plans

courses.title: Production LLM Engineering: Reliability, Latency and Cost
courses.subtitle: For senior engineers running LLM features at real traffic: set SLOs, engineer for provider outages and rate limits, cut latency and cost per request, and operate the system with tracing, budgets and safe rollouts.
courses.summary: The engineering discipline of running LLM-backed features at scale: SLOs and error budgets for probabilistic systems, multi-provider failover and capacity reservations, latency engineering from TTFT to perceived speed, cost engineering with caching, batching and routing, OpenTelemetry GenAI tracing, and safe rollout of prompt and model changes.
courses.description:
Calling an LLM API is easy; keeping a feature fast, available and inside budget when traffic grows, a provider degrades or a model is deprecated is not. This expert course treats the LLM call as a dependency with unusual properties: variable latency measured in seconds, token-based cost, rate limits in two dimensions, silent quality regressions and scheduled model retirements. You will define SLOs for availability, latency and quality, design failover across providers and cloud routes (including Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry) with circuit breakers and hedged requests, and use priority tiers, provisioned throughput and batch APIs where they fit.

Latency and cost are treated quantitatively: decomposing TTFT and generation time, streaming and speculative UI patterns, prompt-prefix design for cache hits, semantic caching and its correctness risks, model cascades and routing, and per-feature unit economics. Operations modules cover OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (still at Development stability, so pinned by version and expected to change), token and cost attribution, load testing against rate limits, and rolling out prompt and model changes with canaries and automatic rollback. Basic caching, retries and batch usage are taught in bld-201, gateway deployment, keys and quotas in bld-270, and self-hosted inference engines in srv-310; this course is about the production system around the model call. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Senior backend and platform engineers responsible for LLM features in production
Site reliability engineers onboarding AI services
Engineering leads accountable for AI feature cost and uptime
outcomes: Define availability, latency and quality SLOs for an LLM feature and manage them with error budgets
Design multi-provider and multi-region failover with circuit breakers, hedging and graceful degradation, and test it with fault injection
Decompose end-to-end latency into queueing, TTFT and generation time and apply the right fix to each
Design prompts and request flows that maximize prompt-cache hit rates and quantify the saving
Build a routing or cascade policy that sends requests to the cheapest model that meets the quality bar, validated by evals
Instrument an LLM service with OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions and attribute token cost to features, tenants and users
Roll out prompt and model changes with canaries, shadow traffic and automatic rollback, and plan for model deprecations
prerequisites: Experience operating a production web service, including on-call and monitoring

courses.title: Guardrails and Safety Engineering for LLM Applications
courses.subtitle: For engineers who own the safety of an LLM product: design layered input, output and action guardrails, choose and tune safety classifiers, measure their false positives and false negatives, and operate them under real traffic.
courses.summary: An engineering course on guardrails as a measured, layered system. Covers policy taxonomies, input and output classifiers (OpenAI moderation, Llama Guard 4, Prompt Guard 2, gpt-oss-safeguard), NeMo Guardrails and Guardrails AI, cloud guardrail services such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, Azure AI Content Safety and Google Cloud Model Armor, grounding and hallucination checks, action guardrails for tools, and how to evaluate, tune and operate them.
courses.description:
Guardrails fail in two directions: they let harmful outputs through, or they block legitimate users until the product is useless. This course teaches how to build guardrails that are explicit about that trade-off. It begins with writing a policy taxonomy specific to your product and mapping it to OWASP and NIST guidance, then works through each layer: input screening for prompt injection and jailbreaks, policy classifiers (from fixed-taxonomy models such as Llama Guard 4 to bring-your-own-policy reasoning classifiers such as gpt-oss-safeguard), PII detection and redaction, output validation against schemas and business rules, grounding and citation checks, and constraints on what tools and agents may do.

You will compare programmable frameworks (NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI) with managed services (Amazon Bedrock Guardrails including Automated Reasoning checks, Azure AI Content Safety with Prompt Shields, now part of Microsoft Foundry, Google Cloud Model Armor) and decide where each fits. The final modules cover measurement and operations: building labelled safety eval sets, choosing thresholds from precision-recall curves, latency budgets for synchronous checks, streaming moderation, user-facing refusal and appeal design, and monitoring for drift and new attack patterns. Offensive red-teaming technique is covered in sec-310; this course is about building and running the defences. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Senior engineers building customer-facing or regulated LLM applications
Trust and safety engineers adapting content policy to generative AI
Security engineers who need guardrails that hold up against adversarial users

Design a layered guardrail architecture spanning input, model, output and action checks with defined failure behaviour

Implement guardrails with NeMo Guardrails or Guardrails AI and with a managed service such as Bedrock Guardrails or Azure AI Content Safety

courses.title: LLM Gateways: Routing, Keys, Quotas and Audit
courses.subtitle: For platform and application engineers: put a gateway between your organization and every model provider to centralize keys, route and fail over traffic, enforce budgets and quotas, and keep an audit trail.
courses.summary: A hands-on course on the LLM gateway pattern. You deploy LiteLLM Proxy and compare it with Envoy AI Gateway, Kong AI Gateway, Azure API Management's AI gateway policies, Cloudflare AI Gateway and Portkey, then implement virtual keys, routing and fallback, token quotas and budgets, caching, guardrail hooks, logging and audit for a multi-team organization.
courses.description:
Once more than one team calls more than one model provider, scattered API keys, unbounded spend and missing audit logs become real problems. An LLM gateway solves them in one place: applications call a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and the gateway handles credentials, routing, limits, caching, policy and logging. This course builds that layer. You start with the architecture and the build-or-adopt decision, then deploy LiteLLM Proxy as a reference implementation and compare it with Envoy AI Gateway, Kong AI Gateway, Azure API Management (llm-token-limit and related policies), Cloudflare AI Gateway, Portkey (now part of Palo Alto Networks) and OpenRouter.

Modules cover identity and virtual keys tied to SSO and teams; routing across OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry and self-hosted vLLM, with fallbacks and load balancing; token-based rate limits, budgets and chargeback; exact and semantic caching; guardrail and data-loss-prevention hooks; and request logging with OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions for audit and cost reporting. A dedicated lesson covers the gateway itself as a high-value target, including the March 2026 compromise of LiteLLM releases on PyPI. Resilience engineering in depth is covered in bld-330. Facts are stated as of October 2026. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Platform engineers building an internal AI platform for several teams
Application engineers who call more than one model provider
Security and FinOps staff who need control over AI usage and spend

Deploy LiteLLM Proxy with a model list spanning hosted APIs, cloud platforms and a self-hosted vLLM endpoint
Issue virtual keys scoped to teams and applications and integrate them with SSO and secret management
Configure routing, load balancing and fallbacks across providers and regions
Enforce token-based rate limits, budgets and chargeback reporting per team

courses.title: Private AI: Deploying an On-Premises Assistant for Your Organization
courses.subtitle: For IT and platform teams: plan, build and operate a self-hosted AI assistant on your own hardware, with open-weight models, a chat front end, single sign-on, document search and governance your security team will accept.
courses.summary: An end-to-end build of a private, on-premises AI assistant. You size GPU hardware, choose open-weight models such as gpt-oss, Qwen, Mistral and Gemma, serve them with vLLM, deploy Open WebUI or LibreChat with SSO and role-based access, connect internal documents for retrieval, and run the service with monitoring, governance and a clear support model.
courses.description:
Many organizations cannot or will not send sensitive data to a public AI service, yet their staff want an assistant as capable as the consumer tools. This course shows how to deliver one on hardware you control. You begin with requirements, the data classes involved and the honest comparison with private cloud options, then size hardware: GPU memory for weights and KV cache, concurrency, and the trade-offs between data-center GPUs, workstation-class cards such as the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, and small appliances.

You select models by license, capability and size, serve them with vLLM (with Ollama for evaluation), and deploy a front end: Open WebUI or LibreChat, including Open WebUI's branding clause for deployments above 50 users. You integrate identity through OIDC with Microsoft Entra ID or Keycloak, map groups to models and tools, connect document search over SharePoint and file shares with permission-aware retrieval, and add tool and MCP integrations carefully. The final modules cover air-gapped installs, model and container supply chain, logging and retention, acceptable-use policy, capacity monitoring and the upgrade cycle. Single-user local tools are covered in ven-290 and serving internals in srv-310. Facts are stated as of October 2026. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.

Platform engineers moving from a pilot on one GPU to a supported service

courses.title: Knowledge Graphs and GraphRAG
courses.subtitle: For engineers building retrieval systems that need relationships, not just similar passages: model and build knowledge graphs, extract them with LLMs, and use them in GraphRAG pipelines you can evaluate and operate.
courses.summary: An expert course on knowledge graphs for LLM applications. You learn property graphs and RDF, query with Cypher, GQL and SPARQL, build graphs from documents with LLM extraction and entity resolution, implement Microsoft GraphRAG, LazyGraphRAG-style and LightRAG-style retrieval, text-to-Cypher and hybrid graph-vector search, and evaluate when a graph actually beats vector RAG.
courses.description:
Vector retrieval finds passages that resemble a question, but it struggles with questions that require following relationships across documents or summarizing a whole corpus. Knowledge graphs make entities and relationships explicit, and GraphRAG uses them to retrieve connected context. This course covers both the long-established discipline and the new LLM techniques. You start with data models: labeled property graphs and Cypher (including Neo4j's Cypher 25 and its alignment with the ISO/IEC 39075 GQL standard), and RDF, OWL, SPARQL and SHACL for semantic graphs, with Amazon Neptune, Neo4j, Memgraph and Graphwise GraphDB (formerly Ontotext GraphDB) as reference stores.

You then build graphs from unstructured text: schema-guided LLM extraction, entity resolution and canonicalization, provenance and incremental updates. The GraphRAG modules implement Microsoft GraphRAG's indexing pipeline with Leiden community detection and its local, global, DRIFT and basic search modes, compare lighter-weight approaches such as LazyGraphRAG and LightRAG, and build text-to-Cypher and hybrid graph-plus-vector retrievers with the Neo4j GraphRAG Python package, LlamaIndex PropertyGraphIndex and LangChain integrations. The course ends with evaluation, cost and operations: when GraphRAG is worth its indexing cost, how to measure it against a strong vector baseline, and how to keep a graph correct as sources change. Facts are stated as of October 2026. It ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: AI engineers whose vector RAG systems fail on multi-hop or global questions
Data engineers and knowledge engineers building enterprise knowledge graphs
Architects deciding whether a graph belongs in their retrieval stack
outcomes: Choose between a property graph and an RDF model and design a schema or ontology for a retrieval use case
Write Cypher, GQL-aligned and SPARQL queries for multi-hop retrieval
Build a knowledge graph from documents with schema-guided LLM extraction, entity resolution and provenance
Implement Microsoft GraphRAG indexing and explain when to use its local, global, DRIFT and basic search modes
Build text-to-Cypher and hybrid graph-plus-vector retrievers with safeguards against invalid or unsafe queries

courses.title: Deep Learning with PyTorch
courses.subtitle: For developers and data scientists who want to build, train, debug and export neural networks in modern PyTorch, from tensors to torch.compile.
courses.summary: A hands-on course in modern PyTorch: tensors and autograd, nn.Module design, data loading, a training loop you understand line by line, GPU and mixed-precision training, torch.compile, and exporting a model for deployment.
courses.description:
Most PyTorch code is copied from tutorials and only half understood, which is why it breaks the first time the data, the GPU or the model changes. This course builds the framework up from tensors, broadcasting and autograd, so that every line of a training loop has a reason. You write modules, datasets and DataLoaders, then train MLPs, CNNs and a small sequence model on real data.

The second half is about doing it properly on a GPU: device placement, bf16 autocast, gradient accumulation and clipping, checkpointing and resuming, and speeding up with torch.compile. You learn to read loss curves, diagnose exploding gradients, NaNs and data-loader bottlenecks, track experiments, and export a trained model with torch.export or ONNX. Library features are current as of October 2026; the course teaches APIs that have been stable across recent PyTorch 2.x releases.
audience: Software engineers moving into machine learning
Data scientists ready to go beyond scikit-learn
ML engineers who learned PyTorch piecemeal and want a solid foundation
outcomes: Manipulate tensors with correct shapes, dtypes, devices and broadcasting, and explain what autograd records
Build models as nn.Module subclasses with parameters, buffers and state_dict handled correctly
Write a Dataset and DataLoader pipeline that keeps a GPU fed, including workers, pinning and collation
Implement a complete training and validation loop with an optimizer, LR schedule, gradient clipping and checkpoint resume
Train with bf16 autocast and torch.compile and measure the speedup honestly
Diagnose common failures such as NaN losses, shape bugs, overfitting and data-loader stalls from logs and loss curves
Export a trained model with torch.export or ONNX for inference outside the training script

courses.title: Transformers from the Ground Up
courses.subtitle: For engineers who want to understand the transformer well enough to implement a GPT-style decoder from scratch and read modern model configs with confidence.
courses.summary: Build a decoder-only transformer piece by piece: tokenization, embeddings, scaled dot-product attention, multi-head and grouped-query attention, positional schemes such as RoPE, and the training and sampling loop, then map it onto real open-weight model architectures.
courses.description:
Transformers are usually explained with diagrams that skip the parts that matter in practice: tensor shapes, masking, normalization placement and how positions are encoded. In this course you implement every component in PyTorch and check it against shape-level reasoning, then assemble a small GPT-style model and train it on a text corpus.

Once the core is clear, the course walks through the architectural choices that distinguish today's open-weight models: pre-norm and RMSNorm, SwiGLU feed-forward blocks, rotary embeddings, grouped-query and multi-head latent attention, mixture-of-experts layers, and the KV cache used at inference time. You finish by reading real Hugging Face config.json files and explaining what each field changes in compute, memory and behavior. Architecture details are current as of October 2026.

Software engineers preparing for fine-tuning or serving work
Researchers and students who want an implementation-level view

courses.title: Classical Machine Learning in Production
courses.subtitle: For data scientists and engineers who need tabular models that are validated honestly, explained to stakeholders and kept healthy after deployment.
courses.summary: Gradient-boosted trees and linear models still win most tabular problems. This course covers leakage-proof pipelines, honest validation, tuning, calibration and explainability, then packaging, serving and monitoring for drift.
courses.description:
For forecasting demand, scoring risk, predicting churn or flagging fraud on structured data, gradient-boosted trees and well-regularized linear models are usually the right tool, and a large language model is usually not. What separates a model that works in production from one that only worked in a notebook is rarely the algorithm. It is leakage, the validation scheme, calibration, and what happens when the data shifts.

This course builds scikit-learn Pipelines and ColumnTransformers that cannot leak, chooses time-based, grouped or stratified cross-validation to match the problem, and compares XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost on the same task. You tune with Optuna, calibrate probabilities, pick thresholds using business costs, and explain predictions with SHAP. The production half covers MLflow tracking and model registry, batch versus online scoring, ONNX export, drift and performance monitoring, and retraining policy. Library features are current as of October 2026.
audience: Data scientists shipping tabular models
ML engineers responsible for model pipelines and monitoring
Analysts moving from notebooks to production

courses.subtitle: For engineers who need to choose, fine-tune, evaluate and deploy image models for classification, detection and segmentation in 2026.

courses.description:
Computer vision has shifted from training a network from scratch to adapting strong pretrained backbones. This course explains the two families underneath almost everything, convolutional networks and vision transformers, and the self-supervised and image-text pretraining (DINOv3, CLIP and SigLIP-style models) that makes small labeled datasets go a long way.

You then work task by task: transfer learning for classification, real-time detection with Ultralytics YOLO and DETR-style detectors such as RF-DETR, and segmentation including Meta's Segment Anything family, whose SAM 3 release added text-prompted concept segmentation. The course covers the unglamorous parts that decide success: annotation formats, augmentation, mAP and IoU done correctly, class imbalance, and error analysis. It ends with export to ONNX and TensorRT, edge latency, and video tracking. Model names and licenses are current as of October 2026; check each checkpoint's license before commercial use.

Developers adding inspection, counting or document vision to products

courses.title: Speech and Audio Models
courses.subtitle: For engineers building transcription, voice and audio-understanding features who need to choose, evaluate, adapt and run open and hosted speech models.
courses.summary: How speech and audio models turn waveforms into text, labels and voices: features and codecs, CTC, transducer and encoder-decoder ASR, diarization, text-to-speech, audio language models, and how to measure word error rate and latency before you ship.
courses.description:
Speech is one of the most mature areas of applied AI and one of the easiest to get wrong in production. Word error rate on a public benchmark says little about accented call-center audio, overlapping speakers or domain vocabulary. This course starts with the signal itself, sampling rates, log-mel spectrograms and neural audio codecs, and then explains the three main ASR architectures: CTC, transducers (RNN-T and TDT, as used by NVIDIA Parakeet) and encoder-decoder models such as Whisper and NVIDIA Canary.

You then build the surrounding pipeline: voice activity detection, chunking for long audio, speaker diarization with pyannote, timestamps, and streaming. The course covers text-to-speech, audio language models such as Mistral's Voxtral family that answer questions about audio, and fine-tuning ASR on domain data. It closes with evaluation (WER, CER, real-time factor, latency), deployment, and the consent and voice-cloning risks of synthesis. Model names and rankings are current as of October 2026 and change often; the course teaches how to re-check them on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard.
audience: ML engineers adding speech recognition or synthesis to products
Developers building voice agents and call analytics
Researchers transcribing interviews, meetings or field recordings

courses.title: Fine-Tuning LLMs: Full, LoRA and QLoRA
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers who need to decide whether to fine-tune an open-weight LLM, then design the data, size the GPUs, run full, LoRA or QLoRA training, and ship an evaluated adapter.
courses.summary: A practitioner's course on adapting large language models: when fine-tuning beats prompting or RAG, how to build the dataset, how much GPU memory full, LoRA and QLoRA training really need, and how to evaluate, merge and serve the result.
courses.description:
Fine-tuning is the most over-requested and under-planned technique in applied AI. This course starts with the decision itself: what fine-tuning can and cannot change, and how to choose a base model and license you can actually ship. It then treats data as the main engineering artifact, covering chat templates, loss masking, deduplication and contamination.

The core of the course is mechanics with numbers attached. You will compute the memory budget for full fine-tuning byte by byte, derive LoRA's parameter count for a real model shape, and see exactly where QLoRA's NF4 quantization, double quantization and paged optimizers save memory. You will run jobs with TRL and PEFT, compare Axolotl and Unsloth, watch for overfitting and forgetting, build an evaluation that would catch a regression, and serve multiple adapters from one base model. The course closes with an overview of preference tuning with DPO. Product facts are current as of October 2026.
audience: ML and applied AI engineers adapting open-weight LLMs
MLOps and platform engineers who provision GPUs for fine-tuning

Select a base model by size, variant and license, including the obligations that open-weight licenses attach to fine-tuned derivatives

courses.title: Alignment: RLHF, DPO and Preference Optimization
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers who post-train open-weight models and need to collect preference data, train reward models, run PPO-style RLHF or DPO-family methods, and prove the result is better and not just longer.
courses.summary: The full preference-optimization stack after SFT: designing and collecting human and AI preference data, Bradley-Terry reward models, PPO-based RLHF with a KL penalty, DPO and its variants (IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO), and the evaluation and failure modes that decide whether alignment worked.
courses.description:
Supervised fine-tuning teaches a model what good outputs look like; preference optimization teaches it which of two plausible outputs is better. This course treats that second step as an engineering discipline. You start with the objective itself, the KL-regularized reward maximization behind RLHF, and derive why DPO can optimize the same objective without an explicit reward model or online sampling.

The course then covers each stage with real tooling. You design preference-data collection, rubrics and annotator agreement, and use AI feedback and constitution-style principles where human labels are too expensive. You train and audit reward models, run PPO with TRL, OpenRLHF or verl, and compare it with DPO, KTO, ORPO and SimPO on cost, stability and data needs. The final modules are about knowing whether it worked: length bias, reward hacking, over-refusal, sycophancy and regressions on capability benchmarks, plus safety tuning and red-team data. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards and GRPO for reasoning are covered in depth in mod-370 and only introduced here. Library features are current as of October 2026.
audience: ML engineers responsible for post-training open-weight LLMs
Research engineers reproducing preference-optimization papers
Applied AI leads deciding how far to go beyond supervised fine-tuning
outcomes: Derive the KL-regularized RLHF objective and explain the role of the reference policy and the KL coefficient

courses.title: Model Evaluation and Benchmarking
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers and evaluation leads who must measure what a model can actually do, compare models fairly, and defend the numbers to skeptics.
courses.summary: Model-level evaluation done rigorously: how benchmarks are scored, why the same model gets different numbers in different harnesses, how contamination and saturation distort leaderboards, how to build your own eval suite with statistics you can defend, and how to evaluate reasoning, agentic and safety capabilities.
courses.description:
Benchmark numbers drive model selection, funding decisions and regulatory filings, yet small changes in prompt format, few-shot examples, answer extraction or sampling settings can move a score by several points. This course teaches evaluation as measurement science. You run the same model through lm-evaluation-harness, lighteval and Inspect, explain why results differ, and learn to report scores with confidence intervals and paired significance tests rather than single numbers.

The course covers the major benchmark families (knowledge, reasoning, math, code, long context, multilingual and agentic tasks), how they saturate and how contamination is detected, and why once-standard benchmarks get retired, as with Hugging Face's Open LLM Leaderboard in 2025 and OpenAI's decision in February 2026 to stop reporting SWE-bench Verified. You then build a private, versioned evaluation suite for your own domain, including LLM-as-judge with calibration against human labels, and pairwise human preference methods such as Elo and Bradley-Terry arenas. The final module covers dangerous-capability and safety evaluations and how evaluation evidence feeds governance, including the EU AI Act obligations for general-purpose models with systemic risk. This course evaluates models; evaluating whole LLM applications is covered in bld-230. Facts are current as of October 2026.

Evaluation and red-team leads building internal benchmark suites
Technical leaders who must interpret vendor benchmark claims

courses.title: Distillation, Pruning and Small Language Models
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers who need a smaller, cheaper model that keeps the capability that matters, by distilling from a teacher, pruning structure away, or picking the right small model to start from.
courses.summary: How small language models get their capability: logit and sequence-level knowledge distillation, on-policy distillation, synthetic-data distillation from a frontier teacher, structured and unstructured pruning with distillation-based recovery, and how to evaluate and choose small models honestly.
courses.description:
Many production workloads do not need the largest model available; they need a model that is good at one job, fast and cheap. This course covers the techniques that produce such models. You start with knowledge distillation in its classic form, matching a teacher's softened output distribution, then move to the variants that matter for language models: sequence-level distillation, on-policy and generalized KD that train on the student's own samples, and reasoning-trace distillation from a large teacher.

The pruning half explains unstructured, semi-structured 2:4 and structured pruning, how importance is estimated from weights, activations or gradients, and the prune-then-distill recipe used by NVIDIA's Minitron work and implemented in Model Optimizer, where depth and width are cut and the model is retrained against its parent. You learn how to evaluate a compressed model against the teacher on your own task, how teacher-output licensing terms constrain what you may train, and how to choose among small open-weight families. Quantization is touched on only as a complementary step; it is taught in depth in srv-320. Model and library facts are current as of October 2026.
audience: ML engineers compressing models for cost, latency or on-device deployment
Applied AI teams replacing a frontier API call with a specialized small model

courses.title: Diffusion Models
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers who want to understand diffusion and flow-matching generators mathematically, train and fine-tune them, control them, and sample from them fast.
courses.summary: From the forward noising process and score matching to latent diffusion, diffusion transformers and rectified flow: how modern image and video generators work, how to train and fine-tune them with Diffusers, how to steer them with guidance and control adapters, and how to make sampling fast.
courses.description:
Diffusion and flow-matching models generate today's leading images and video and are increasingly used for audio, 3D, proteins and materials. This course builds the theory you need to work on them rather than only prompt them. You derive the DDPM forward and reverse processes, connect noise prediction to score matching and stochastic differential equations, and then see how flow matching and rectified flow, the formulation used by Stable Diffusion 3 and the FLUX family, recast generation as learning a velocity field.

The practical half uses Hugging Face Diffusers. You train a small model from scratch, examine the latent-diffusion stack (VAE, text encoders, U-Net or diffusion transformer), and fine-tune large open-weight generators with LoRA and DreamBooth-style personalization. You then control generation with classifier-free guidance, ControlNet-style conditioning, image-prompt adapters and editing, and make it fast with modern samplers, distillation to few-step models, caching and TensorRT. The course ends with evaluation (FID, CLIP score and human preference) and with provenance, licensing and safety for generated media. Model names and licenses are current as of October 2026; each open checkpoint carries its own license.

Research engineers working on generative models
Applied scientists using diffusion for molecules, materials or simulation

courses.title: Pretraining a Language Model
courses.subtitle: For research and ML engineers who need to plan and run a language-model pretraining run end to end: data, tokenizer, architecture, optimizer, stability, evaluation and handoff to post-training.
courses.summary: The model-side craft of pretraining: building a web-scale data pipeline with filtering and deduplication, training a tokenizer, choosing architecture and hyperparameters from small-scale experiments, keeping a large run stable, scheduling data and learning rate, and evaluating base-model checkpoints.
courses.description:
Pretraining is where a model's knowledge and most of its capability come from, and where most of its compute is spent. This course follows a pretraining project from decision to handoff. You start with the questions that decide whether to do it at all: pretraining from scratch versus continued pretraining of an open base model, the token and compute budget, and what open recipes such as AI2's OLMo and Hugging Face's FineWeb and SmolLM work have shown publicly.

The data module is the largest: extraction from Common Crawl, language identification, heuristic and model-based quality filtering, MinHash and exact deduplication, PII and toxicity handling, decontamination, and mixing with code, math and multilingual sources using datatrove. You then train a byte-level BPE tokenizer and make architecture and hyperparameter choices using small proxy models and maximal-update parametrization (muP) for transfer. The training modules cover AdamW and newer optimizers such as Muon, warmup-stable-decay schedules, loss spikes and their mitigations (z-loss, QK-norm, gradient clipping, rollback), annealing on high-quality data, and context-length extension. Parallelism, cluster operations and scaling-law compute planning are covered in trn-310, trn-330 and trn-320; this course uses them rather than re-teaching them. Facts are current as of October 2026.

courses.title: Reinforcement Learning Fundamentals
courses.subtitle: For engineers and data scientists who want to frame problems as sequential decisions, implement the core RL algorithms in PyTorch, and train and debug agents with Gymnasium and Stable-Baselines3.
courses.summary: The foundations of reinforcement learning taught by building them: Markov decision processes, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning, deep Q-networks, policy gradients and PPO. Every algorithm is implemented or trained on Gymnasium environments, with the experiment discipline that RL demands.
courses.description:
Reinforcement learning is the branch of machine learning where an agent learns from the consequences of its own actions rather than from labeled examples. It powers game-playing systems, robot controllers and, increasingly, the post-training of large language models. It is also notoriously easy to get wrong: results swing with random seeds, reward functions get exploited, and a bug can look exactly like a hard problem.

This course builds the field from the ground up. You formalize problems as Markov decision processes, solve small ones exactly with value and policy iteration, then move to learning from experience with Monte Carlo, SARSA and Q-learning. The second half goes deep: DQN and its stabilizers, REINFORCE, actor-critic methods with generalized advantage estimation, and PPO, the algorithm that also underpins much of LLM alignment. You implement the core algorithms in PyTorch in the CleanRL single-file style, train them on Gymnasium and MuJoCo environments, compare against Stable-Baselines3, and learn to report results across seeds with proper confidence intervals. The final module connects these foundations to reward design and to how RL is used for language models, which mod-320 and mod-370 cover in depth. Library details are current as of October 2026.
audience: ML engineers moving from supervised learning to sequential decision-making
Data scientists evaluating RL for control, recommendation or operations problems
Engineers preparing for LLM post-training work (RLHF, RLVR) who need the RL foundations first

courses.title: Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning: RLVR, GRPO and Reward Design
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers who want to train reasoning behavior into open-weight LLMs with verifiable rewards, run GRPO-family algorithms at scale, and tell genuine capability gains from reward hacking.
courses.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, end to end: building verifiers for math, code and tool use, the GRPO objective and its successors (Dr. GRPO, DAPO, GSPO), distributed rollout systems, reward design for partially verifiable tasks, and the evaluation discipline that separates real reasoning gains from hacked rewards and contaminated benchmarks.
courses.description:
Since DeepSeek-R1 showed that large-scale reinforcement learning against automatically checkable rewards could produce long chain-of-thought reasoning, RL from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard stage of LLM post-training. It is also a different engineering problem from preference-based RLHF: rewards come from programs rather than human judges, rollouts are long and expensive, and the most common failure is not instability but a model that learns to satisfy the checker instead of solving the problem.

This course treats reasoning RL as a system. You build verifiers and sandboxes for math answers, unit-tested code and multi-turn tool use; derive GRPO from PPO and study the fixes later work made to its normalization, clipping and length behavior; and run training with verl, TRL's GRPOTrainer, OpenRLHF or NeMo RL using vLLM or SGLang rollouts. You learn the cold-start and curriculum choices behind R1-style recipes, the infrastructure trade-offs of colocated versus disaggregated and asynchronous rollouts, and how to design rewards when only part of a task is verifiable. The last module is about proof: pass@k versus pass@1, contamination checks, format and length hacking, and when distilling a strong reasoner beats running RL at all. Preference-based alignment (RLHF, DPO) is covered in mod-320; RL foundations in mod-206. Library and model facts are current as of October 2026.

courses.title: Interpretability and Model Internals
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers and researchers who want to look inside transformer language models, find the features and circuits behind a behavior, and use that understanding to debug, steer and audit models.
courses.summary: A practical course in mechanistic interpretability: hooking model activations with TransformerLens and nnsight, probing and the logit lens, activation and attribution patching, sparse autoencoders and transcoders with SAELens and Gemma Scope 2, attribution graphs for circuit tracing, and using these tools for steering, safety audits and model debugging.
courses.description:
Behavioral evaluation tells you what a model does; interpretability tries to tell you why. Over the last few years the field has moved from toy models to tooling that works on real open-weight LLMs: libraries that expose every activation, sparse dictionaries that decompose those activations into human-readable features, and attribution graphs that trace how a specific answer was computed. Used carefully, these tools can find the cause of a failure, suppress or amplify a behavior, and support safety claims with evidence. Used carelessly, they produce convincing stories that do not survive a control experiment.

This course teaches both the techniques and the skepticism. You start with the residual-stream view of the transformer and the classic findings (induction heads, superposition). You then work through the experimental toolkit: linear probes, the logit and tuned lens, activation patching and attribution patching, and causal scrubbing-style hypothesis tests. The middle of the course covers sparse autoencoders and transcoders: training them with SAELens, using the open Gemma Scope 2 suite for Gemma 3, browsing and labeling features on Neuronpedia, and building attribution graphs with the open circuit-tracer library. The final modules apply interpretability to steering, refusal and deception audits, and model debugging, and close with what interpretability evidence can and cannot support. Tool and release facts are current as of October 2026.
audience: ML engineers who debug or audit open-weight language models
Research engineers entering mechanistic interpretability
AI safety and evaluation practitioners who need evidence beyond behavioral tests

courses.title: Training Multimodal Models
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers who build or adapt vision-language and other multimodal models and need to choose an architecture, assemble image-text data, run the pretraining and instruction-tuning stages, and evaluate the result.
courses.summary: How modern multimodal models are trained: contrastive encoders (CLIP, SigLIP 2), connector-based vision-language models (LLaVA, Qwen-VL, Molmo), native and early-fusion designs, the web-scale and synthetic data pipelines behind them, staged pretraining and visual instruction tuning, extension to video and audio, and evaluation that catches hallucination and benchmark leakage.
courses.description:
Most frontier and open-weight models now accept images, and many accept video and audio. Under the hood, nearly all of them combine a pretrained encoder for each modality with a language model, then train the combination in stages: align the representations, teach broad multimodal understanding, then instruction-tune for the tasks users care about. The design choices along the way, such as how images become tokens, which parameters are frozen, how resolution is handled and what data is used, decide both quality and cost.

This course walks the full pipeline with open tools and open recipes. You train and evaluate a contrastive image-text encoder and understand why SigLIP's sigmoid loss displaced softmax CLIP training at scale. You study connector architectures from LLaVA's projector to cross-attention and native-resolution designs in the Qwen-VL family, and contrast them with early-fusion models that tokenize images directly. You build an image-text data pipeline with DataComp-style filtering, recaptioning and dense-caption data such as PixMo, then run alignment pretraining and visual instruction tuning with Hugging Face Transformers and TRL, including LoRA fine-tuning of an open VLM on document and chart data. Later modules extend the recipe to video and speech, then cover evaluation with VLMEvalKit and lmms-eval, object-hallucination testing, and preference tuning for multimodal outputs. Image and video generation are covered in mod-350. Model and library facts are current as of October 2026.

Research engineers training multimodal models from pretrained components
Technical leads deciding between fine-tuning an open VLM and calling a hosted multimodal API

Train and evaluate a CLIP- or SigLIP-style contrastive encoder with OpenCLIP and zero-shot retrieval metrics
Design the vision-language connector, token budget and resolution strategy for a VLM
Build an image-text training corpus with filtering, deduplication, recaptioning and license review

courses.title: Robotics and Embodied AI: Foundation Models for Action
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers moving into robotics who need to collect demonstration data, train and fine-tune imitation and vision-language-action policies, use simulation and world models, and deploy policies on real robots safely.
courses.summary: The learning side of modern robotics: robot data and teleoperation, imitation learning with ACT and diffusion policies, vision-language-action models such as OpenVLA, pi0 and Isaac GR00T, simulation and sim-to-real with Isaac Lab and MuJoCo, world models, and the evaluation and safety practice needed before a learned policy controls real hardware.
courses.description:
Robotics is going through the same shift language went through: from task-specific models trained from scratch to large pretrained models that are adapted with a modest amount of task data. Vision-language-action (VLA) models take camera images and an instruction and output robot actions; open models and toolchains now let a small team fine-tune one on its own robot. But robots are not chatbots. Data is expensive to collect, actions must run at control rates on embedded compute, evaluation happens in the physical world, and mistakes break hardware or hurt people.

This course covers that whole loop. You start with how robots are represented for learning: observation and action spaces, control frequencies, embodiments and the LeRobot dataset format. You collect demonstrations by teleoperation and train behavior-cloning policies, including Action Chunking with Transformers and diffusion policies. You then study VLA architectures (OpenVLA's tokenized actions, flow-matching action experts in pi0, pi0.5 and Isaac GR00T, SmolVLA for low-cost arms) and fine-tune an open VLA with LeRobot or openpi. Simulation and world models get their own module: Isaac Lab and MuJoCo Playground for RL and data generation, domain randomization for sim-to-real, and video world models such as NVIDIA Cosmos for synthetic data. The course ends with real-robot evaluation protocols, latency and on-robot inference, and safety engineering for learned controllers. Hardware selection is covered in hw-207. Model and toolkit facts are current as of October 2026.

courses.title: GPU Programming Fundamentals with CUDA
courses.subtitle: For Python and C++ developers who want to understand how GPU kernels really run and leave able to write, measure and fix their own.
courses.summary: A hands-on introduction to CUDA C++: the execution model, the memory hierarchy, the classic parallel patterns, streams and CUDA Graphs, and profiling with Nsight. It finishes with the kernels deep learning actually needs, written in CUDA, Triton and the tile-based cuTile Python DSL and plugged into PyTorch.
courses.description:
Most AI engineers use GPUs through frameworks that hide the hardware. That works until a model is slow, runs out of memory or needs an operation the framework does not fuse. This course gives you the mental model and the hands-on skills underneath: how a kernel launch becomes a grid of blocks scheduled onto streaming multiprocessors, why memory access patterns usually matter more than arithmetic, and how to tell from a profiler which of the two is limiting you.

You will write and progressively optimize real kernels (vector operations, a transpose, a reduction, a scan and a tiled matrix multiply), overlap transfers with compute using streams, cut launch overhead with CUDA Graphs, and find race conditions with Compute Sanitizer. The final module moves to deep-learning kernels: a fused operation in Triton, the same idea in cuTile Python, the Python DSL for NVIDIA's CUDA Tile programming model introduced in CUDA 13.1, and registering a custom operator so PyTorch and torch.compile can call it. Toolkit specifics are stated against CUDA 13.x as of the review date.

C and C++ developers moving into GPU computing
HPC engineers porting numerical code to NVIDIA GPUs
outcomes: Write, compile and launch CUDA C++ kernels with a launch configuration chosen for the problem size and the GPU
Explain how threads, warps, blocks and streaming multiprocessors map onto the hardware and how this affects occupancy
Restructure memory accesses for coalescing and use shared memory tiling without bank conflicts
Implement reductions, scans and tiled matrix multiplication and explain why vendor libraries such as cuBLAS still outperform them

courses.title: Mixed Precision, Memory and Training Performance
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers who train models on one GPU or one node and want them to fit in memory, stay numerically stable and run fast.
courses.summary: The single-node foundations of fast training: what FP32, TF32, BF16, FP16, FP8, MXFP8 and NVFP4 actually trade away, how to use autocast and FP8 recipes safely, where every gigabyte of GPU memory goes, and the techniques (checkpointing, accumulation, compiled and fused kernels) that make a step fit and run faster.
courses.description:
Before a job is worth distributing, it should be efficient on one GPU. This course teaches the three levers that decide that: numeric precision, memory and per-step speed. You will learn the range and precision of each training format, why BF16 replaced FP16 loss scaling for most work, how FP8 training works with per-tensor and block scaling, and what the Blackwell-generation MXFP8 and NVFP4 formats change. You will apply them with torch.autocast, Transformer Engine and torchao and learn to recognise the loss curves that signal a precision problem.

The memory half uses PyTorch's own tooling (the caching allocator statistics and memory snapshots) to show where memory goes, then fits larger models with activation checkpointing, gradient accumulation and memory-light optimizers. The speed half covers torch.compile, scaled dot-product attention backends including FlashAttention and FlexAttention, fused kernels and losses, and the data loader. Multi-GPU sharding and parallelism are covered in trn-310; deep profiling methodology in trn-340.

Researchers hitting out-of-memory errors or slow steps on a single node
Platform engineers supporting training teams on shared GPUs

courses.description:
Distributed training is a chain of trade-offs between memory, compute and communication. This course teaches you to reason about each link with numbers rather than folklore. You will account for every byte a GPU holds during training, compute what each collective costs on NVLink and InfiniBand, and see exactly what DDP buckets, ZeRO stages, FSDP2 sharding, Megatron tensor and pipeline parallelism, context parallelism and expert parallelism change in that budget.

The second half is operational. You will choose a parallel layout for a large model with a worked calculation, launch it with torchrun and Slurm, tune NCCL for the fabric, write sharded checkpoints you can actually resume from, measure model FLOPs utilization and scaling efficiency honestly, and diagnose the failures that dominate real runs: hangs, NCCL timeouts, desynchronised ranks and stragglers. Code, launch scripts and configuration are shown against current PyTorch, DeepSpeed and Megatron-Core APIs as of the review date.

courses.title: Scaling Laws and Compute Planning
courses.subtitle: For research leads and ML infrastructure engineers who must decide how big a model to train, on how many tokens, on what cluster and for how long.
courses.summary: How to turn the scaling-laws literature into a defensible compute plan: counting training FLOPs, what Kaplan, Chinchilla and their replications actually found, when to deliberately train past compute-optimal, how to fit your own laws from small runs, and how to convert a model and token budget into GPUs, weeks, risk buffers and cost.
courses.description:
Every large training run starts with a bet: a parameter count, a token count and a compute budget. Scaling laws are the best tool for making that bet, but they are often quoted as slogans rather than used as methods. This course goes to the source papers and their assumptions. You will count training compute with the 6ND approximation and its corrections, read the Kaplan et al. (2020) and Hoffmann et al. (2022, Chinchilla) results closely, and see why later replications and analyses revised the fitted coefficients.

You will then go beyond compute-optimal: training smaller models on far more tokens to cut inference cost, scaling when unique data runs out, and how mixture-of-experts models change the accounting. The practical core is fitting your own scaling law from a ladder of small runs, with honest uncertainty, and transferring hyperparameters with muP. The course ends by building a complete compute plan, from loss target to cluster size, wall-clock time, failure and ablation overhead, and a go/no-go milestone schedule. Published results are presented as their authors reported them; no figures are invented.

ML infrastructure engineers sizing clusters and calendars for training teams

courses.title: Checkpointing and Fault Tolerance for Long Training Runs
courses.subtitle: For engineers who run multi-day or multi-week training jobs and need them to survive node failures, hangs and bad data without losing days of progress.
courses.summary: An engineering course on keeping long training runs productive: measuring goodput, choosing checkpoint intervals, capturing complete and reshardable training state, saving fast with asynchronous and in-memory checkpoints, detecting hangs, bad nodes and silent corruption, and recovering automatically through job restarts, in-process restarts and elastic training.
courses.description:
On a large cluster, failure is a matter of when, not if. GPUs throw XID errors, links flap, nodes hang inside a collective, and a single bad batch can spike the loss. What separates a productive run from an expensive one is how much work each failure costs. This course treats that as an engineering problem with a metric, goodput, and a toolkit.

You will start with the failure taxonomy and the Young/Daly reasoning for checkpoint intervals, then define exactly what a resumable checkpoint must contain, including data-loader position and RNG state, and how to reshard it onto a different parallel layout. The fast-checkpointing module covers asynchronous saving with PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint, Megatron-Core distributed checkpointing, local and replicated in-memory checkpoints, and the storage bandwidth they need. Detection covers heartbeats, the NCCL watchdog and PyTorch's flight recorder, DCGM health gates and loss-spike monitoring. Recovery covers Slurm requeue and hot spares, the NVIDIA Resiliency Extension's fault-tolerance and in-process restart features, and replica-level recovery with torchft. Feature maturity is stated as of the review date, since several of these tools are evolving quickly.

courses.title: Profiling and Optimizing Training Throughput
courses.subtitle: For ML and performance engineers who need to find out why a training job is slow and make it measurably faster without changing its results.
courses.summary: A methodical approach to training performance: define the right metrics, classify a step as compute-, memory-, launch-, input- or communication-bound, capture and read traces with the PyTorch Profiler, Nsight Systems, Nsight Compute and Holistic Trace Analysis, then fix the bottleneck on the host, the GPU or the network and prove the gain is real.
courses.description:
Performance work fails in two common ways: tuning by folklore, and declaring victory on a noisy measurement. This course teaches a repeatable method instead. You will build a benchmark harness that controls warm-up, variance and loss equivalence, then learn to read every layer of evidence: PyTorch Profiler and Kineto traces in Perfetto, Nsight Systems timelines annotated with NVTX, Nsight Compute kernel analysis, Holistic Trace Analysis across many ranks, and DCGM profiling metrics from the fleet.

Each fix is tied to a diagnosis. Host-side problems (slow input pipelines, launch-bound steps, hidden synchronisations) are fixed with prefetching, CUDA Graphs and removing syncs. GPU-side problems are fixed with torch.compile, better attention and GEMM shapes, and, when justified, custom kernels in Triton, CUTLASS or the CuTe DSL. Communication problems are exposed in distributed traces and addressed with bucketing, prefetch and overlap. The course closes with a worked optimization campaign on a hypothetical model, continuous performance testing and how to report results honestly.
audience: ML performance engineers and research engineers responsible for training efficiency
Infrastructure engineers asked why expensive GPUs sit idle
Framework developers tuning models for new GPU generations

courses.title: Collective Communication: NCCL and the Network
courses.subtitle: For ML infrastructure and network engineers who need to understand, measure and tune the collectives that distributed training depends on.
courses.summary: A deep course on how collectives move data across GPUs: the algorithms and cost models, NCCL's internals (channels, algorithms, protocols and topology search), NVLink and rack-scale NVLink domains, InfiniBand and RoCE scale-out networks, rigorous measurement with nccl-tests and NCCL observability, and newer device-initiated and all-to-all patterns used by mixture-of-experts training.
courses.description:
Distributed training is only as fast as its slowest collective. This course explains what actually happens when a framework calls all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter or all-to-all. You will derive the cost of ring and tree algorithms with an alpha-beta model, learn why nccl-tests reports bus bandwidth rather than algorithm bandwidth, and map each kind of parallelism to the collectives it generates.

You will then open up NCCL: communicators, channels and proxy threads; the Ring, Tree, CollNet, NVLS and PAT algorithms and the Simple, LL and LL128 protocols; and how topology detection builds its graph from PCIe, NVLink and NIC placement. The network modules cover NVLink and NVLink SHARP inside a node or rack-scale domain, GPUDirect RDMA and NIC affinity, then the scale-out fabric from NCCL's side: its IB verbs transport and network plugins, PXN, how adaptive routing, congestion and SHARP in-network reduction show up in collective performance, the RoCE settings NCCL depends on, Spectrum-X, and where the Ultra Ethernet Consortium specification fits. Operating the fabric itself (subnet managers, PFC and DCQCN tuning, switch configuration) is covered in inf-320. The course closes with measurement and tuning, NCCL logging and profiler plugins, device-initiated communication with the NCCL Device API (experimental as of NCCL 2.28) and NVSHMEM, all-to-all kernels for expert parallelism, and a structured approach to debugging collective timeouts. AMD's RCCL is noted where it differs. Version-specific NCCL features are stated as of the review date.
audience: ML infrastructure engineers who own distributed training performance
HPC and data-center network engineers supporting GPU clusters
Framework and kernel engineers working on communication-heavy models such as mixture-of-experts

Explain how NCCL selects algorithms, protocols and channels from the detected topology

courses.description:
When an AI project stalls, the cause is often something nobody on the business side can see: a GPU quota that was never approved, a model too large for the memory of the server it was given, a storage system that cannot keep up, or a rack that cannot be powered. This course gives non-specialists a working mental model of AI infrastructure so they can follow those conversations and ask useful questions.

You follow a single request from a chat window down through the serving layer, the GPU server, the cluster network, the storage system and the data center building, and then back up through how training jobs are scheduled and how capacity is bought in the cloud or on premises. The course closes with a checklist of questions to ask your infrastructure team. Product names are given as of October 2026 as examples; the concepts are built to outlast them. Deeper treatment of every topic is available in inf-201 and the rest of the infrastructure track.

courses.subtitle: For system administrators and infrastructure engineers who are taking ownership of GPU servers and leave able to choose, install, monitor, share, size and power them with confidence.
courses.summary: The operator's view of data-center GPUs: what the current NVIDIA and AMD systems are, how they are packaged and connected, how the driver, CUDA/ROCm and container stack fit together, how to monitor and triage failing GPUs, how to share and size GPU memory, and what power, cooling and sourcing decisions follow.
courses.description:
Most organisations now own or rent GPUs, and the people who keep them running are usually Linux administrators who were never taught what makes a GPU server different. This course gives you the working model and the commands. It starts with why AI work runs on GPUs and the handful of architectural ideas an operator actually needs, then surveys the current data-center lineup (NVIDIA Hopper, Blackwell and Rubin; AMD Instinct MI300 through MI400 series) and how those chips are packaged into PCIe cards, HGX and OAM baseboards and rack-scale NVLink systems.

The middle of the course is hands-on operations: the driver, CUDA and Fabric Manager compatibility rules that cause most failed upgrades; containers with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and CDI; the AMD ROCm equivalent; reading nvidia-smi and amd-smi properly; fleet telemetry and diagnostics with DCGM; and a triage runbook for ECC, row remapping, XID errors and thermal throttling. The final modules cover GPU sharing (MIG, time-slicing, MPS), memory sizing for inference and training with worked examples, power and cooling arithmetic, and a structured cloud-versus-on-premises comparison. Chip microarchitecture in depth is left to hw-201; this course is about running the hardware. Product facts are stated as of October 2026.

Platform and MLOps engineers who run GPU nodes for data science teams
Technical leads comparing on-premises GPUs with cloud capacity

courses.title: Linux Administration for AI Clusters

courses.summary: The Linux skills that differ on an AI cluster: choosing and imaging the OS, packaging GPU and RDMA drivers that survive kernel updates, NUMA and PCIe topology tuning, cgroup v2 isolation, shared identity and file systems, scientific software environments with Lmod, Spack and containers, and patching a fleet without breaking jobs.
courses.description:
A GPU compute node is a Linux server, but the habits that work for web servers break on it. A routine kernel update can strand the NVIDIA driver; a wrong IOMMU or PCIe ACS setting can quietly halve GPU-to-NIC bandwidth; a user's job can land its memory on the far NUMA node; and a hundred researchers need a hundred conflicting Python and CUDA versions on the same machines. This course teaches the node-level administration that keeps an AI cluster fast and boring.

You start with distribution choice and lifecycle (RHEL 10 and its rebuilds Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS), then stateless and stateful provisioning with Warewulf, NVIDIA Base Command Manager and Ansible. The core modules cover the NVIDIA driver in its packaging variants (open kernel modules, DKMS and precompiled streams), DOCA-OFED for InfiniBand and RoCE, Fabric Manager and persistence; then hardware-aware tuning with hwloc, numactl, tuned profiles, hugepages, IOMMU and ACS for GPUDirect peer-to-peer and RDMA. The later modules cover cgroup v2 resource isolation, SSSD/LDAP identity and Munge, NFS and parallel file system clients, user software environments with Lmod, Spack, EasyBuild, Apptainer and Enroot, and the patching, logging and kdump practices that let you change a fleet safely. Facts are stated as of October 2026.

Research computing staff supporting scientists on shared clusters
DevOps engineers who now own bare-metal GPU servers
Platform engineers building node images for AI workloads

courses.description:
Kubernetes was designed for stateless services that scale one pod at a time. AI work is different: a training job needs 64 GPUs to start together or not at all, an inference replica may span two nodes, GPUs are too expensive to leave reserved but idle, and the fast network is RDMA that the default pod network knows nothing about. This course teaches the components and patterns that close that gap.

You begin with the GPU node: the NVIDIA GPU Operator and the AMD GPU Operator, the device plugin, and Dynamic Resource Allocation, whose core APIs became generally available in Kubernetes 1.34. You then share GPUs with MIG and time-slicing, attach InfiniBand or RoCE interfaces with the Network Operator and Multus, and schedule batch work with Kueue quotas, JobSet, the Kubeflow Trainer and NVIDIA's open-source KAI Scheduler or Volcano. Later modules cover multi-node inference with LeaderWorkerSet, KServe and the Gateway API Inference Extension, Ray on KubeRay, storage through CSI drivers, GPU telemetry with the DCGM exporter, and how managed EKS, GKE and AKS differ. Facts are stated as of October 2026.

courses.title: Slurm for AI and HPC
courses.subtitle: For cluster administrators and power users who leave able to configure, tune and troubleshoot Slurm for GPU-heavy AI and HPC workloads.
courses.summary: Slurm from the daemons up, with an AI focus: slurm.conf and gres.conf for GPUs, cgroup v2 confinement, topology-aware placement including block topology for NVLink racks, fair share, QOS and preemption, containers with Pyxis and Enroot, multi-node launch with PMIx and NCCL, accounting and reporting, and safe upgrades.
courses.description:
Slurm schedules a majority of the world's largest AI and HPC systems, and since NVIDIA acquired SchedMD in December 2025 it has remained open source on a six-month major release cadence (25.11 and 26.05 are the current lines as of October 2026). Yet many clusters still run defaults that waste GPUs: jobs that can see GPUs they were not allocated, eight-GPU jobs spread across switches, priority rules nobody can explain, and node health problems discovered by users rather than by the scheduler.

This course works through a Slurm deployment as an administrator would. You configure slurmctld, slurmd, slurmdbd and slurmrestd; describe GPUs with gres.conf and NVML autodetection; confine jobs with cgroup v2; and describe the network with the tree and block topology plugins so jobs land inside a switch or an NVLink domain. You then design fair-share, QOS and preemption policies, run containers with Pyxis and Enroot or Apptainer, launch multi-node PyTorch with srun and PMIx, and use prolog, epilog and HealthCheckProgram hooks. The course closes with accounting and reporting with sacct and sreport, troubleshooting stuck jobs and drained nodes, rolling upgrades, and where Slurm and Kubernetes meet, including Slinky. Facts are stated as of October 2026.

Infrastructure engineers adding GPU partitions to an existing cluster
ML engineers who submit large multi-node training jobs
Administrators migrating from PBS, LSF or Grid Engine

Design partitions, QOS, fair-share and preemption policies for a stated mix of research and production users

courses.title: Cloud GPU Platforms Compared
courses.subtitle: For architects and engineering leads choosing where to rent GPUs, who leave able to compare hyperscaler and specialist GPU clouds on hardware, networking, storage, capacity mechanisms and managed tooling.
courses.summary: A structured comparison of where to rent GPUs as of October 2026: the instance families on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle, the specialist GPU clouds, how their cluster networks and managed storage differ, how to actually obtain scarce capacity, and the managed cluster services that sit on top.
courses.description:
Renting GPUs looks simple until you need 256 of them in one placement group next week. The providers differ less in which NVIDIA chip they offer than in how their instances are connected, how capacity is reserved, what managed file systems sit next to the GPUs, and how much of the cluster tooling you must build yourself. This course gives you a comparison method and the current facts to apply it.

You first learn to read an instance specification: GPUs, GPU memory, host memory, local NVMe, and scale-out bandwidth. You then compare the main families: AWS P5, P6-B200, P6-B300 and the P6e GB200/GB300 UltraServers with EFA; Azure ND H100/H200 v5, ND MI300X v5 and ND GB200/GB300 v6 with InfiniBand; Google Cloud A3, A4, A4X and A4X Max alongside TPUs; and Oracle's RDMA superclusters, followed by specialist clouds such as CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius and Crusoe. The second half covers capacity mechanisms (on-demand, reservations, AWS Capacity Blocks for ML, Google's Dynamic Workload Scheduler, spot and committed spend), managed storage (FSx for Lustre, Azure Managed Lustre, Google Cloud Managed Lustre), and managed cluster layers (SageMaker HyperPod, AWS ParallelCluster, Azure CycleCloud, Google Cluster Director), ending with a scored provider selection exercise. Instance names change often, so every fact is dated to October 2026 and the method is built to be reused.

courses.title: On-Premises vs Cloud AI: Cost and Capacity Planning
courses.subtitle: For infrastructure, finance and engineering leads who must decide where AI compute should live and leave able to build a defensible total-cost model and a capacity plan.
courses.summary: A practical method for the build-versus-rent decision: forecasting GPU demand, modelling the full cost of owned capacity (hardware, facilities, power, network, storage, staff and refresh), modelling cloud cost honestly (reservations, egress, idle time), finding the utilization break-even, and turning the answer into a staged, hybrid capacity plan.
courses.description:
Most on-premises versus cloud comparisons are wrong in the same few ways: they compare an owned server at 100% utilization with an on-demand cloud price, leave out power, cooling, networking and staff, assume a five-year life for hardware whose useful life for frontier work may be shorter, or ignore that cloud capacity at the scale needed may simply not be available on the date needed. This course teaches a total-cost and capacity method that survives a finance review.

You start by forecasting demand in GPU-hours from real workloads: training runs, fine-tuning, inference traffic and experimentation. You then build an owned-capacity model covering capital cost, depreciation, colocation or facility cost, power at a stated PUE, network and storage, support contracts, staff and refresh, and a cloud model covering on-demand, reserved and committed pricing, capacity blocks, storage, egress and the cost of idle reservations. The break-even module shows how sensitive the answer is to utilization, power price and hardware life. The final modules turn the decision into a staged capacity plan with procurement lead times, power and space constraints, hybrid bursting and review triggers, using hypothetical worked examples throughout. All numbers in examples are illustrative; learners bring their own quotes.

FinOps and finance partners reviewing GPU spend
Research computing leads deciding between grants for hardware and cloud credits
Architects writing the business case for a GPU cluster
