courses.title: HPC Cluster Design for AI: Compute, Fabric and Storage
courses.subtitle: For infrastructure architects and senior HPC engineers who must turn an AI workload brief into a buildable, testable cluster design and defend it to a review board.
courses.summary: How to design a GPU cluster for AI from requirements to acceptance: compute node selection, rail-optimized fat-tree fabrics with real port and switch counts, InfiniBand versus RoCE, parallel storage sized for checkpoints and data loading, provisioning and scheduling, burn-in, power and cooling. Ends with a full 128-node reference design and an architecture review.
courses.description:
Most AI cluster problems are designed in long before the first job runs: a fabric that collapses onto a few inter-switch links, a storage system that benchmarked well because the test fit in cache, a rack row that cannot shed the heat of the nodes it was bought for. This course teaches the design discipline that prevents them. You start from the workload — training, inference or mixed research HPC — and derive concrete targets for GPU count, memory, checkpoint bandwidth, data-loading bandwidth and failure tolerance.

From there you design each layer with numbers: compute nodes (HGX-class 8-GPU servers, rack-scale NVL72 systems and PCIe GPU servers), the three networks every cluster needs, rail-optimized fat-trees with leaf, spine, cable and transceiver counts, InfiniBand versus RoCE and Spectrum-X, and tiered storage across node-local NVMe, parallel file systems (IBM Storage Scale, Lustre, WEKA, VAST) and object. You learn to run benchmarks that cannot lie to you, provision with NVIDIA Base Command Manager, schedule with topology-aware Slurm alongside Kubernetes, accept the system with HPL, NCCL tests, IOR and mdtest, and plan power, cooling and day-2 operations. The final module walks through a complete hypothetical 128-node design, its variations, and how to defend it. Product facts are stated as of October 2026.

Senior cluster and storage engineers moving into AI-scale design
Research computing leads planning a GPU cluster purchase

courses.title: High-Performance Networking: InfiniBand, RoCE and Ethernet for AI
courses.subtitle: For network and HPC engineers who run AI fabrics and leave able to configure, tune and troubleshoot InfiniBand and lossless Ethernet so collective communication runs at line rate.
courses.summary: The protocol and operations layer of AI networking: how RDMA and collectives load the fabric, InfiniBand subnet management, routing engines, partitions and SHARP, lossless RoCEv2 with PFC, ECN and DCQCN, Spectrum-X and Ultra Ethernet transport, NCCL and RCCL tuning, multi-tenant isolation and a disciplined method for finding the cause of a slow or flapping fabric.
courses.description:
A fabric that passes cable checks can still deliver half its bandwidth to a training job. The causes live above the physical layer: a routing engine that concentrates flows, adaptive routing switched off, PFC storms, ECN thresholds copied from a storage network, a NIC on the wrong PCIe root, or NCCL choosing a ring when a tree or NVLink SHARP would win. This course is about those layers. Physical design, optics and switch counts are covered in hw-203 and inf-310; here you operate and tune the fabric.

You start from the traffic itself: RDMA verbs, GPUDirect RDMA and the all-reduce, all-gather and all-to-all patterns that training and mixture-of-experts inference generate. The InfiniBand modules cover the subnet manager and UFM, routing engines (fat-tree, up/down and adaptive routing), partitions and P_Keys, SHARP in-network reduction and Quantum-X800 era features. The Ethernet modules cover RoCEv2 lossless configuration with PFC, ECN and DCQCN, buffer and QoS design, Spectrum-X adaptive routing and congestion control, SONiC-based and merchant-silicon fabrics, and the Ultra Ethernet 1.0 transport. You then tune NCCL and RCCL, isolate tenants, and work through a troubleshooting method using perftest, NCCL tests, ibdiagnet and switch telemetry. Facts are stated as of October 2026.

HPC administrators who operate InfiniBand subnets
Data center network architects moving AI traffic onto Ethernet
Performance engineers chasing slow multi-node training

courses.title: Parallel Storage for AI: Storage Scale, Lustre, WEKA and VAST
courses.subtitle: For storage and HPC engineers who run AI data platforms and leave able to configure, tune, benchmark and troubleshoot the four leading parallel storage systems for training and inference.
courses.summary: An operator's deep dive into parallel storage for AI: the I/O patterns of data loading, checkpointing and KV-cache offload; IBM Storage Scale internals and tuning; Lustre with LNet, DNE, PFL and Data-on-MDT; WEKA NeuralMesh and VAST's disaggregated shared-everything design; GPUDirect Storage; benchmarking that cannot fool you; and day-2 operations such as tiering, quotas, snapshots and replication.
courses.description:
Storage decides whether expensive GPUs compute or wait. AI workloads mix millions of small random reads during data loading, bursts of very large sequential writes during checkpoints, metadata storms from tokenized shards, and increasingly the offload of inference KV cache to shared storage. Each of the leading parallel systems handles that mix differently, and each has tunables that matter and many that do not. Cluster-level storage tiering and sizing are introduced in inf-310; this course goes inside the file systems themselves.

You start with the I/O physics of AI workloads, then work through each platform as an administrator: IBM Storage Scale (NSDs, Erasure Code Edition and Storage Scale System, filesets, the policy engine, AFM and the data acceleration tier introduced in Storage Scale 6.0); Lustre (MDTs and OSTs, LNet, DNE, Progressive File Layouts, Data-on-MDT and the features of the 2.16 and 2.17 releases, including DDN EXAScaler packaging); WEKA NeuralMesh; and VAST Data's DASE architecture and its AI-oriented data services. Cross-platform modules cover GPUDirect Storage and RDMA clients, client-side tuning, benchmarking with fio, IOR, mdtest and the MLPerf Storage benchmark while defeating cache effects, and operations: tiering to object, quotas, snapshots, replication, upgrades and failure handling. Facts are stated as of October 2026.

HPC engineers operating IBM Storage Scale (GPFS) or Lustre

Performance engineers diagnosing slow data loading or checkpoints

courses.title: Data Center Power and Liquid Cooling for AI
courses.subtitle: For data center, facilities and infrastructure engineers who must host high-density GPU racks and leave able to design, commission and operate the power and liquid-cooling systems they need.
courses.summary: Power and cooling for AI racks measured in tens to hundreds of kilowatts: the electrical chain from utility to GPU, rack power shelves and the move toward 800 VDC distribution, GPU power dynamics and capping, direct-to-chip liquid cooling with CDUs and ASHRAE W- and S-class temperatures, immersion and rear-door alternatives, retrofitting air-cooled halls, commissioning and operations.
courses.description:
An 8-GPU air-cooled HGX-class server draws roughly 10 to 15 kW; rack-scale systems such as GB200 and GB300 NVL72 bring a single rack well past 100 kW and require liquid cooling, and vendor roadmaps point toward racks near a megawatt. Facilities designed for 8 to 15 kW per rack cannot simply absorb that. This course teaches the electrical and thermal engineering behind AI racks so infrastructure and facilities teams can plan, build and run them safely.

The power modules trace the chain from utility and medium voltage through UPS, switchgear, busway and PDUs to rack power shelves, then examine GPU power behaviour: fast load swings during training, power capping and smoothing, and the redundancy schemes that fit AI loads. You study the industry move from 54 V in-rack distribution toward 800 VDC architectures announced by NVIDIA and its partners. The cooling modules cover heat transfer basics, direct-to-chip liquid cooling with coolant distribution units, technology cooling system and facility water loops, ASHRAE's W-class and S-class temperature definitions, fluids, filtration and leak detection, then immersion and rear-door heat exchangers, heat reuse and water use. The course closes with retrofit strategies, commissioning and integrated system testing, and day-2 operations including monitoring, maintenance and incident response. Facts are stated as of October 2026; this course does not replace licensed engineering design.
audience: Data center and critical facilities engineers
Infrastructure architects planning GPU deployments in existing buildings
Colocation and AI-cloud operations teams
Mechanical and electrical consultants moving into AI facilities
outcomes: Trace the electrical chain from utility to GPU and calculate rack, row and hall power for a stated AI deployment
Explain GPU power dynamics during training and choose power capping, smoothing and redundancy strategies accordingly
Explain the rationale and trade-offs of 800 VDC distribution versus 54 V in-rack and AC architectures
Design a direct-to-chip liquid cooling loop with CDUs and specify facility and technology cooling system temperatures using ASHRAE classes
Compare direct-to-chip, immersion, rear-door heat exchanger and air cooling for a given density and building

Write a commissioning and integrated systems test plan and a day-2 operations runbook for liquid-cooled racks

courses.title: AI Cluster Operations: Monitoring, Health Checks and Incidents
courses.subtitle: For SREs and cluster operators who run production GPU clusters and leave able to build the telemetry, automated health checks and incident practice that keep GPU availability high.
courses.summary: Operating GPU clusters at production standard: defining availability and goodput SLOs, building a telemetry pipeline across GPUs, fabric, storage, schedulers and facilities, automating node health checks and drains, triaging GPU, fabric and storage failures at fleet scale, running incidents and post-incident reviews, and managing node lifecycle, spares and RMA.
courses.description:
In a large training run, a single GPU with a degrading link or a node with a slow file system mount can stall thousands of GPUs, and every hour of that stall is paid for. Operations for AI clusters is therefore less about whether servers are up and more about whether jobs make progress. This course teaches the operational system around the hardware: what to measure, how to detect and remove bad nodes before jobs hit them, how to respond when they do, and how to learn from it. Single-GPU diagnostics and error codes are covered in inf-201; here you run them across a fleet.

You begin by defining SLOs that matter for AI: GPU availability, job goodput, time to detect and time to remove a bad node. You then build a telemetry pipeline with the DCGM exporter, node exporters, fabric and storage collectors, Slurm and Kubernetes metrics, Prometheus or a compatible long-term store, Grafana and log aggregation, and design alerts that page on symptoms. The health modules cover layered checks (boot, prolog, periodic, epilog), Node Health Check, DCGM diagnostics, NCCL and storage probes, and automated drain-and-repair loops, with notes on vendor suites such as NVIDIA Mission Control and Base Command Manager. Further modules cover fleet-scale triage of XID patterns, fabric and file system degradation, checkpoint-restart and job resilience, structured incident response and blameless reviews, and node lifecycle management with spares, RMA and burn-in on return. Facts are stated as of October 2026.

HPC operations teams supporting large training runs
Infrastructure managers accountable for GPU availability

courses.title: Green AI: Energy, Carbon and Efficient Compute
courses.subtitle: For infrastructure, ML and sustainability practitioners who need to measure the energy and carbon of AI training and inference, report it credibly, and cut it without hurting results.
courses.summary: How to measure, account for and reduce the energy, carbon and water footprint of AI: GPU and node power telemetry, PUE and WUE, location- and market-based carbon accounting, embodied emissions, the SCI and SCI for AI specifications, EU reporting requirements, and the engineering levers (efficient models, precision, batching, power capping and carbon-aware scheduling) that actually reduce impact.
courses.description:
AI's energy demand has become a planning constraint for utilities, a reporting obligation for operators, and a question every customer and regulator now asks. Answers are often wrong in both directions: headline numbers that ignore idle power, cooling and embodied emissions, or offsets that hide real consumption. This course teaches practitioners to produce numbers they can defend and reductions that are real.

You start by measuring: GPU power through NVIDIA DCGM and NVML, node and rack power, estimation tools such as CodeCarbon and Zeus, and Kubernetes-level attribution with Kepler. You then convert energy into carbon and water using grid intensity data, PUE and WUE, and the GHG Protocol's location-based and market-based Scope 2 methods, and add the embodied carbon of servers and GPUs. A reporting module covers the Software Carbon Intensity standard (ISO/IEC 21031:2024) and the Green Software Foundation's SCI for AI, the EU Energy Efficiency Directive's data-centre reporting database and the A-to-G rating scheme the Commission adopted in September 2026, and the energy documentation expected of general-purpose AI model providers under the EU AI Act. The second half is about reduction: choosing smaller and distilled models, quantization and efficient serving, GPU power capping and frequency tuning, and carbon-aware and time-shifted scheduling. Facility power and cooling design is covered in depth in inf-340. Regulatory and tool facts are current as of October 2026; this course is educational and not legal advice.

ML engineers asked to report or reduce the footprint of training and inference

courses.title: AI FinOps: Measuring and Controlling AI and GPU Spend
courses.subtitle: For FinOps practitioners, platform engineers and engineering managers who need to see where AI money goes, allocate it to teams and products, and cut waste in GPU, model-API and token spend.
courses.summary: FinOps applied to AI: the cost anatomy of GPU infrastructure and model APIs, normalizing bills with the FOCUS specification, tagging and allocating shared GPU clusters and token spend, unit economics such as cost per inference and per resolved task, commitment and capacity strategy for GPUs, and the engineering levers (caching, batching, routing, right-sizing) that reduce AI spend without losing quality.
courses.description:
AI spend behaves differently from the cloud spend most FinOps practices were built for. GPU capacity is scarce and often bought in reserved blocks; model APIs bill per token with prices that change by model, cache state and batch mode; shared clusters make it hard to say which team used what; and the business value of an AI feature is rarely in the bill at all. This course adapts the FinOps Foundation's framework to that reality.

You start with the cost anatomy of AI: accelerated instances, storage and networking, managed AI platforms, and per-token model APIs, including how prompt caching, batch processing and reasoning tokens change the bill. You then build visibility: ingesting cloud and AI-vendor bills into a FOCUS-aligned dataset, tagging and metadata for AI workloads, and allocating shared GPU clusters by GPU-hours with OpenCost or Slurm accounting and shared model gateways by token usage with LiteLLM-style metering. The middle of the course covers unit economics and showback or chargeback models that teams accept. The optimization modules cover GPU utilization and right-sizing, commitments, spot and capacity reservations, and token-level levers such as model routing, caching, prompt compression and batch APIs. The course ends with forecasting, budgets and anomaly detection, and an AI FinOps operating model. Build-versus-buy and on-premises break-even analysis are covered in inf-260. Pricing and product facts are current as of October 2026.

courses.description:
Most ML projects that fail in production fail for operational reasons: nobody can reproduce the training run, the feature logic differs between training and serving, a model is promoted without a check, or accuracy quietly decays as the data shifts. This course teaches the discipline that prevents those failures, using open tooling you can run yourself — Git and DVC for versioning, MLflow for experiment tracking and the model registry, Kubeflow Pipelines and Airflow for orchestration, Feast for features, and Evidently for drift monitoring — and maps each practice onto the managed platforms (Amazon SageMaker AI, Azure Machine Learning, Google's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform — formerly Vertex AI — and Databricks).

The final module extends the same ideas to LLM applications, where the versioned artifact is often a prompt, a retrieval index and a model choice rather than trained weights, and where evaluation datasets replace a single accuracy metric. Tool facts are stated as of October 2026.

courses.description:
A model in a notebook is not a product. The second half is about running the service. You deploy on Kubernetes with resource requests, probes and GPU scheduling, autoscale with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, KEDA or Knative on signals that actually track load, handle cold starts and scale-to-zero, and release new model versions with canary and shadow traffic and a fast rollback. Managed options (Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints, Cloud Run with GPUs, Azure Machine Learning online endpoints) are compared on the same criteria. Product facts are stated as of October 2026.

courses.subtitle: For ML platform and infrastructure engineers who must run open-weight LLMs in production and leave able to size, tune, benchmark, scale and cost an inference service.
courses.summary: The engineering of LLM inference from first principles to production: why decode is memory-bound, how to size the KV cache, how continuous batching, PagedAttention, prefix caching, quantization and speculative decoding change the economics, and how to run vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and Dynamo at scale. Ends with load testing, Kubernetes autoscaling and a defensible cost per million tokens.
courses.description:
Serving a large language model is a memory-bandwidth and scheduling problem far more than a compute problem, and most expensive mistakes in production come from not knowing that. This course builds the mental model first — prefill versus decode, the KV cache and the arithmetic that decides how many users a GPU can hold — and then walks through every major technique the engines use to push that boundary: continuous batching, PagedAttention, prefix caching, chunked prefill, FP8 and INT4 quantization, speculative decoding, multi-LoRA, tensor/pipeline/expert parallelism and disaggregated prefill/decode.

The second half is operational. You configure vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM (trtllm-serve), Triton Inference Server, NVIDIA Dynamo and llama.cpp with real commands; expose OpenAI-compatible endpoints; measure TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput and goodput with proper load tests; plan capacity against an SLO; autoscale on Kubernetes using queue-depth signals rather than GPU utilisation; and compute the cost per million tokens of a self-hosted deployment so it can be compared honestly with API pricing. Engine facts are stated as of October 2026.

courses.title: Quantization and Inference Optimization
courses.subtitle: For ML and performance engineers who must make a model smaller and faster without losing the quality that matters, and prove it with measurements.
courses.summary: The numerics and engineering of making models cheaper to run: number formats from FP16 to FP4, post-training quantization algorithms such as GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant, quantization-aware training, KV cache quantization, and the compiler and kernel work (torch.compile, TensorRT, fused attention, CUDA graphs) that turns smaller numbers into real speed. Every technique is paired with a way to measure what it costs in quality.
courses.description:
Quantization is the single biggest lever on inference cost, and also the easiest way to ship a model that is quietly worse. This course starts with the numerics — integer and floating-point formats, scales and zero points, per-tensor, per-channel and group-wise granularity, and the microscaling block formats (MXFP4, MXFP8, NVFP4) supported by recent NVIDIA and AMD accelerators — and explains why outlier activations make LLMs hard to quantize.

You then apply the main post-training methods (round-to-nearest, GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, rotation-based methods) with LLM Compressor, NVIDIA Model Optimizer (formerly TensorRT Model Optimizer) and torchao, compare them with quantization-aware training, and produce checkpoints in the formats engines load: compressed-tensors, Hugging Face, GGUF and ONNX. The second half covers optimization beyond quantization — graph compilation, kernel fusion, FlashAttention-style kernels, CUDA graphs and custom kernels in the Triton language — and closes with an evaluation protocol that catches regressions perplexity misses. Engine-level serving (batching, scheduling, speculative decoding) is covered in srv-310, and pruning and distillation as model-design techniques in mod-340. Format and tool support is stated as of October 2026.
audience: ML performance and inference engineers
MLOps engineers producing quantized checkpoints for serving
Researchers deploying their own models on constrained GPU budgets
HPC engineers moving into inference optimization
outcomes: Explain how scale, zero point, granularity and format (INT8, INT4, FP8 E4M3/E5M2, MXFP4, NVFP4) determine quantization error and hardware support
Choose between weight-only, weight-and-activation and KV cache quantization for a memory-bound or compute-bound workload
Apply GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant with a calibration set and explain why each method handles outliers differently
Decide when quantization-aware training is worth its cost over post-training quantization
Produce quantized checkpoints in the format a target engine loads and verify that it loads the intended kernels
Use graph compilation, kernel fusion and CUDA graphs to remove overhead, and identify the bottleneck with a profiler before optimizing
Design an evaluation protocol that detects task-level quality loss from quantization, not only perplexity change
prerequisites: Python and PyTorch fluency; trn-201 helps for the kernel module

courses.title: LLM Observability and Monitoring
courses.subtitle: For engineers and SREs running LLM applications and agents in production who need to see what the system did, why it failed, what it cost, and whether quality is drifting.
courses.summary: How to instrument, monitor and debug LLM systems end to end: distributed traces across prompts, retrieval, tool calls and agent steps; token, latency and cost metrics; online evaluation of live traffic; and the alerting, privacy controls and incident practice that make it operable. Built on OpenTelemetry so the skills transfer across vendors.
courses.description:
Traditional monitoring tells you a request succeeded in 2 seconds; it cannot tell you that the answer was wrong, that retrieval returned the wrong document, or that an agent looped through eleven tool calls and spent your daily budget. This course teaches observability for systems whose failures are semantic as well as operational. You instrument applications with OpenTelemetry and the GenAI semantic conventions (still marked Development as of October 2026, so you will learn how to cope with attribute churn), add auto-instrumentation from OpenLLMetry or OpenInference, and send traces to an LLM-focused backend such as Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, LangSmith or MLflow Tracing alongside Prometheus, Grafana or Datadog.

From there you build the metrics that matter — TTFT, inter-token latency, tokens, cost per request and per tenant, cache hit rate, error and refusal rates — and the serving-layer and GPU signals beneath them. You add online evaluation with sampled LLM-as-judge and user feedback, detect drift in inputs and quality, design SLOs and alerts for non-deterministic systems, and handle prompts and outputs that contain personal data. The course closes with debugging real failure patterns in RAG pipelines and agents from their traces. Product facts are stated as of October 2026.
audience: SREs and platform engineers responsible for LLM applications
AI engineers operating RAG systems and agents in production
ML platform teams building shared telemetry for many AI apps
Engineering managers who own AI reliability and spend

courses.title: Edge and On-Device AI
courses.subtitle: For engineers who must run models on phones, laptops, embedded boards and edge servers, and leave able to choose a runtime, compress a model to fit, ship it, and keep it updated in the field.
courses.summary: The software side of edge AI: deciding what should run on the device, fitting models into tight memory and power budgets, converting them for ExecuTorch, LiteRT, Core ML, ONNX Runtime and OpenVINO, targeting NPUs and GPUs, running small language models locally, and operating a fleet of devices with secure model updates. Hardware selection is covered in hw-206.
courses.description:
On-device inference trades the data center's abundance for privacy, offline operation, low latency and zero per-token cost — but only if the model fits the device's memory, thermal and battery budget. This course teaches that trade-off and the engineering behind it. You start with a decision framework for on-device, edge-server and hybrid designs, then work through the compression and conversion path: quantizing and pruning for the target, exporting with torch.export, and lowering to ExecuTorch, LiteRT, Core ML, ONNX Runtime and OpenVINO, including how NPU delegates and execution providers decide which operators actually run on accelerated hardware.

Dedicated modules cover small language models on device — llama.cpp and GGUF, MLC LLM, MLX on Apple silicon, and the platform models exposed through Apple's Foundation Models framework and Android's Gemini Nano via ML Kit — and edge vision and sensor pipelines on NVIDIA Jetson with TensorRT and DeepStream. App-level integration in Swift and Kotlin is covered in dev-211; this course is about the model, runtime and fleet engineering beneath it. The course ends with operations: benchmarking on real devices, fleet model delivery and rollback, protecting model files, and hybrid routing between device and cloud. Platform facts are stated as of October 2026; several mobile AI APIs change at each annual OS release.
audience: Mobile, desktop and embedded engineers adding on-device AI
ML engineers deploying models outside the data center
Edge and IoT platform architects
Product engineers weighing on-device versus cloud inference for privacy or latency

courses.title: Data Engineering for AI
courses.subtitle: For data and ML engineers who feed models: build reproducible pipelines that collect, store, clean, deduplicate, version and serve data for training, fine-tuning, retrieval and evaluation.
courses.summary: How data pipelines for AI differ from analytics pipelines, and how to build them: lakehouse storage with Parquet and Iceberg or Delta, distributed processing with Spark, Ray Data and DuckDB, text cleaning, filtering and MinHash deduplication at corpus scale, dataset versioning, orchestration with Airflow or Dagster, and feeding GPUs efficiently at training time.
courses.description:
Models are bounded by the data they see, and AI data work has requirements that analytics pipelines rarely face: unstructured and multimodal inputs, corpus-scale near-duplicate detection, exact reproducibility of a training set months later, and loaders that must keep expensive GPUs busy. This course builds the full path. You will design storage on object stores using Parquet with Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake tables, choose between Spark, Ray Data, Daft and DuckDB for a processing job, and orchestrate pipelines with Airflow or Dagster using data-aware scheduling.

The core of the course is the preparation pipeline used for pretraining and fine-tuning corpora: language identification, heuristic and model-based quality filtering, exact and MinHash-LSH near-duplicate removal, PII scrubbing and decontamination against evaluation sets, with reference to open tooling such as Hugging Face datatrove and NVIDIA NeMo Curator. You will then version datasets with table snapshots or lakeFS, package them in Hugging Face datasets, WebDataset or MosaicML Streaming formats, and measure loader throughput on GPU nodes. Streaming ingestion with Kafka for retrieval freshness rounds out the course. Governance and lineage are covered in depth in dat-320. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Data engineers moving from analytics pipelines to AI workloads
ML engineers who own training and fine-tuning datasets
Platform engineers building the data layer for an AI team

Design object-store lakehouse storage with Parquet and Iceberg or Delta tables, including partitioning and schema evolution

courses.title: Document Processing and Unstructured Data Pipelines
courses.subtitle: For engineers turning PDFs, scans, Office files, email and web pages into clean, structured, searchable data: choose parsers and OCR, extract tables and fields reliably, and run the pipeline at volume.
courses.summary: Build production pipelines for unstructured documents: format detection and text extraction, layout analysis and reading order, OCR and vision-language parsers, table and form extraction, schema-driven field extraction with LLMs, human review loops, and running it all at scale with measured accuracy and cost.
courses.description:
Most enterprise knowledge lives in PDFs, scans, slide decks, spreadsheets and email threads, and most AI projects stall at turning it into clean data. This course teaches the pipeline end to end. You will start with format detection and native text extraction using tools such as PyMuPDF and Apache Tika, then move to layout-aware parsers (Docling, Unstructured, LlamaIndex's LlamaParse) that recover reading order, headings, tables and figures, and to OCR choices ranging from Tesseract and PaddleOCR to Mistral OCR and the cloud services Azure Document Intelligence (now in Microsoft Foundry Tools), Amazon Textract and Google Document AI.

The middle modules focus on getting structure out: tables that survive extraction, key-value fields from forms and invoices, schema-driven extraction with LLMs and validation, classification and splitting of mixed document batches, and confidence-based routing to human review. The final modules cover operating the pipeline: building ground-truth sets and measuring field-level accuracy, handling email, Office and HTML sources, PII redaction, idempotent re-processing when a parser improves, and cost and throughput at millions of pages. How RAG systems chunk and retrieve parsed content is covered in bld-210. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Data and ML engineers building ingestion for RAG, analytics or automation
Intelligent document processing teams modernizing OCR-based workflows
Platform engineers running document pipelines at volume

courses.title: Data Labeling and Annotation Operations
courses.subtitle: For teams that need labelled data they can trust: write annotation guidelines, choose tools and workforce models, measure agreement, use model-assisted labelling and run preference and evaluation labelling for LLMs.
courses.summary: Run annotation as an operation with measurable quality: task design and guidelines, labelling tools such as Label Studio, CVAT and Argilla, in-house versus vendor workforces, inter-annotator agreement, gold questions and adjudication, model-assisted and active-learning workflows, and the human preference and rubric labelling used for LLM post-training and evaluation.
courses.description:
Labelled data is still the bottleneck for supervised models, fine-tuning, evaluation and preference optimization, and most labelling problems are specification problems. This course starts with task design: turning a fuzzy requirement into label definitions, edge-case rules and a guideline document that annotators can apply consistently, then piloting and revising it. It covers the main task types (classification, span and entity annotation, bounding boxes, polygons and segmentation, audio and video, and LLM-specific pairwise preference and rubric scoring) and tools to run them: open-source Label Studio, CVAT and Argilla, Prodigy, and managed platforms and vendors such as Labelbox, Scale AI, SuperAnnotate and Encord.

Quality gets the most attention: inter-annotator agreement with Cohen's and Fleiss' kappa and Krippendorff's alpha, gold and honeypot items, review and adjudication workflows, and annotator feedback. You will also cut cost with model-assisted pre-labelling, active learning and LLM-as-annotator with human verification, while measuring the bias these introduce. The final module covers workforce ethics and pay, data protection for annotators handling sensitive data, documentation for EU AI Act data-governance expectations, and budgeting a labelling programme. Regulatory notes are educational, not legal advice. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: ML engineers and data scientists who commission or manage labelling
Annotation and data operations leads
Product and domain experts writing labelling guidelines

courses.title: Synthetic Data Generation
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers and data scientists who need more, safer or more targeted data than they can collect: generate synthetic text, tabular and instruction data with LLMs and statistical models, verify it, and know when it will hurt rather than help.
courses.summary: An expert course on generating and validating synthetic data: LLM-generated instruction, reasoning and tool-use data (Self-Instruct, Evol-Instruct, persona-driven and verifier-filtered generation), distillation, synthetic evaluation sets, tabular synthesis with SDV and differential privacy, fidelity, utility and privacy metrics, model-collapse risk, and the licence terms that govern using model outputs.
courses.description:
Synthetic data now sits inside most post-training pipelines and many privacy programmes, but generated data inherits the generator's blind spots and can quietly degrade a model. This course teaches generation and verification together. For language data you will work through seed-based expansion (Self-Instruct, Evol-Instruct), persona- and taxonomy-driven diversity, multi-turn and tool-use trajectory synthesis, rejection sampling with verifiers and reward models, and distillation from larger teacher models, using open tooling such as NVIDIA NeMo Data Designer and the community-maintained distilabel alongside hosted APIs. You will also build synthetic evaluation sets and learn why they need human audit.

courses.subtitle: For data leaders and senior engineers accountable for the data behind AI systems: enforce quality with contracts and tests, trace lineage from source to model, document datasets, and meet EU AI Act, GDPR and copyright-driven data obligations.
courses.summary: An expert course on making AI data trustworthy and auditable: AI-specific quality dimensions, data contracts and automated tests with Great Expectations, Soda and dbt, column- and dataset-level lineage with OpenLineage and catalogs such as DataHub and Unity Catalog, dataset documentation with datasheets and Croissant, and the data obligations in the EU AI Act, GDPR and copyright opt-out regimes.
courses.description:
When a model misbehaves, the first questions are about data: what it was trained or grounded on, where that came from, who approved it and whether it was fit for purpose. This course builds the capabilities to answer them. It starts with quality dimensions that matter for AI beyond classic completeness and validity: representativeness, label quality, freshness for retrieval, leakage and contamination. You will encode them as data contracts and automated checks with Great Expectations, Soda and dbt tests, wire them into pipelines as blocking gates, and monitor drift in production data.

The lineage modules use OpenLineage events and catalogs such as DataHub, Unity Catalog and Apache Atlas to trace data from source systems through feature and embedding pipelines to model versions, so you can answer impact and deletion questions. Documentation modules cover datasheets for datasets, data cards and MLCommons Croissant metadata. The regulatory module covers EU AI Act Article 10 data governance for high-risk systems, the Commission's template for the public summary of training content for general-purpose AI models, GDPR lawful basis and erasure requests against trained models and vector stores, and text-and-data-mining opt-outs. Regulatory content is educational, not legal advice. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.

courses.title: AI Security Fundamentals: The OWASP Top 10 for LLMs
courses.subtitle: For security engineers, AppSec teams and developers who need to find, explain and fix the security risks that LLM features add to real applications.
courses.summary: A practitioner course on securing applications that use large language models, organized around the 2026 OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Every risk comes with a hypothetical scenario, the root cause, and concrete defenses in code and configuration.
courses.description:
Adding a language model to an application changes its attack surface in ways that classic AppSec checklists miss: instructions and data share one channel, retrieved documents and tool results can carry commands, the model's output is untrusted input to everything downstream, and an agent can turn a clever sentence into a database write. This course teaches you to reason about those risks precisely and to fix them with architecture rather than hope.

You start with why LLMs change the attack surface and how to draw trust boundaries for chat, RAG and agent designs. You then work through all ten risks in the 2026 OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (released August 2026), with a crosswalk to the 2025 numbering that many tools and reports still use: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency, supply chain, data and model poisoning, unbounded consumption, misinformation, hidden context exposure (formerly system prompt leakage), vector and embedding weaknesses, and improper output handling. Each lesson pairs hypothetical scenarios with mitigations you can implement. The final module maps the risks to MITRE ATLAS techniques and the NIST AI 100-2 E2025 adversarial machine learning taxonomy, introduces adversarial testing, and gives you secure design patterns and a reusable security review checklist for any LLM feature. Framework facts are current as of October 2026.

Software developers building chat, RAG or agent features
Security architects writing standards for AI use in products
Penetration testers extending web and API testing to LLM applications

Describe each risk in the 2026 OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and map it to its 2025 equivalent

Implement defenses for sensitive data exposure, hidden context exposure, and vector store authorization in RAG systems
Constrain agent tools with least privilege, user-scoped authorization, approval gates and budgets

courses.title: Prompt Injection and Agent Security
courses.subtitle: For security engineers, AI developers and red teamers who need to understand prompt injection deeply and build agents that stay safe when injection succeeds.
courses.summary: A deep course on prompt injection: why it exists, how direct, indirect and multimodal payloads turn into data exfiltration and goal hijack in agents, why filters alone fail against adaptive attackers, and which architectural patterns and tests actually reduce risk.
courses.description:
Prompt injection sits at the top of the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and drives the first entry of the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack). It persists because a language model reads instructions and data through the same channel, so any content the model processes can try to steer it. This course explains the mechanism precisely, then follows payloads from documents, web pages, email, tool results, images and encoded text through to real impact: exfiltration through rendered links and tool calls, hijacked agent goals, and poisoned memory that persists across sessions. Public disclosures such as EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) are used as case studies.

You will evaluate detection approaches (input and output classifiers, spotlighting and delimiting, instruction hierarchy) and learn why adaptive attacks defeat them when used alone. The core of the course is architecture: the lethal trifecta of private data, untrusted content and an exfiltration path; plan-then-execute, dual-LLM and capability-based designs such as CaMeL; egress control; and confirmation steps people do not rubber-stamp. You finish by building an injection test corpus and automated probes with PyRIT, garak and promptfoo and tracking attack success rate as a regression metric. Broader agent identity, tool authorization and MCP hardening are covered in sec-220. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course; it is not endorsed by OWASP, MITRE, NIST or any vendor named here.

Developers building RAG and agent features
AI red teamers and penetration testers
Security architects

AI red teaming borrows the discipline of traditional red teaming but adds targets that are probabilistic, conversational and connected to tools. This course teaches you to run engagements that produce findings developers can fix and leaders can trust. It starts with scope: separating security testing from safety and misuse evaluation, obtaining written authorization, and setting rules of engagement for systems that may touch production data or take real actions. You will work through jailbreak families, indirect injection and exfiltration chains, retrieval manipulation and corpus poisoning, and tool and agent abuse. You will automate with PyRIT, garak and promptfoo, use attacker models and multi-turn strategies such as PAIR, TAP and Crescendo, and score results with classifiers, LLM judges and human review. The course extends beyond the prompt to model-level testing, APIs, serving infrastructure and multimodal inputs, then covers attack success rates with confidence intervals, actionable reporting and coordinated disclosure. It closes with continuous red teaming in CI, building the team, and a capstone engagement against a hypothetical agentic application. All techniques are taught for authorized testing of systems you are permitted to assess. courses.title: Securing the AI Supply Chain
courses.subtitle: For security architects, MLOps and platform engineers who must verify where models, datasets, libraries and agent tools came from and stop tampered artifacts reaching production.
courses.summary: An expert course on AI supply chain security: the threats to base models, adapters, datasets, ML libraries, containers and agent tools; safe serialization and model scanning; signing with the OpenSSF Model Signing specification and Sigstore; SLSA provenance; AI bills of materials; and a registry with promotion gates.
courses.description:
Few organizations train their own foundation models. They download weights from model hubs, fine-tune with open datasets, install fast-moving ML libraries, pull inference containers and connect agent tools and MCP servers written by others. Every one of those links can be tampered with, and some, such as pickle-based model files, can execute code the moment they are loaded. This course teaches you to secure that chain with the same rigour mature teams apply to software, using frameworks current as of October 2026: SLSA v1.2 (build and source tracks), NIST SP 800-218 and its generative AI profile SP 800-218A, the OpenSSF Model Signing (OMS) specification with Sigstore, CycloneDX ML-BOM and the SPDX 3.0 AI and Dataset profiles.

You will learn why safetensors and similar formats reduce risk, what model scanners can and cannot detect, and why backdoored weights are hard to find by inspection. You will sign and verify model artifacts, capture provenance for training and fine-tuning pipelines, enforce verification at deployment with admission policies, and maintain AI BOMs, model cards and licence records through retraining. The course covers ML framework and inference server vulnerabilities, third-party model APIs, and agent tools and MCP servers as supply chain, then closes with a model registry and promotion gates, incident response for a compromised artifact, and a maturity roadmap. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course; it is not endorsed by OWASP, MITRE, NIST or any vendor named here.

Third-party risk and procurement security teams

courses.title: Privacy-Preserving AI
courses.subtitle: For ML engineers, privacy engineers and security architects who must train and deploy models on sensitive data while limiting what those models can reveal.
courses.summary: An expert course on privacy-preserving machine learning: privacy attacks on models, differential privacy and DP-SGD, federated learning and secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, secure computation and confidential computing, privacy in LLM applications, and how to audit privacy claims.
courses.description:
A model trained on sensitive data can leak it: attackers can infer whether a record was in the training set, reconstruct attributes, or extract memorized text from a generative model. NIST AI 100-2 E2025 classes these as privacy attacks alongside evasion, poisoning and misuse. This course teaches the techniques that reduce that leakage and, just as important, how to tell what guarantee each one really provides.

You will learn differential privacy from first principles (epsilon, delta, composition), train and fine-tune with DP-SGD using Opacus, choose and evaluate privacy budgets with NIST SP 800-226 (final, March 2025), and generate differentially private synthetic data. You will examine federated learning with frameworks such as Flower, what secure aggregation does and does not protect, and attacks on federated updates. The cryptographic and hardware module compares homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation and confidential computing on CPUs and GPUs by cost, latency and trust assumptions. For LLM systems you will design de-identification before training and retrieval, privacy-preserving inference gateways, and assess machine unlearning. The course closes with LINDDUN privacy threat modeling, mapping techniques to GDPR and EU AI Act data governance duties, and auditing models with attack simulations. The course is educational and is not legal advice. Operational data security for RAG stores and logs is covered in sec-230. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course; it is not endorsed by OWASP, MITRE, NIST or any vendor named here.

courses.title: Threat Modeling and Secure Design for LLM Applications
courses.subtitle: For security architects, AppSec engineers and tech leads who need to threat model LLM features before they ship and turn the results into concrete design decisions.
courses.summary: A hands-on course in threat modeling chat, RAG and agent features: data flow diagrams with real trust boundaries, threat enumeration with STRIDE, MITRE ATLAS and NIST AI 100-2, risk rating for probabilistic components, and secure design patterns that hold up when the model is fooled.
courses.description:
Most LLM security failures are design failures: the model was given more data, more authority or more reach than any input-handling control could safely contain. This course teaches you to find those problems on a whiteboard, before code review. You will model chat, retrieval-augmented and agent architectures as data flow diagrams, mark trust boundaries that account for retrieved content and tool results, and enumerate threats using STRIDE alongside AI-specific catalogs: MITRE ATLAS (v2026.09 at review), the NIST AI 100-2 E2025 adversarial machine learning taxonomy and the OWASP Top 10 lists for LLM and agentic applications.

You will then learn how to rate likelihood and impact when outputs are non-deterministic, how to analyse blast radius, and how to choose between mitigating, accepting and transferring risk. The design module covers privilege separation patterns (dual-LLM, plan-then-execute, quarantined context), deterministic controls around the model, identity propagation, and where guardrail classifiers help. You will turn threat models into testable security requirements, align them to the CISA/NCSC Guidelines for Secure AI System Development, ETSI EN 304 223 and NIST SP 800-218A, and work through two complete hypothetical threat models. This course goes deeper on design than sec-201, which surveys the OWASP risks one by one. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course; it is not endorsed by OWASP, MITRE, NIST or any vendor named here.

courses.description:
An agent is software that decides at run time which tools to call with which arguments, so the security question shifts from what the user can do to what the agent can be talked into doing. This course treats agents as identities with privileges. You start with agent anatomy, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (ASI01 to ASI10, released December 2025) and the Five Eyes joint guidance Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (May 2026). You then design agent identity and authorization: workload identities, on-behalf-of access with scoped OAuth tokens, user-scoped authorization enforced outside the model, and least agency through allowlists, parameter constraints and budgets.

A full module covers the Model Context Protocol as of the 2026-07-28 specification: its trust model, OAuth-based authorization and audience-bound tokens, confused-deputy risks, tool poisoning and rug pulls, and how to vet, pin and host servers. You will design execution sandboxes (containers, gVisor, microVMs) with egress and secret controls, secure inter-agent communication including A2A, contain cascading failures and rogue agents, and lock down coding agents in developer environments. The course ends with audit-grade tracing, kill switches and a pre-production checklist. Prompt injection mechanics are covered in depth in sec-210. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course; it is not endorsed by OWASP, MITRE, NIST or any vendor named here.

courses.description:
AI systems multiply copies of sensitive data: training and fine-tuning sets, embeddings in vector databases, cached prompts and completions, evaluation sets and observability logs. Each copy needs an owner, an access model and an integrity story. This course maps that lifecycle and anchors it to the joint CISA, NSA and FBI information sheet AI Data Security: Best Practices for Securing Data Used to Train and Operate AI Systems (May 2025), which centres data supply chain risk, poisoned data and drift, together with the OWASP entries on data and model poisoning, sensitive information disclosure and vector and embedding weaknesses.

You will establish provenance with integrity hashes and signed datasets, screen curated and scraped corpora for poisoning, and scrub secrets and personal data before training. The retrieval module is the heart of the course: enforcing source-system permissions at query time, isolating tenants in vector databases, understanding what embeddings reveal, and hardening ingestion pipelines. You then address leakage through conversation history, caches and fine-tuned model memorization, design data loss prevention for AI traffic, log prompts without creating a breach target, and assess vendor retention, training-use and deletion terms. Formal privacy techniques such as differential privacy are covered in sec-330. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course; it is not endorsed by OWASP, MITRE, NIST or any vendor named here.

courses.subtitle: For ML engineers and security researchers who need to attack and defend machine learning models directly: evasion, poisoning, backdoors and model extraction, evaluated rigorously.

courses.description:
Long before chatbots, machine learning models in fraud detection, malware classification and computer vision were being fooled, poisoned and copied. Those attacks still apply, now joined by their generative AI counterparts. This course teaches adversarial machine learning with the vocabulary of NIST AI 100-2 E2025 (attacker goals, knowledge and capabilities across the lifecycle) and maps it to MITRE ATLAS techniques.

You will implement gradient-based evasion (FGSM, PGD, Carlini-Wagner), black-box and transfer attacks, and domain-specific evasion against tabular fraud models and malware classifiers where feature constraints matter. You will study availability and targeted poisoning, backdoor trigger design, and poisoning of web-scale, fine-tuning and instruction data. The extraction module covers stealing models through prediction APIs and distilling LLM behaviour, with defenses such as rate limiting, output perturbation and watermarking. The defense module treats adversarial training, certified robustness and randomized smoothing, and above all how to evaluate defenses correctly against adaptive attacks and gradient masking, using the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox and RobustBench. The course closes with prioritizing robustness work, building it into model release, and a capstone on a hypothetical fraud classifier. Privacy attacks are covered in sec-330 and application-level prompt attacks in sec-210. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course; it is not endorsed by OWASP, MITRE, NIST or any vendor named here.

courses.title: Securing AI Infrastructure: GPU Clusters, Model Serving and MLOps Pipelines

courses.description:
AI infrastructure concentrates valuable assets in one place: proprietary model weights, sensitive training data and expensive accelerators. It is also built from components that were designed for trusted research environments, such as distributed compute frameworks, experiment trackers and notebook servers, several of which have had serious vulnerabilities or been found exposed to the internet (MITRE ATLAS added a technique for misconfigured or publicly exposed AI services in its September 2026 release). This course applies infrastructure security practice to that environment, drawing on Wirewalk's HPC and AI infrastructure work.

You will assess GPU multi-tenancy options (MIG, time-slicing, whole-node allocation) and their isolation limits, harden Slurm and Kubernetes for AI workloads, control access on InfiniBand and RoCE fabrics and parallel file systems, and manage node images, drivers and firmware. You will harden inference servers such as vLLM and Triton, put gateways, authentication and quotas in front of endpoints, and protect weights at rest, in transit and in use. The MLOps module secures notebooks, experiment trackers, registries, CI runners and feature stores. You will evaluate GPU confidential computing with attestation and air-gapped or sovereign deployments, design telemetry, map controls to NIST SP 800-53, the draft NIST Cyber AI Profile (IR 8596) and CIS Benchmarks, and finish with a capstone review of a hypothetical 64-node training cluster. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course; it is not endorsed by OWASP, MITRE, NIST or any vendor named here.

courses.description:
Attacks on AI systems leave evidence, but usually not in the places a SOC already watches. An indirect prompt injection shows up as a retrieved document followed by an unusual tool call; model extraction looks like a patient, high-volume query pattern; a poisoned dataset may surface weeks later as a behaviour change. This course teaches you to instrument AI systems, detect those patterns and respond. It is about defending AI systems; using AI to run security operations is covered in cyb-201.

You will map MITRE ATLAS techniques and the OWASP LLM and agentic risks to observable events, design telemetry for prompts, completions, retrieval, tool calls and infrastructure (including OpenTelemetry's generative AI semantic conventions), and balance forensic value against the privacy risk of logging conversations. You will write and test detections for injection and jailbreak attempts, anomalous agent tool use, scraping, extraction and runaway consumption. Playbooks cover injection-led exfiltration, compromised models, datasets or MCP servers, and agents taking unauthorized actions. You will reconstruct incidents from traces, handle non-deterministic reproduction, preserve model and log evidence, eradicate by rotating credentials and rolling back models, and handle notification duties such as serious incident reporting under the EU AI Act. The course ends with incident sharing, tabletop exercises and maturity metrics. Regulatory content is educational and is not legal advice. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course; it is not endorsed by OWASP, MITRE, NIST or any vendor named here.

courses.description:
Almost every security product now advertises AI, and most security teams are being asked what it actually does. This course gives you the vocabulary and mental models to answer. It starts with the security basics AI is applied to (the attack lifecycle, MITRE ATT&CK, alerts and telemetry), then separates the two very different kinds of AI in security: machine learning models that have scored malware, spam and anomalies for over a decade, and the large language model assistants and agents that arrived more recently in products such as Microsoft Security Copilot, Gemini in Google Security Operations, CrowdStrike Charlotte AI and SentinelOne Purple AI.

You will walk through each layer of a typical defense stack (email, endpoint, identity, network, SIEM and SOC) to see where AI adds value and where it does not, and look at the attacker side: AI-written phishing, voice and video deepfakes, and faster vulnerability discovery. The course closes with practical judgment: questions to ask a vendor, why false-positive rates and base rates matter, what an AI-assisted security career looks like, and the next courses in the Security by AI pathway. Product details are reviewed as of October 2026. It ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.

courses.title: Using AI Assistants Safely in Security Work
courses.subtitle: For security practitioners who use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot or in-product security assistants day to day and need clear rules for what to paste, what to trust and what to record.
courses.summary: Practical rules for using general-purpose and security-specific AI assistants in security work: classifying what can be shared, sanitizing logs and malware samples, verifying output before acting, handling untrusted content that may carry prompt injection, and keeping an auditable record. Ends with a one-page team policy you can adopt.
courses.description:
Security people handle the most sensitive data in an organization: credentials in logs, customer records in incident evidence, unreleased vulnerabilities, and malware. Pasting any of that into the wrong AI tool can create a breach of its own, and acting on a confident but wrong answer can take down production. This course teaches the everyday discipline of using AI assistants in security work without creating those problems.

You will learn how consumer, business and enterprise tiers differ in data retention and training use, and how to read a provider's data terms; how to classify security data and redact or tokenize it before use; and how to verify AI output such as commands, queries, regex, CVE details and indicators before you rely on it. Because security work involves reading attacker-controlled content, the course covers why phishing emails, web pages and malware strings can carry instructions aimed at your assistant, and how to work with them safely. It closes with record-keeping for investigations and a ready-to-adapt team policy. Provider terms are reviewed as of October 2026; it ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.

Security engineers and administrators
GRC and audit staff who draft policies and reports
Security team leads writing acceptable-use rules for AI

courses.subtitle: For SOC analysts, detection engineers and IR leads who want to use LLMs and ML to triage faster, hunt and detect better, and automate response without trusting AI output blindly.
courses.summary: A practitioner course on using AI in the security operations center: LLM-assisted triage and enrichment, incident summaries and timelines, natural-language hunting with KQL, SPL and ES|QL, AI-assisted Sigma detection engineering, SOAR playbooks with approval gates, and honest measurement. Every technique comes with prompts, queries or playbook snippets, and the course closes with a hands-on lab on synthetic logs.
courses.description:
AI is now built into most SIEM, XDR and SOAR products, and every security team is being asked what it is getting for it. This course teaches the work underneath the marketing. It starts with where AI genuinely helps a SOC and where it fails, how LLM security assistants are wired to your data, and how they differ from the machine learning anomaly detection that SOCs have used for years. You then apply LLMs to the core analyst loop: triaging and enriching alerts, summarizing incidents into timelines, and keeping every claim grounded in evidence so hallucinated indicators never reach a block list.

The middle of the course is hands-on query and detection work: turning analyst questions into KQL, SPL and ES|QL, validating generated queries before trusting their results, running hypothesis-driven hunts, drafting Sigma rules with an LLM, and testing them against true-positive and benign data. The final modules survey the vendor landscape as of October 2026 (Microsoft Security Copilot, Gemini in Google Security Operations, CrowdStrike Charlotte AI, SentinelOne Purple AI, Splunk's AI capabilities and open-source options), show how to put LLM steps into SOAR playbooks behind human approval gates, cover prompt injection through logs and emails and the handling of sensitive telemetry, and explain how to measure MTTD, MTTR, analyst time and false-positive rates without fooling yourself. A capstone lab ties it together on a synthetic phishing-to-endpoint intrusion dataset you can build and run on a laptop.

Detection engineers who write and tune SIEM and EDR rules

Threat intelligence teams face more reporting than they can read, in more languages than they speak, and consumers who want answers in hours. LLMs are well suited to reading, extracting and summarizing, and poorly suited to judging source reliability or inventing confidence. This course teaches where that line sits.

courses.description:
Choosing a security AI platform is mostly a decision about where your security data already lives, how the vendor's AI reaches it, and what it costs to run. This course gives you the architecture view and the evaluation method to make that decision well, rather than a feature checklist that will be outdated next quarter.

Each platform module explains how the AI is grounded in the vendor's data (for example, Microsoft Security Copilot across Defender XDR, Sentinel and its data lake and Entra; Gemini and its triage and investigation agent in Google Security Operations; Charlotte AI across CrowdStrike Falcon and Next-Gen SIEM; Purple AI in SentinelOne Singularity; AI assistants in Splunk Enterprise Security and Elastic Security including Attack Discovery), what it can do on its own, what it can take action on, how it is licensed or metered, and where data is processed. You will also look at bring-your-own-model options using MCP servers and open-source stacks. The course closes with a proof-of-value method: success criteria, test datasets, scoring rubrics, cost modeling and governance (roles, approvals and audit logs). The first half covers exposure management: why CVSS alone misprioritizes, how EPSS probability scores, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and SSVC decision trees combine with asset criticality and reachability, and how to use an LLM to normalize advisories and summarize remediation for owners. The second half turns to code: triaging SAST and SCA findings with LLM context, running AI-assisted secure code review against CWE classes and the OWASP Top 10, and generating fixes with tools such as GitHub Copilot Autofix for CodeQL alerts or Semgrep and Snyk AI features, with tests and re-scans as verification gates. The final module covers AI-driven vulnerability discovery, from LLM-guided fuzzing harnesses to research efforts such as Google's Big Sleep and the DARPA AI Cyber Challenge, and what that means for patch velocity. courses.subtitle: For identity security, fraud and detection teams who use behavioral analytics and machine learning to catch account takeover, insider risk and fraud, and need to tune and explain those models.

courses.description:
Stolen credentials and session tokens are among the most common ways in, and fraud teams face the same problem: the attacker looks like a legitimate user. Behavioral analytics and machine learning are the main tools for telling them apart, and they generate a lot of noise when poorly tuned. This course explains how these systems work so you can deploy, tune and defend them.

You will study identity attack patterns (password spraying, MFA fatigue, adversary-in-the-middle phishing, token theft and consent abuse) and how identity threat detection works in products such as Microsoft Entra ID Protection, Okta and CrowdStrike Falcon Identity Protection. You will build baselines and peer groups, compare statistical and machine learning anomaly detectors in Python with scikit-learn and PyOD, apply graph analytics to fraud rings and lateral movement, and learn how risk-based authentication and step-up decisions use model scores. The course places heavy weight on operations: precision at a fixed alert budget, feedback loops, concept drift, explaining an alert to an analyst, and the privacy and employment-law care that insider risk monitoring requires. Product details are reviewed as of October 2026.

courses.title: AI-Assisted Digital Forensics and Incident Investigation
courses.subtitle: For incident responders and forensic examiners who want AI to speed up triage, timeline analysis and reporting without compromising evidence integrity, chain of custody or courtroom defensibility.
courses.summary: Apply AI to digital forensics and incident investigation while keeping forensic discipline: evidence acquisition and chain of custody, AI-assisted triage of endpoints with Velociraptor, super-timelines with Plaso and Timesketch, LLM-assisted log, memory and malware analysis, and defensible reporting that documents every AI-assisted step.
courses.description:
Investigations generate enormous volumes of artifacts, and the bottleneck is usually an examiner reading timelines, logs and memory output. AI can shorten that work considerably, but forensics has rules that most AI demos ignore: evidence must be preserved and verifiable, methods must be repeatable, and conclusions must survive challenge from the other side. This course teaches AI-assisted investigation inside those rules.

The course opens with forensic fundamentals that do not change with AI: order of volatility, acquisition, hashing, write-blocking, chain of custody documentation and evidence handling per accepted guidance such as NIST SP 800-86 and ISO/IEC 27037. You will then use AI where it helps: scoping and triaging many endpoints with Velociraptor, building super-timelines with Plaso and analyzing them in Timesketch (including LLM-assisted analysis), summarizing cloud and identity logs, interpreting Volatility memory output, and getting a first-pass explanation of scripts and malware in an isolated environment. courses.title: Building Machine Learning Detection Models for Security Data
courses.subtitle: For detection engineers and security data scientists who need to build, evaluate, deploy and maintain ML detectors on real security telemetry, and know when a rule would do better.
courses.summary: An end-to-end engineering course on ML detection for security data: framing detection problems, labeling with scarce and noisy ground truth, feature engineering on process, network, authentication and URL data, model choice from gradient boosting to sequence models and embeddings, evaluation at realistic base rates, adversarial robustness, deployment into SIEM pipelines, and monitoring for drift.
courses.description:
Most security ML projects fail for reasons that have little to do with model architecture: the labels are wrong, the evaluation ignores base rates, the features leak the answer, or the model cannot be explained to the analyst who receives its alert. This course is built around those failure points.

You will frame detection problems (supervised classification, anomaly detection, ranking) and decide when ML beats a Sigma rule and when it does not. You will build labeled datasets from incident history, red-team exercises and public resources such as the OTRF Security Datasets and the EMBER malware feature set, and normalize telemetry to schemas such as OCSF and the Elastic Common Schema. Hands-on modules cover feature engineering for process trees, command lines, DNS and URL strings, and authentication sequences; gradient-boosted trees, sequence models and text embeddings for command-line and script classification; and evaluation with time-based splits, precision at alert budget, and cost-weighted metrics. The final modules address adversarial evasion and poisoning of security models, explainability for analysts, deployment patterns into SIEM and streaming pipelines (including Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic and Splunk machine learning tooling), and drift monitoring and retraining. Code is in Python with scikit-learn, XGBoost and PyTorch.

Security data scientists and ML engineers in security teams
Security product engineers building detection features
Technical SOC leads who own detection quality

Build labeled datasets from incident history, red-team data and public datasets while avoiding leakage
Engineer features from process, command-line, network, DNS and authentication telemetry normalized to a common schema
Train and compare gradient-boosted, sequence and embedding-based models for security classification

courses.title: The Agentic SOC: Autonomous Investigation and Response with Guardrails
courses.subtitle: For SOC architects, security automation engineers and SOC leaders who are designing, buying or building AI agents that investigate and act, and must keep autonomy bounded, observable and reversible.
courses.summary: Design and operate AI agents that investigate and respond in a SOC: autonomy levels, agent architecture and tool design over MCP, investigation planning and evidence handling, bounded response actions with approvals and rollback, evaluation harnesses and red-teaming of the agents themselves, and the operating model changes an agentic SOC requires.
courses.description:
Security vendors now ship agents that triage alerts, run multi-step investigations and recommend or take response actions, and many teams are building their own on top of general-purpose models. The engineering question is no longer whether an agent can investigate, but how much it should be allowed to do on its own, and how you will know when it is wrong.

This course starts with an autonomy model for SOC work (from assistant to autonomous action) and maps common tasks to the level each one can safely reach. You will design agent architecture: planning and tool use, least-privilege tool design exposed through the Model Context Protocol, read-only versus state-changing tools, memory and case context, and multi-agent handoffs. You will study how commercial agents in Microsoft Security Copilot, Google Security Operations, CrowdStrike Charlotte AI and SentinelOne Purple AI are scoped, as of October 2026, and when to build your own. The core of the course is guardrails: action allowlists, blast-radius limits, approval gates sized to impact, dry runs and rollback, defenses against prompt injection arriving through alerts and evidence, and full audit trails. You will build an evaluation harness from replayed incidents, measure verdict accuracy and investigation completeness, red-team the agent, and design the operating model: staffing, escalation, accountability and incident response for the agent itself. This course assumes the SOAR and LLM triage fundamentals from cyb-201.
audience: SOC architects and security automation engineers
SOC managers and directors planning agent adoption
MDR and MSSP engineering leads
Security engineers integrating AI agents with SIEM, EDR and identity tools
outcomes: Classify SOC tasks by safe autonomy level and justify the level using impact, reversibility and evidence quality
Design an investigation agent architecture with planning, least-privilege tools, case memory and audit logging
Expose security tools to agents through MCP or equivalent interfaces with scoped credentials and read/write separation
Implement response guardrails: allowlists, blast-radius limits, impact-sized approvals, dry runs and rollback

courses.title: AI for Authorized Penetration Testing and Offensive Security
courses.subtitle: For professional penetration testers and red team leads who want to use AI to work faster within written authorization, agreed scope and rules of engagement, and to control the new risks AI tools bring into an engagement.
courses.summary: Use AI in authorized security testing only: legal authorization, scope and rules of engagement come first; then AI assistance for reconnaissance analysis, web application testing, code and binary review, and reporting, with strict controls on autonomous tools, client data handling and out-of-scope actions. Taught against PTES, the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide and NIST SP 800-115.
courses.description:
Penetration testing is legal only because the system owner has authorized it in writing, for a defined scope and under agreed rules of engagement. AI tools do not change that, but they do create new ways to break it: an autonomous agent that wanders out of scope, client data sent to an unapproved model provider, or a generated exploit run without the review a human tester would apply. This course teaches AI-assisted offensive security entirely inside an authorized engagement.

The first module is the legal and contractual foundation: written authorization from someone with authority over the systems, statements of work, scope definitions down to IP ranges, domains, accounts and cloud tenants, third-party and cloud provider testing policies, rules of engagement including testing windows, prohibited actions, stop conditions and emergency contacts, and frameworks such as TIBER-EU style threat-led testing. Educational, not legal advice. Later modules apply AI to the testing workflow: analyzing open-source reconnaissance output, prioritizing attack surface, assisting web application testing alongside tools such as Burp Suite, reviewing source code and reverse-engineering binaries with Ghidra and LLM assistance, and mapping findings to MITRE ATT&CK. A dedicated module covers autonomous and agentic testing tools: how to constrain them with scope enforcement, action allowlists and human approval, and how to log everything they do. The course closes with AI-assisted reporting that keeps findings accurate and client data protected. It does not teach attacks against systems you are not authorized to test.

Offensive security and red team leads
Security consultancies running testing engagements
Internal security teams commissioning or overseeing tests

courses.title: Defending Against AI-Enabled Attacks: Deepfakes, AI Phishing and Automated Exploits
courses.subtitle: For security leaders, architects and senior analysts who must adapt controls, detection and response to attackers using generative AI for impersonation, social engineering and faster exploitation.
courses.summary: A threat-informed course on how adversaries use generative AI and how to defend against it: voice and video deepfake fraud, AI-scaled phishing and help desk social engineering, accelerated vulnerability exploitation, AI-assisted malware, and attacks on your own AI-enabled workflows. Emphasizes process and identity controls that hold regardless of how convincing the fake is.
courses.description:
Generative AI lowers the cost of convincing impersonation and speeds up parts of the attack chain. Public reporting from model providers and government agencies, including threat reports published by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Microsoft on misuse of their models, gives defenders an evidence base for what attackers are actually doing, as opposed to speculation. This course starts from that evidence and builds defenses that do not depend on spotting the fake.

You will model AI-enabled adversaries against MITRE ATT&CK and the attack lifecycle, then work through each threat class. For voice and video deepfakes you will design out-of-band verification, callback and dual-control procedures for payments and help desk resets, and evaluate deepfake detection and content provenance (C2PA Content Credentials) realistically. For AI-scaled phishing you will move from content inspection toward phishing-resistant authentication with FIDO2 passkeys and identity-centric detection. For faster exploitation you will compress patch and mitigation timelines and prioritize by exploitation evidence. You will also look at AI-assisted malware and living-off-the-land tradecraft, and at attacks that target your own AI assistants and agents as an entry point (handed off in depth to the AI Security pathway). The course closes with tabletop exercises and an executive briefing on AI-enabled threats that avoids hype. Reporting is reviewed as of October 2026.

Fraud, treasury and finance control owners
Threat intelligence and red team staff modeling AI-enabled adversaries
