courses.description:
Cloud and network telemetry is high-volume and mostly benign, which makes it a natural target for machine learning and a hard place to get signal. This course teaches how to turn that data into detections and investigations, using both the managed AI-driven services the cloud providers offer and analytics you build yourself.

You will start with the data: AWS CloudTrail, Azure activity and Entra logs, Google Cloud audit logs, VPC and network flow logs, Kubernetes audit logs, and network metadata from Zeek and Suricata, normalized into a security data lake with OCSF (for example via Amazon Security Lake) or your SIEM's schema. Hands-on modules cover anomaly detection on control-plane API activity and flows, beaconing and DNS tunneling detection, encrypted-traffic analysis with JA4-style fingerprints and flow features, graph-based attack-path analysis combining posture and identity data as in cloud-native application protection platforms such as Wiz, and LLM-assisted investigation of cloud incidents that turns raw API sequences into readable narratives. The course ends with cost-aware architecture and detection coverage mapped to the ATT&CK Cloud and Containers matrices. Service details are reviewed as of October 2026.

courses.title: AI Compliance Essentials for Every Employee
courses.subtitle: For any employee who uses AI tools at work and needs to know which rules apply, what they may share, and when to stop and escalate.

The core of the course is a working knowledge of the two frameworks most programs anchor to: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage, the Playbook and the Generative AI Profile) and the ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system standard (clauses 4 to 10, Annex A controls and the Statement of Applicability), with ISO/IEC 23894 and ISO/IEC 42005 as companions. You will crosswalk them to each other and to the EU AI Act, run an impact assessment end to end, define lifecycle gates and third-party controls, design metrics for leadership, and leave with a 90-day plan and templates for intake fields, a risk register and a RACI. courses.title: The EU AI Act in Practice
courses.subtitle: For compliance, legal, product and engineering leads who must classify AI systems under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and turn its obligations into a working compliance programme.
courses.summary: A practitioner's walk through the EU AI Act: who it reaches, which role you hold, what is prohibited, how to classify high-risk systems, and what providers, deployers and general-purpose AI model providers must actually do. Includes the timeline as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) and worked classification examples.
courses.description:
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is now partly in application: the prohibitions and AI literacy duty since February 2025, the general-purpose AI (GPAI) model rules since August 2025, and the Article 50 transparency rules since August 2026. In July 2026 the Digital Omnibus on AI moved the high-risk deadlines to 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I), added new prohibitions and softened several duties. This course teaches you to read the Regulation article by article, decide what it means for a specific system, and separate what is law from what was only proposed.

You will work through scope and extraterritorial reach, the five operator roles and how roles shift, Article 5 prohibitions, Article 4 AI literacy, Article 50 transparency and the Code of Practice on AI-generated content, the two routes to high-risk classification, every provider obligation from risk management to serious incident reporting, deployer duties and the fundamental rights impact assessment, the GPAI and systemic-risk regime with the GPAI Code of Practice, the AI Office and national authorities, and penalties. The course ends with a compliance roadmap and a set of worked classification cases you can reuse. Content reflects the consolidated position as of October 2026; it is educational, not legal advice.
audience: Compliance, risk and privacy professionals
In-house counsel and legal operations
Product managers and engineering leads shipping AI into the EU
AI governance leads and internal auditors
outcomes: Determine whether the AI Act applies to a system and organisation, including non-EU providers whose outputs are used in the EU
Assign the correct operator role (provider, deployer, importer, distributor, authorised representative) and identify when Article 25 turns another operator into a provider
Screen use cases against the Article 5 prohibitions and the Article 50 transparency obligations
Classify a system as high-risk or not via Annex I or Annex III, and document an Article 6(3) assessment
Map the full set of high-risk provider and deployer obligations, including the FRIA, post-market monitoring and serious incident reporting deadlines
Explain GPAI and systemic-risk model obligations and the role of the GPAI Code of Practice
State the applicable dates after the Digital Omnibus on AI and distinguish adopted law from proposals
Build a prioritised compliance roadmap with an AI inventory, role register and evidence plan
prerequisites: Working familiarity with how AI systems are built and deployed in your organisation

courses.title: US AI Regulation: Federal, State and Sector Rules
courses.subtitle: For compliance, legal and product teams who must map a fast-moving patchwork of US federal policy, state AI statutes and sector rules onto the AI systems they build or buy.
courses.summary: A practitioner's map of US AI regulation as of October 2026: federal executive orders and the preemption push, enforcement under existing FTC, civil rights and sector law, the state statutes from Colorado, Texas, California and New York, and employment, insurance and healthcare rules. Ends with a multi-state compliance tracker you can maintain.
courses.description:
The US has no single AI statute. Instead, organisations face federal executive policy that changed direction in 2025, an Executive Order (EO 14365) and a March 2026 National Policy Framework that push Congress toward preempting state law, active enforcement of existing consumer protection and civil rights statutes, and a growing body of state laws that are being enacted, amended, delayed and challenged in court at the same time. This course teaches you to tell what is in force from what is proposed, paused or under challenge.

You will work through federal policy (EO 14179, EO 14365, America's AI Action Plan and OMB memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22), FTC Section 5 enforcement and AI-washing actions, credit and employment law, sector regulators, the Colorado AI Act and its 2026 repeal-and-reenactment as SB 26-189 (signed May 2026, effective January 1, 2027), Texas TRAIGA, the California CCPA automated decisionmaking technology regulations, California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act for frontier developers, content provenance and deepfake laws, NYC Local Law 144 and other hiring-tool rules, the NAIC model bulletin for insurers, and state healthcare AI disclosure laws. Content reflects the position as of October 2026 and dates are stated as such; it is educational, not legal advice.
audience: Compliance and privacy professionals
In-house counsel and legal operations
Product and HR technology leads deploying AI in the US
AI governance leads at multi-state organisations

courses.description:
Many AI policies fail in one of two ways: they are so broad that nobody can tell what is allowed, or they ban tools that staff then use anyway on personal accounts. This course teaches you to write policy that is specific enough to act on, proportionate to risk, and enforceable with the controls you already have.

You will learn where AI rules belong in a policy hierarchy, how to define scope so it covers AI features embedded in SaaS products, how to tier tools and map data classification levels to them, and how to write output rules for verification, disclosure and records retention. Higher-risk uses get their own clauses: coding assistants with repository access, agents and MCP-connected tools that can take actions, customer-facing bots, and decisions about people. You will map clauses to ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A, NIST AI RMF GOVERN and applicable law, handle labour consultation, and design enforcement through SSO, tenant restrictions, DLP and CASB controls, training and attestation. The course is educational, not legal advice; the Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course only.

courses.title: AI Vendor Risk and Third-Party Due Diligence
courses.subtitle: For third-party risk, procurement, security and legal teams who must assess AI suppliers and AI features in existing products, contract for them, and monitor them after signature.
courses.summary: How to run due diligence on AI vendors and on AI features that appear inside software you already buy: tiering, questionnaires such as SIG and the CSA AI-CAIQ, reading SOC 2 reports and ISO/IEC 42001 certificates, technical data-flow and security review, AI-specific contract clauses, regulatory overlays, and ongoing monitoring through model changes and deprecations.
courses.description:
AI changes third-party risk in ways a standard security questionnaire misses. A supplier may train on your data by default, route prompts through sub-processors in other regions, swap the underlying model without notice, ship an agentic feature that can act in your tenant, or retire the model your process depends on. This course gives third-party risk and procurement teams a method for finding and controlling those risks.

You will tier AI vendors by data sensitivity, decision impact and dependency; choose and adapt questionnaires including the Shared Assessments SIG and the Cloud Security Alliance AI Controls Matrix and AI-CAIQ; read SOC 2 reports, ISO/IEC 27001 and 42001 certificates and model or system cards for what they actually cover; review data flows, retention and zero-data-retention options; request security and red-team evidence; and negotiate data-use, IP indemnity, model-change and exit clauses. You will apply regulatory overlays including EU AI Act value-chain duties, the 2023 US interagency third-party risk guidance (and the replacement the agencies proposed in September 2026), DORA and HIPAA business associate rules, then set up monitoring and offboarding. The course is educational, not legal advice; the Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course only and does not imply endorsement by any organisation named.

Procurement and sourcing leads
Security assessors and GRC analysts

courses.title: Responsible AI: Fairness, Bias and Explainability
courses.subtitle: For data scientists, model reviewers and responsible AI leads who must measure bias, choose and defend a fairness definition, mitigate disparities and explain model decisions to regulators and affected people.
courses.summary: A hands-on course on the measurable parts of responsible AI: where bias enters, how group fairness metrics work and conflict, testing with Fairlearn and AIF360, bias evaluation for LLMs, mitigation trade-offs, explainability with SHAP, LIME and counterfactuals, adverse action reason codes, and the standards and documentation that make the work auditable.
courses.description:
Fairness and explainability are where responsible AI stops being a values statement and becomes engineering and evidence. This course teaches you to find bias, quantify it with the right metric for the decision at hand, decide what to do about it, and explain individual and overall model behaviour in terms a regulator or an affected person can use.

You will trace bias through the lifecycle, compute and compare demographic parity, equalised odds and calibration, connect them to disparate treatment, disparate impact and the four-fifths rule, and run assessments with the open-source Fairlearn and AI Fairness 360 toolkits. You will handle missing protected attributes, test LLM applications with counterfactual prompts and benchmark suites, apply pre-, in- and post-processing mitigations, and document a search for less discriminatory alternatives. On explainability you will compare SHAP, LIME, partial dependence and counterfactual explanations, generate adverse action reasons for credit decisions, and learn the limits of LLM self-explanation. Standards covered include NIST SP 1270, ISO/IEC TR 24027 and ISO/IEC TS 6254:2025. Worked examples are hypothetical. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course only.
audience: Data scientists and ML engineers
Model validators and responsible AI reviewers
Compliance staff in lending, hiring, insurance and healthcare
Product managers for AI that affects people
outcomes: Trace the sources of bias across data collection, labelling, modelling and deployment for a given system
Compute and interpret group fairness metrics and justify which definition fits a specific decision

courses.title: Copyright, IP and Licensing in Generative AI
courses.subtitle: For counsel, content leaders, product managers and engineering leads who need to judge the IP risk of training, using and shipping generative AI, and set a workable clearance process.
courses.summary: Where generative AI and intellectual property law meet as of October 2026: human authorship and registration, fair use and the training cases from Bartz v. Anthropic to the Third Circuit's Thomson Reuters v. Ross affirmance, EU and UK positions, output infringement, open-weight model licences, provider indemnities and an IP clearance workflow.
courses.description:
Generative AI raises three separate IP questions that are often blurred together: whether training on protected material is lawful, whether output infringes someone else's rights, and whether anyone owns the output at all. Courts have begun answering pieces of each, often in narrow and fact-specific ways. This course teaches you to separate the questions, read the leading decisions accurately, and turn them into practical rules for your organisation.

You will cover the human authorship requirement (Thaler v. Perlmutter and the US Copyright Office's Copyright and Artificial Intelligence reports, including the pre-publication Part 3 on training), registration with AI-generated material, the fair use analysis in Bartz v. Anthropic, Kadrey v. Meta and Thomson Reuters v. Ross (including the Third Circuit's September 2026 affirmance), the significance of how training data was acquired, the EU text and data mining opt-out, Getty Images v. Stability AI in the UK and GEMA v. OpenAI in Germany. You will then assess output risk from memorisation, characters, trademarks and likeness, open-source contamination in generated code, and compare model licences (Apache 2.0, which Google adopted for Gemma 4 in April 2026, the Llama community licence, the custom terms on earlier Gemma releases, and OpenRAIL) and provider indemnity programmes. The course ends with EU AI Act GPAI copyright duties and a clearance workflow. Case status is stated as of October 2026 and many matters remain on appeal. It is educational, not legal advice; the Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course only.
audience: In-house counsel and IP professionals
Marketing, creative and content leaders
Product managers shipping generative features
Engineering leads using code generation or open-weight models
outcomes: Separate training, output and ownership questions and identify which legal doctrines govern each
Explain the human authorship requirement and how to register works that contain AI-generated material

courses.title: Implementing ISO/IEC 42001: Building an AI Management System
courses.subtitle: For AI governance leads, ISMS managers and implementation consultants who must build an ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system from scoping through to a successful certification audit.
courses.summary: An implementation course for ISO/IEC 42001: defining scope and roles, gap assessment, integrating with an existing ISO management system, building the risk and impact assessment methods, implementing Annex A controls in engineering workflows, assembling documented information, running internal audit and management review, and preparing for Stage 1 and Stage 2 certification audits under ISO/IEC 42006.
courses.description:
Knowing what ISO/IEC 42001 says is different from building a management system that survives a certification audit. This course picks up where gov-201 leaves off and walks through implementation as a project: what to decide first, which artefacts auditors expect, how to embed controls in the engineering and procurement processes that actually create AI systems, and how to keep the system running after the certificate is issued.

You will scope the AI management system under Clause 4.3 and record your organisation's roles using ISO/IEC 22989 terminology, run a gap assessment, and integrate with ISO/IEC 27001 or ISO 9001 using the harmonised structure. You will design the AI risk assessment method with ISO/IEC 23894, the impact assessment process with ISO/IEC 42005, and a Statement of Applicability that justifies inclusions and exclusions. You will implement Annex A controls for lifecycle, data, information for interested parties, responsible use and third parties; assemble documented information and change control for models and prompts; and run monitoring, internal audit, management review and corrective action. The final module covers choosing a certification body accredited against ISO/IEC 42006, the Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits, surveillance, and adjacent schemes such as CSA STAR for AI. courses.description:
Audit teams are being asked for assurance over AI before the criteria and techniques have settled. This course gives auditors a working method: what to audit against, how to scope, which evidence is sufficient for systems that are probabilistic and change frequently, and how to report in a way that boards and regulators can act on.

You will compare internal audit, second-line review and external assurance; draw criteria from NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act and the IIA's AI Auditing Framework, applied alongside the Global Internal Audit Standards; and distinguish engagement types such as ISAE 3000 and SSAE-based attestation, SOC 2 reports covering AI services, ISO certification audits and statutory bias audits. You will build an AI audit universe from the inventory, write audit programmes for predictive, generative and agentic systems, and test governance, data lineage, validation evidence, change management and vendor controls. Technical modules cover reperforming accuracy, robustness and fairness tests, inspecting prompt logs, guardrail configurations and red-team evidence, sampling, and using AI tools within the audit itself. The course closes with findings, ratings, audit committee reporting, independence and competence. Scenarios are hypothetical. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course only and is not a professional audit credential.

courses.title: Model Risk Management for AI
courses.subtitle: For model risk managers, validators and model owners in banks, insurers and other regulated firms who must extend model risk management to machine learning, LLM applications, vendor models and agents.
courses.summary: Model risk management for modern AI as of October 2026: the April 2026 US interagency guidance (Fed SR 26-2, OCC Bulletin 2026-13, FDIC FIL-15-2026) that replaced SR 11-7 and expressly leaves generative and agentic AI outside its scope, the UK PRA SS1/23 and Canada's OSFI E-23, then inventory and tiering, conceptual soundness for ML, validation of LLM applications and black-box vendor models under a firm's own extended framework, ongoing monitoring, change control and board reporting.
courses.description:
For fifteen years SR 11-7 anchored model risk management in US banking and far beyond it. In April 2026 the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC replaced it with revised, non-binding interagency guidance (SR 26-2, OCC Bulletin 2026-13, FDIC FIL-15-2026) that states generative and agentic AI models are not within its scope, while the UK PRA's SS1/23 and Canada's OSFI Guideline E-23 (effective May 2027) set principles-based expectations that reach AI explicitly. At the same time, firms are deploying machine learning, foundation-model applications and agents that strain classic validation techniques. This course teaches you to apply proportionate model risk management to all of them, including how to govern the generative and agentic systems the US guidance carves out, where firms must rely on their broader risk management and third-party, fair lending and consumer protection obligations rather than on the model risk guidance itself.

You will compare the three supervisory frameworks and decide what counts as a model, including vendor models, LLM-based tools and agentic workflows. You will design inventory and materiality tiering, assign roles across the three lines, assess conceptual soundness for ML, and set documentation and reproducibility standards. Validation modules cover benchmarking, sensitivity, stability and explainability for ML; task-specific evaluation, hallucination and prompt-sensitivity testing for LLM applications; and approaches for black-box vendor models. You will set up ongoing monitoring with population stability and outcomes analysis, manage overrides and change control for retraining and model version upgrades, address fair lending, and report aggregate model risk to senior management and the board. Read the primary supervisory texts for binding detail; this course is educational, not legal or regulatory advice. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course only.

courses.title: Privacy Law and AI: GDPR, CCPA and HIPAA
courses.subtitle: For privacy counsel, DPOs and privacy engineers who must apply GDPR, California and other US state privacy law, and HIPAA to the full AI lifecycle from training data to deployed agents.
courses.summary: Expert-level treatment of privacy law for AI as of October 2026: where personal data sits in models and pipelines, EDPB Opinion 28/2024, lawful basis and Article 22 after the CJEU's Dun & Bradstreet ruling, DPIAs and the FRIA, data subject rights against models, the Digital Omnibus proposals, the CCPA ADMT and risk assessment regulations, other state laws, and HIPAA for health AI.
courses.description:
Privacy law reaches AI at every stage: when training data is collected, when prompts and logs are stored, when a model may itself contain personal data, and when outputs drive decisions about people. Regulators in the EU and US have started to say how existing law applies, and new rules are layering on top. This course teaches you to analyse each stage under the three regimes most organisations face.

Under the GDPR you will work through EDPB Opinion 28/2024 on AI models, the legitimate-interest test for training and deployment, Article 22 and the right to an explanation of automated decisions after CJEU Case C-203/22 (Dun & Bradstreet Austria), DPIAs and their interplay with the EU AI Act fundamental rights impact assessment, data subject rights against trained models, international transfers, and enforcement actions by data protection authorities. You will separate what has been adopted (the 2026 AI Omnibus amending the AI Act) from the Digital Omnibus GDPR amendments that remain under negotiation. In the US you will apply the CCPA regulations on automated decisionmaking technology, risk assessments and cybersecurity audits, other state privacy laws with profiling opt-outs, and sensitive-data statutes such as Illinois BIPA and Washington's My Health My Data Act. For health AI you will cover business associate agreements, de-identification, ambient scribing, the Section 1557 rule on patient care decision support tools, and the pending HIPAA Security Rule update. Educational, not legal advice; the Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course only.

courses.title: AI Incident Management and Reporting
courses.subtitle: For incident managers, AI governance leads, security responders and counsel who must prepare for, run and report incidents involving AI systems, including the regulatory reporting clocks that now apply.
courses.summary: End-to-end AI incident management as of October 2026: defining AI incidents and hazards, building a plan that extends NIST SP 800-61r3, the telemetry you need beforehand, detection and severity classification, containment by rollback, kill switch and tool revocation, root cause analysis for non-deterministic systems, regulatory reporting under the EU AI Act, GDPR, NIS2, DORA, SEC rules, California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act, and post-incident learning.
courses.description:
AI incidents rarely look like a classic breach. A customer-facing assistant gives harmful advice, a model upgrade silently degrades a credit decision, an agent follows instructions planted in a document and emails data out, or a meeting summariser leaks a board discussion. Each needs a responder who can tell whether it is a security, safety, privacy, rights or quality event, contain it without destroying evidence, and work out which reporting clocks started when.

You will define AI incidents, hazards and near misses using the OECD definitions, build a taxonomy and an AI annex to an incident response plan aligned with NIST SP 800-61r3, and specify the logging needed before anything goes wrong: prompts, outputs, tool calls, retrieval sources and model versions. You will write playbooks, use guardrail alerts, evaluation regressions and MITRE ATLAS techniques as detection signals, classify severity, and contain incidents through feature flags, model rollback and credential or tool revocation. Investigation modules cover root cause analysis when outputs are not reproducible, evidence preservation and privilege, and re-release criteria. You will map overlapping notification duties, including EU AI Act Article 73 serious incident reporting, GDPR breach notification, NIS2, DORA, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05, and frontier-developer incident reporting under California SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act. The course ends with blameless reviews, disclosure and tabletop exercises. Scenarios are hypothetical; educational, not legal advice. The Wirewalk Institute certificate attests to completion and assessment of this course only.

courses.description:
Most AI business cases fail in one of three places: they count time saved as cash saved, they leave out the costs that arrive after the pilot, or they never measure what happened after launch. This course gives executives a disciplined method for each step. You will build a value driver tree that links an AI use case to revenue, cost, risk or capital; baseline the current process before anything is built; and cost the solution fully, from per-seat assistants and usage-based API pricing to committed capacity, integration, evaluation, human review and change management.

The second half covers uncertainty and proof. You will model scenarios and sensitivities (NPV, payback and the breakeven adoption rate), risk-adjust the case for error rates and slow adoption, design pilots with control groups that produce real evidence, and instrument unit economics per task or document. The final module covers funding models, presenting to a CFO or investment committee, and benefits realisation reviews that decide whether to scale, fix or stop. All examples are labelled hypothetical scenarios; vendor pricing structures are described as of October 2026.
audience: Executives sponsoring AI investments
Finance business partners and FP&A leads
Transformation and strategy office leaders
Product and operations leaders preparing AI funding requests
outcomes: Build a value driver tree that links an AI use case to a measurable financial or risk outcome
Establish a baseline for the current process before an AI solution is funded
Estimate the total cost of ownership of an AI solution across seat, usage-based and committed-capacity pricing, including hidden run costs
Distinguish released time from realised cash benefit and model scenarios, sensitivities and breakeven adoption
Design a pilot with a control group that produces decision-grade evidence
Choose a funding model and present an AI case that withstands CFO and investment committee challenge
Run a benefits realisation review that leads to a scale, fix or stop decision

courses.title: The AI Operating Model: Teams, Talent and Change
courses.subtitle: For executives and HR and transformation leaders who must organise for AI and leave able to set decision rights, staff the right roles, redesign work and lead adoption.
courses.summary: How to organise a company for AI: choosing between a centre of excellence, federated and embedded models, setting decision rights, defining new roles, sourcing talent, meeting AI literacy duties, redesigning work for humans and agents, and leading adoption with employees and their representatives.
courses.description:
AI value depends less on the model than on the organisation around it. This course helps executives design that organisation deliberately. It starts with structure: when a centre of excellence, a federated model or fully embedded teams fit, who holds decision rights over use cases, models, data access and spend, and what a Chief AI Officer should and should not own. It then covers the roles that matter now, from AI product managers and evaluation leads to AI risk leads, how to hire, upskill or partner for them, and how to run tiered AI literacy programmes, including the EU AI Act Article 4 literacy duty, which the 2026 Digital Omnibus recast as a duty on providers and deployers to take measures that support AI literacy.

The second half is about work and people. You will decompose roles into tasks to automate, augment or keep, design teams where people supervise AI agents with clear accountability, and plan redeployment. You will learn why adoption stalls, how champions networks and incentives work, and how to engage works councils, unions and employees early. The course closes with platform and enablement teams and the health metrics that tell you when the model needs to change. Content is current as of October 2026; regulatory references are educational, not legal advice.

courses.title: Buying AI: Procurement, Contracts and Vendor Negotiation
courses.subtitle: For executives, procurement leaders and commercial counsel who buy AI products and services and leave able to run a sound evaluation, secure the contract terms that matter and negotiate from strength.
courses.summary: A practical guide to buying AI: outcome-based requirements, market scanning, proof-of-value on your own data, AI-specific due diligence, the contract terms that matter (data use, IP indemnities, model change, SLAs), pricing and negotiation levers, lock-in avoidance and post-signature vendor management.
courses.description:
Buying AI is different from buying ordinary software. The product changes underneath you when the vendor updates its models, pricing is often metered in tokens or committed spend, your data may be used in ways the standard terms allow, and the vendor's regulatory role affects your own obligations. This course gives executives and procurement leaders a working method. It starts before the RFP: defining requirements as outcomes and risk tiers, scanning a market of model providers, hyperscaler platforms, SaaS products with embedded AI and integrators, and running a proof of value on your own data with your own evaluation set.

The core of the course is due diligence and contracting: vendor questionnaires on model provenance and sub-processors, assurance evidence such as SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 42001, provider and deployer roles under the EU AI Act, and the clauses that matter most, including no-training commitments, IP indemnities for generated output, model change notification and SLAs. It uses the EU model contractual clauses for AI procurement (MCC-AI) and US OMB memorandum M-25-22 as reference points. The final modules cover pricing structures, negotiation levers, portability and the EU Data Act switching rules, and managing the vendor through renewal or exit. Content is current as of October 2026 and is educational, not legal advice.

CIOs and CTOs approving AI purchases

courses.summary: Decision-level guidance on AI infrastructure: sizing workloads, choosing between frontier APIs, open-weight models, cloud GPUs, reserved capacity and on-premises clusters, reading the NVIDIA and AMD roadmaps, planning for power and liquid cooling, modelling TCO, and building an internal AI platform and roadmap.
courses.description:
AI infrastructure decisions now carry multi-year, multi-million commitments: reserved GPU capacity, rack-scale systems that need liquid cooling, data centre power that takes years to secure, and platform choices that shape every AI product built on top. This course gives technology executives the judgment to make those decisions without getting lost in specifications. It starts from workloads (training, fine-tuning, batch and real-time inference, agents) and how to size demand in tokens, concurrency and latency targets, then compares frontier APIs, hyperscaler model platforms, open-weight models, cloud GPU instances, neoclouds, reserved capacity, colocation and owned clusters.

A hardware module reads the current roadmap at decision level, including NVIDIA Blackwell, Blackwell Ultra and the Vera Rubin generation, AMD Instinct and rack-scale Helios systems, and custom silicon such as Google TPU and AWS Trainium, along with the networking and storage costs that sit beyond the GPU. Further modules cover power density, liquid cooling and grid lead times; TCO models built on utilisation, depreciation and cost per token; supply, obsolescence, sovereignty and security risk; and the internal AI platform of gateways, routing, observability and guardrails. The course ends with a three-year roadmap you can take to the board. Product facts are stated as of October 2026.

courses.title: AI Regulatory and Compliance Exposure: An Executive Briefing
courses.subtitle: For executives, general counsel and compliance leaders who must know where AI law actually reaches their business and leave able to map exposure and prioritise a compliance programme.
courses.summary: An executive briefing on AI regulatory exposure: supply-chain roles, building an exposure map from your AI inventory, the EU AI Act after the 2026 Digital Omnibus, GPAI obligations, US federal, state and sector rules, other major jurisdictions, standards, liability, and how to prioritise and report a compliance programme.
courses.description:
AI regulation is no longer hypothetical, but it is uneven: some obligations already apply, some were moved by the EU's 2026 Digital Omnibus, and in the United States the picture is a mix of federal policy, a federal push to preempt state AI laws, agency enforcement, state statutes and sector rules. Executives need to know which of these actually reach their business and what to do first. This course starts with exposure, not statutes: the provider, deployer, importer and distributor roles, how to build an exposure map from an AI inventory, and the jurisdictional triggers that bring a company into scope.

It then briefs the EU AI Act obligations by risk tier, the compliance dates as adjusted by the Digital Omnibus, the general-purpose AI model obligations and Code of Practice, and how the Act interacts with GDPR, the Data Act and product law. The US module covers federal posture, including the December 2025 executive order directing challenges to state AI laws, and agency enforcement; state laws such as Colorado's (whose 2024 AI Act was repealed and replaced in 2026), California, Texas, Illinois and New York City Local Law 144, and sector overlays in healthcare, financial services and employment. A short international module contrasts the UK, Canada, China, South Korea and Japan and shows how ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI RMF serve as common currency. The course closes with penalties and liability, including the revised EU Product Liability Directive, and a method for prioritising and reporting a compliance programme. Content is current as of October 2026 and is educational, not legal advice.
audience: C-suite executives and business-unit heads
General counsel and chief compliance officers
Chief risk and privacy officers
Product leaders shipping AI features internationally
outcomes: Determine the organisation's role (provider, deployer, importer or distributor) for each AI system it builds, buys or sells
Build a regulatory exposure map from an AI inventory and identify jurisdictional triggers

courses.description:
Many organisations have run generative AI pilots and bought assistant licences without changing how work gets done. This course is for the executives responsible for closing that gap. It begins with why programmes stall after the pilot and how to write an ambition that balances efficiency, growth and new products, then maps where to transform first, function by function.

The middle of the course is practical: what enterprise assistants such as Microsoft 365 Copilot, Gemini Enterprise, ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Enterprise do well and poorly; how agent platforms such as Microsoft Copilot Studio, Salesforce Agentforce and Google's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform differ from custom-built agents; why retrieval over company knowledge decides quality; and how to redesign end-to-end processes in customer service, software delivery and the back office with sensible human review. The final modules cover the leader's role: using generative AI visibly, talking honestly about jobs and productivity, measuring adoption depth rather than logins, and running a transformation steering cadence that survives rapid model and vendor change. All scenarios are labelled hypothetical; product facts are as of October 2026.

courses.description:
CFOs carry two AI jobs at once. The first is transforming their own function: close and reconciliation agents, AI-assisted forecasting and variance commentary, and the AI features now embedded in ERP and EPM suites. The second is governing AI spend for the whole company, where seat licences, token-metered APIs, GPU capacity and data work grow faster than most budgets anticipate. This course covers both.

The first modules map AI to record-to-report, procure-to-pay, order-to-cash and FP&A, compare embedded options such as SAP Joule, Oracle Fusion Applications AI agents, Workday Illuminate agents and Finance agents in Microsoft 365 Copilot against general-purpose assistants, and set out the internal controls, model risk practices and auditor conversations that AI-assisted processes require. The later modules break down AI spend, apply FinOps practices (showback, chargeback, budgets and unit cost per outcome) and the FOCUS billing data specification, and address accounting questions: capitalising internal-use software under ASC 350-40 as amended by ASU 2025-06, IAS 38 for IFRS reporters, cloud commitments and depreciation of AI hardware, and investor disclosure that avoids AI washing. courses.title: AI Risk for CISOs and Chief Risk Officers
courses.subtitle: For CISOs, CROs and their deputies who must fold AI into security and enterprise risk programmes and leave able to set controls, measure AI risk and report it to the board.
courses.summary: How security and risk leaders govern AI: the new threat model of prompt injection, data leakage and agent autonomy, OWASP and MITRE ATLAS taxonomies, NIST CSF 2.0 and the draft Cyber AI Profile, model risk management, agent identity and data controls, red teaming, shadow AI, AI vendor risk, key risk indicators, incident response and board reporting.
courses.description:
AI changes both sides of the CISO's and CRO's job. Internally, generative AI and agents introduce prompt injection, sensitive data leakage, model abuse and autonomous actions with real permissions. Externally, attackers use AI for deepfake fraud, convincing phishing and faster exploitation. This course gives security and risk executives a programme-level response rather than a list of tools.

It maps the AI risk surface using the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications and MITRE ATLAS, then integrates AI into existing structures: NIST CSF 2.0 and NIST's draft Cyber AI Profile (IR 8596), enterprise risk management and the three lines model, and model risk management under the April 2026 interagency guidance (Federal Reserve SR 26-2), which superseded SR 11-7 and explicitly leaves generative and agentic AI outside its scope. The controls module covers non-human identities and least privilege for agents and MCP tool access, data loss prevention and AI gateways, and red teaming and continuous evaluation. The course closes with shadow AI discovery, AI vendor assessment, key risk indicators tied to risk appetite, AI incident playbooks and regulatory notification, and reporting AI risk to the executive committee and board. Framework and standard references are current as of October 2026.

courses.title: Data Strategy for the AI Era
courses.subtitle: For executives and chief data officers who must make the company's data usable for AI and leave able to set architecture direction, governance, data rights and a funded roadmap.
courses.summary: Data strategy rebuilt for AI: what AI-ready data means, unstructured data as an asset, honest thinking about data moats, lakehouse and open table formats, platform choices, retrieval, data products and ownership, metadata and lineage as guardrails, data rights under GDPR, CCPA and the EU Data Act, and a funded roadmap.
courses.description:
Data strategies written for dashboards and reporting rarely serve AI well. Generative AI turns documents, email, call recordings and images into usable assets, and every AI use case asks whether specific data is fit for that purpose. This course helps executives rethink data strategy for that reality. It starts with what AI-ready data means (fitness for a specific use, demonstrated continuously), how unstructured data changes the picture, and which data advantages are real and which are not a moat.

The architecture module stays at executive level: the lakehouse pattern and open table formats such as Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake, the catalog decision, platform choices among Databricks, Snowflake, Microsoft Fabric, Google BigQuery and AWS, and retrieval and vector search for feeding company knowledge to models. Governance covers data products and domain ownership, metadata, lineage and access control as AI guardrails, and data quality for AI. The rights module addresses lawful basis and purpose limitation under GDPR and CCPA, the EU Data Act, data licensing, synthetic data, and copyright in training and retrieval. The course ends with funding the data foundation through AI use cases and a roadmap with progress metrics. Content is current as of October 2026; legal topics are educational, not legal advice.
audience: Chief data, digital and information officers
C-suite executives sponsoring AI programmes
Heads of data platforms and analytics
Data governance and privacy leaders
outcomes: Explain what AI-ready data means and assess fitness of data for a specific AI use case
Identify unstructured data assets and judge which data advantages are defensible
Set architecture direction on lakehouse, open table formats, catalogs and platforms at executive level
Establish data product ownership and use metadata, lineage and access control as AI guardrails
Assess the legal basis, licensing and copyright position for using data in AI training and retrieval
Fund data foundation work through specific AI use cases
Build a data strategy roadmap with metrics that show progress

courses.title: AI for HR and People Leaders
courses.subtitle: For CHROs and senior people leaders who must decide how AI is used in hiring, performance and workforce planning, and answer for its legal, fairness and employee-trust consequences.
courses.summary: An executive briefing on AI in the people function, in two directions: AI used on employees and candidates (screening, assessment, performance and monitoring) and AI changing the work employees do. It covers the employment-AI legal map as of October 2026, vendor accountability, works councils and employee trust, and workforce redesign.
courses.description:
People leaders now own two AI agendas at once. The first is AI applied to people decisions: résumé screening, video and skills assessments, internal mobility matching, performance insights and workplace monitoring, now increasingly delivered as agents inside Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle HCM and Microsoft 365. These are among the most heavily regulated uses of AI anywhere. The second agenda is AI changing jobs themselves, which forces decisions about reskilling, role redesign, headcount planning and how to talk honestly with employees about it.

This course gives you the judgment for both. It sets out the legal map as of October 2026: the EU AI Act's treatment of employment AI as high-risk (with the Annex III obligations now deferred to December 2027) and its ban on workplace emotion recognition, New York City's Local Law 144 bias audits, Illinois's amendment to its Human Rights Act, California's Civil Rights Council and CPPA automated-decision rules, Colorado's narrower replacement AI law (SB 26-189, effective 2027), and the vendor-liability theories being tested in Mobley v. Workday. It then covers vendor due diligence, bias testing, works-council consultation, an employee AI policy and a workforce transition plan. Content is educational and is not legal advice.
audience: Chief people officers and CHROs
HR vice presidents and heads of talent acquisition
Employment counsel and HR compliance leaders
Executives reshaping roles and workforces around AI
outcomes: Classify the organisation's HR AI uses by legal and fairness risk, separating AI used on people from AI used by people
Brief the executive team on employment-AI obligations under the EU AI Act and key US federal, state and city rules as of October 2026
Set requirements for HR technology vendors on bias testing, explainability, audit rights and liability allocation
Decide where human review is mandatory in hiring, promotion, performance and termination decisions
Plan employee consultation, including works councils, and an internal AI-use policy that sustains trust
Build a workforce transition plan that links AI adoption to reskilling, role redesign and headcount decisions

courses.title: AI in Mergers, Acquisitions and Due Diligence
courses.subtitle: For corporate development leaders, private-equity partners, deal counsel and boards who must value and diligence AI companies and assets, and use AI to run deals faster.
courses.summary: An executive program on AI in deals from both sides: diligencing and valuing AI targets (models, data rights, compute, talent and regulatory exposure) and using AI to accelerate diligence itself. It covers acqui-hires and licensing structures, antitrust and national-security review, AI-specific representations and warranties, and post-merger integration.
courses.description:
AI shows up in almost every deal now, either as the asset being bought or as the tool used to run the process. When it is the asset, the questions are unfamiliar: Does the target actually own or license the data its models were trained on? Is its product a thin wrapper on a third-party API with a pricing risk? Are its GPU commitments an asset or a liability? Who keeps the talent? What does the EU AI Act or a pending copyright suit do to the forecast? This course gives deal leaders a structured AI diligence framework and the questions that separate durable AI capability from a demo.

It also covers how deals themselves are changing: acqui-hires and licence-and-hire structures and the antitrust scrutiny they now attract, HSR and CFIUS review, the US outbound investment rules (and the COINS Act, enacted in December 2025, which codifies and expands them once Treasury issues implementing rules) for AI investments in countries of concern, and AI-specific representations, warranties, indemnities and insurance. On the other side of the table, it shows how AI in virtual data rooms and contract-review tools such as Datasite, Intralinks, Kira (Litera), Luminance and Harvey can speed diligence, and where its errors can cost you. Regulatory and market facts are as of October 2026; this course is educational and is not legal, tax or investment advice.
audience: Corporate development and M&A leaders
Private equity and venture partners
General counsel and deal lawyers
CFOs and board members approving acquisitions
outcomes: Apply a structured AI diligence framework covering models, data rights, compute, talent, security and regulatory exposure
Distinguish proprietary AI capability from dependence on third-party models and quantify the resulting concentration and margin risks
Evaluate deal structures for AI targets, including acqui-hires and licence-and-hire arrangements, against antitrust and national-security review risk
Specify AI-related representations, warranties, indemnities and closing conditions for a purchase agreement
Use AI tools to accelerate data-room review and contract analysis while controlling for confidentiality and extraction errors

courses.title: AI in Healthcare and Life Sciences
courses.subtitle: For health system, payer and pharma professionals who must select, validate and govern AI under FDA, ONC, HIPAA and CMS rules rather than just pilot it.
courses.summary: How AI is actually deployed across hospitals, payers and drug developers as of October 2026, and the rules that govern it: FDA device software oversight and change control plans, ONC decision-support transparency, HIPAA, CMS prior authorization policy, Section 1557 and GxP. Ends with a working governance and local-validation process for clinical AI.
courses.description:
Healthcare AI is no longer a research topic: ambient documentation tools such as Microsoft Dragon Copilot, Epic AI Charting and Abridge are in daily clinical use, payers use models in utilization management, and drug developers use AI from trial design to regulatory submissions. Each of these uses sits under a different regulator and a different evidence standard. This course teaches you to tell which rules apply to which system and what good evaluation looks like before and after go-live.

You will work through clinical data foundations (HL7 FHIR, DICOM, claims), HIPAA and business associate agreements, FDA oversight of AI-enabled device software including the clinical decision support criteria as revised in FDA's January 2026 CDS guidance and predetermined change control plans, the ONC HTI-1 decision support intervention requirements and the pending HTI-5 proposal to scale them back, the EU AI Act and Medical Device Regulation interface, CMS prior authorization policy including CMS-0057-F and the WISeR model, the HHS Section 1557 rule on patient care decision support tools, FDA's draft guidance on AI used to support drug and biologic regulatory decisions, and GxP validation. It closes with health-system governance built on the Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI (CHAI) Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare guidance. Regulatory status is stated as of October 2026; the course is educational, not legal or clinical advice.

Health system IT, data and analytics teams
Payer utilization management and revenue cycle leaders
Pharma and biotech regulatory, clinical operations and quality staff
Compliance and privacy officers in healthcare
outcomes: Map a proposed healthcare AI use case to the regulators and rules that apply, including FDA device status, ONC certification, HIPAA, CMS and Section 1557
Determine whether clinical decision software is likely a regulated device or exempt CDS, and explain what a predetermined change control plan allows
Design a pilot and evaluation for an ambient documentation or chart-summarization tool with clinician review and an error taxonomy

courses.subtitle: For bank, fintech, wealth and capital-markets professionals who build, validate or approve AI under fair lending, model risk, financial crime and conduct rules.
courses.summary: A practitioner's course on AI in banking, payments, wealth and capital markets as of October 2026: credit decisioning and adverse action, fraud and AML models, model risk management after the April 2026 rescission of SR 11-7, supervising generative AI in advice and communications, and EU, UK and operational resilience rules.
courses.description:
Financial services has used statistical models for decades, which is exactly why AI here is judged against mature expectations: reason codes a consumer can act on, disparate impact testing, independent validation, recordkeeping and third-party risk management. Generative and agentic AI add new questions those frameworks were not written for. This course teaches you to apply existing rules to new models and to recognise where the rules have recently changed.

You will cover gradient-boosted credit models and explainability, ECOA and Regulation B adverse action requirements and what the CFPB's May 2025 withdrawal of Circular 2023-03 did and did not change, less discriminatory alternative searches, real-time payment fraud and authorized push payment scams, ML-assisted transaction monitoring, deepfake and synthetic identity fraud, the revised interagency model risk guidance that replaced SR 11-7 in April 2026 and its carve-out of generative and agentic AI, FINRA Regulatory Notice 24-09 and communications supervision, SEC and FTC AI-washing enforcement, EU AI Act high-risk treatment of creditworthiness assessment under the revised 2027 timeline, DORA third-party risk, and the UK FCA's Consumer Duty and accountability regime. Dates and regulatory status are stated as of October 2026; the course is educational, not legal advice.
audience: Credit risk, fraud and AML analytics teams
Model risk management and validation staff
Compliance and fair lending officers
Technology and product leads at banks, credit unions, fintechs and asset managers
outcomes: Explain how an ML credit model can meet ECOA and Regulation B adverse action requirements, and identify reason-code practices regulators have rejected
Design disparate impact testing and a less discriminatory alternative search for a lending model
Evaluate fraud and AML model changes for detection gains, false-positive cost and defensibility to examiners

courses.description:
Legal AI has moved from novelty to infrastructure: research platforms such as Westlaw Advantage with CoCounsel Legal and Lexis+ with Protégé, firm-wide platforms such as Harvey and Legora, and general-purpose assistants under enterprise terms are all in daily use. Sanctions for fabricated citations continue to be reported, and courts and bars keep issuing guidance. This course goes beyond basic tool use to the professional, evidentiary and operational questions a practice has to answer.

You will work through ABA Formal Opinion 512 on generative AI, state bar guidance and judicial standing orders, verification protocols that prevent hallucinated authority, technology-assisted review and continuous active learning, validation sampling and recall estimates for defensible review, authentication of AI-generated and deepfake evidence under Federal Rule of Evidence 901 and the status of proposed Rule 707, contract review and diligence workflows, privilege and work-product risk when vendors store prompts, ethical walls in retrieval systems, supervision under Model Rules 5.1 and 5.3, and billing for AI-assisted work. Positions are stated as of October 2026; the course is educational, not legal advice.

Law firm innovation, IT and risk teams

Manufacturing AI fails for practical reasons more often than modelling ones: data trapped in historians and PLCs, defects too rare to learn from, cameras and lighting that change, maintenance models that never reach a work order, and planning tools no one trusts. You will cover ISA-95, OPC UA, MQTT and the unified namespace, edge versus cloud inference, IEC 62443 for connecting AI to OT networks, anomaly detection for rare defects and in-line deployment of vision models, vibration and current-signature condition monitoring and remaining-useful-life models, soft sensors and process optimization, digital twins and synthetic data with NVIDIA Omniverse and OpenUSD, sim-to-real for robots and AMRs, statistical, ML and foundation time-series forecasting, AI-assisted planning in tools such as SAP IBP, Kinaxis and o9, supplier risk sensing, industrial copilots such as Siemens Industrial Copilot, and the EU Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 and its interface with the AI Act for AI safety components. Product and regulatory facts are stated as of October 2026.

courses.summary: Running AI at a university as of October 2026: campus licensing for ChatGPT Edu, Gemini for Education, Claude for Education and Microsoft 365 Copilot, academic integrity after generative AI, GPU services built on Slurm and Open OnDemand, national resources such as NAIRR and ACCESS, research data security and funder rules, and sustainable funding models.
courses.description:
Universities face two AI problems at once. On the enterprise side, every student and staff member wants an AI assistant, and the institution has to choose, license and protect data in it. On the research side, faculty need GPUs, hosted open-weight models and help, at a scale few departmental budgets can fund. This course covers both, from the perspective of the people who have to run the services.

You will cover campus agreements for ChatGPT Edu, Gemini for Education, Claude for Education and Microsoft 365 Copilot, FERPA and vendor terms, assessment redesign and the limits of AI detection, sizing a shared or condo GPU cluster, Slurm GPU scheduling and fair-share, Open OnDemand for Jupyter and RStudio, hosting open-weight models with vLLM behind a campus gateway, the National AI Research Resource and its new operations center, ACCESS allocations, DOE facilities and the Genesis Mission, CUI and NIST SP 800-171 enclaves, IRB and export control questions, NIH notice NOT-OD-25-132 on AI-developed applications, confidentiality in peer review, publisher AI disclosure policies, and cost recovery for GPU services. Program and policy status is stated as of October 2026.
audience: Research computing and HPC center staff
University CIOs, IT architects and enterprise application teams
Research administration and sponsored programs offices
Provosts' offices and teaching and learning centers
outcomes: Compare campus-wide AI assistant offerings on data protection, identity integration and licensing, and draft FERPA-aware terms
Size and design a shared GPU service with Slurm scheduling, fair-share policy and Open OnDemand access
Plan a hosted open-weight model service for researchers with authentication, quotas and logging
Guide researchers to the right national resource, such as NAIRR, ACCESS or DOE facilities, and help write a compute justification
Apply CUI, IRB, export control and funder AI rules to a research AI workflow
Build a cost recovery and support model that keeps an AI research service sustainable
prerequisites: Working familiarity with university IT or research administration

courses.title: AI in Government and the Public Sector
courses.subtitle: For federal, state and local government staff and their contractors who must buy, deploy and account for AI in public services under public-sector mandates.
courses.summary: How public bodies adopt AI as of October 2026: OMB M-25-21 and M-25-22 in practice, use case inventories, buying through GSA schedules, OneGov and FedRAMP 20x, service delivery use cases, due process in automated eligibility decisions, records and security obligations, and lessons from international public-sector frameworks.
courses.description:
Government AI carries obligations private deployments do not: public transparency, due process for people denied benefits, public records retention, appropriations-driven budgets, and procurement rules designed for accountability rather than speed. This course is about delivering AI in that environment. It deliberately avoids re-teaching the US regulatory map covered in gov-220 and focuses instead on the agency practitioner.

You will work through OMB M-25-21 (Chief AI Officers, AI strategies and minimum practices for high-impact AI) and M-25-22 (acquisition), use case inventories, state and local AI policies, GSA Multiple Award Schedule and OneGov agreements, the USAi evaluation platform, FedRAMP 20x and its AI prioritization track, GovRAMP for state and local buyers, contact center and casework use cases, plain-language and multilingual access, automated eligibility decisions and appeal rights, lessons from Australia's Robodebt scheme and the Dutch childcare benefits scandal, EU AI Act fundamental rights impact assessments for public bodies, records laws for prompts and outputs, classified and sovereign deployments, public safety uses, and Canada's Directive on Automated Decision-Making and the UK Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard. Positions are stated as of October 2026; the course is educational, not legal advice.
audience: Agency CIOs, Chief AI Officers and their staff
Program and service delivery managers
Government procurement and contracting officers
Government contractors and systems integrators
outcomes: Classify a proposed agency use as high-impact under OMB M-25-21 and list the minimum practices it triggers
Plan an AI acquisition using OMB M-25-22, GSA vehicles and FedRAMP or GovRAMP authorization status
Design an AI-assisted casework or contact-center service with human review, notice and appeal
Identify due process and fairness failure modes using documented public-sector algorithm failures
Apply records retention, security and transparency obligations to prompts, outputs and use case inventories
Build a pilot evaluation that reports outcomes appropriators and oversight bodies can use

courses.title: AI in Retail and E-commerce
courses.subtitle: For e-commerce, merchandising, marketing and store operations teams who want AI that lifts conversion and margin without breaking consumer protection rules.
courses.summary: AI across retail as of October 2026: semantic search and recommendations, agentic commerce and the protocols that let AI agents shop (ACP, UCP and AP2), demand forecasting and markdowns, personalized pricing under New York's Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act, generative product content, service agents, computer vision in stores, and FTC rules on fake reviews.
courses.description:
Retail has been running recommendation and forecasting models for years. What changed is that customers increasingly arrive through AI assistants, sometimes with an agent completing the purchase, and that pricing and review practices driven by algorithms now draw specific laws and enforcement. This course covers both the established toolkit and the new channel.

You will cover semantic product search and LLM catalog enrichment, two-tower retrieval and ranking for recommendations, honest experimentation, how AI shopping agents discover products through feeds and structured data, the Agentic Commerce Protocol from OpenAI and Stripe, Google's Universal Commerce Protocol, and the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) that Google created and handed to the FIDO Alliance in 2026, fraud and chargeback questions when an agent is the buyer, forecasting and markdown optimization, the New York Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act and antitrust risk from shared pricing software, uplift modeling for promotions, generative product copy and imagery, returns and order-status agents, shelf monitoring and loss prevention, the FTC rule on fake reviews and testimonials, and biometric privacy in stores. Protocol and legal status are stated as of October 2026 and change quickly; the course is educational, not legal advice.
audience: E-commerce and digital product managers
Merchandising, pricing and planning analysts
Retail marketing and CRM teams
Store operations and loss prevention leads
outcomes: Improve product discovery with semantic search, catalog enrichment and a recommendation design matched to the data available
Prepare a catalog and checkout for AI shopping agents and compare the main agentic commerce protocols
Design an A/B or uplift test that measures the incremental effect of personalization or promotions
Assess a dynamic or personalized pricing program against disclosure laws and algorithmic collusion risk
Deploy generative content and customer service agents with review, escalation and brand controls
Identify consumer protection and biometric privacy obligations for reviews, chatbots and in-store vision

courses.title: AI in Insurance
courses.subtitle: For underwriting, claims, actuarial and compliance professionals who must deploy AI in insurance under state regulators' growing expectations for governance, testing and vendor oversight.
courses.summary: AI across the insurance value chain as of October 2026: ML in pricing and underwriting alongside GLMs, external consumer data, unfair discrimination testing, claims automation and fraud scoring, the NAIC Model Bulletin and state adoption, Colorado's SB 21-169 framework, the NAIC third-party data and model vendor work, EU AI Act treatment of life and health insurance pricing, and generative AI in distribution and claims.
courses.description:
Insurance is regulated state by state, and regulators have moved from general statements to concrete expectations: a written AI systems program, testing for unfair discrimination, documented oversight of third-party data and models, and answers ready for market conduct examinations. At the same time, generative AI is reaching agents, adjusters and policyholders. This course connects the technical work to those expectations.

You will cover where AI sits from distribution to claims, how gradient-boosted models are filed and explained alongside GLMs, telematics, aerial imagery and other external consumer data and information sources, proxy discrimination testing, automated underwriting, first notice of loss automation, photo-based damage estimation, fraud scoring and SIU referral, the NAIC Model Bulletin on the Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems by Insurers and its adoption, Colorado SB 21-169 and its life insurance governance and testing regulations, the NAIC Third-Party Data and Models (H) Working Group's vendor registry proposal, EU AI Act high-risk treatment of risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, algorithmic denial litigation and state physician-review laws in health utilization review, adjuster copilots, and preparing for regulator data calls. Status is stated as of October 2026; the course is educational, not legal advice.
audience: Underwriting and pricing actuaries
Claims and special investigations unit leaders
Insurance compliance, legal and regulatory affairs staff
Insurtech product and data science teams
outcomes: Map AI uses across distribution, underwriting, claims and fraud to the regulatory expectations that apply to each
Explain how ML pricing models are documented and defended in rate filings alongside GLMs
Design unfair discrimination and proxy testing for a model that uses external consumer data
Build claims and fraud workflows where AI informs but does not alone determine adverse outcomes
Write an AI systems program aligned with the NAIC Model Bulletin, including inventory, risk tiers, vendor oversight and board reporting

courses.title: AI in Energy and Utilities
courses.subtitle: For utility, grid operator and energy company professionals who apply AI to forecasting, assets and customers, and who now also have to serve AI data centers as some of the largest loads on the grid.

courses.description:
Energy is both a user of AI and the industry most affected by it. Utilities apply machine learning to forecasting, inspection, wildfire risk and customer service, under reliability and security rules that make control-room AI different from office AI. At the same time, AI data centers are arriving as very large, fast-changing loads that strain interconnection queues and grid stability. This course covers both sides.

You will cover generation, transmission, distribution and market basics for AI practitioners, SCADA, AMI, PMU, GIS and outage management data, NERC CIP implications for models touching control systems, load, solar and wind forecasting including weather foundation models, DERMS and virtual power plants, human-in-the-loop decision support for operators, satellite and LiDAR vegetation management, drone inspection, transformer health analytics, data center load forecasting and interconnection queues, FERC's large load interconnection rulemaking and 2026 orders to grid operators, and state large-load tariffs, data center ride-through and flexibility, customer operations, price forecasting, oil and gas subsurface and pipeline analytics, EU AI Act classification of critical infrastructure safety components, the EPRI Open Power AI Consortium and SAFERai.power initiative, and securing utility AI. Status is stated as of October 2026.

Utility data science and IT/OT teams
Energy traders and market analysts
Data center developers and energy procurement leads working with utilities

courses.title: AI in Life Sciences Research: Proteins, Genomics and Imaging
courses.subtitle: For bench and computational scientists, core-facility staff and research IT teams who want to run and critically judge AI models for protein structure and design, genomics and biological imaging.
courses.summary: A practitioner's tour of the AI models reshaping life-science research: AlphaFold 3 and its open alternatives for structure prediction, RFdiffusion3, ProteinMPNN and BoltzGen for design, DeepVariant, AlphaGenome and Evo 2 for genomics, and Cellpose-SAM, micro-SAM and MONAI for imaging. It stresses confidence metrics, validation, licensing, compute and biosecurity.
courses.description:
AI models are now part of routine life-science research, but each family comes with its own failure modes and fine print. This course starts with structure prediction: how AlphaFold 3, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and OpenFold3 predict complexes, how to read pLDDT, PAE and ipTM, and when a confident prediction is still wrong. It moves on to generative protein design with RFdiffusion3, ProteinMPNN and BoltzGen, and to protein language models such as ESM, before turning to genomics: variant calling with DeepVariant and NVIDIA Parabricks, variant-effect prediction with AlphaMissense and AlphaGenome, DNA foundation models such as Evo 2, and single-cell foundation models.

The imaging module covers cell and nucleus segmentation with Cellpose-SAM and micro-SAM in napari, medical and preclinical imaging with MONAI, and AI-assisted cryo-EM model building. The final module is about doing this responsibly and at scale: licences that restrict commercial use of weights or training data, running models on GPU clusters with containers and Slurm, reproducibility and reporting, and dual-use and biosecurity obligations including nucleic-acid synthesis screening. Model versions, licences and availability are stated as of October 2026.
audience: Structural and molecular biologists
Bioinformaticians and computational biologists
Imaging and microscopy core staff
Research computing and HPC teams supporting life-science labs
outcomes: Run a biomolecular complex prediction and interpret pLDDT, PAE and ipTM to decide how far to trust it
Choose between AlphaFold 3, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and OpenFold3 given licence, input types and compute constraints
Describe a generative protein-design pipeline from backbone generation to sequence design and in-silico filtering
Select appropriate AI tools for variant calling, variant-effect prediction and regulatory-genomics questions, and state their limits
Segment microscopy images with a generalist model, fine-tune it on lab data and validate the result quantitatively

Apply licensing, reproducibility and biosecurity checks before publishing or sharing AI-derived results

courses.title: AI in Media and Entertainment
courses.subtitle: For producers, studio and network executives, post-production leads and content-rights professionals who need to use generative AI in production while respecting talent contracts, copyright and disclosure rules.
courses.summary: A working course on generative AI across the media value chain: development, previsualisation, VFX and post, dubbing and localisation, and marketing. It pairs the tools (Adobe Firefly, Runway, Google Veo and Flow, ElevenLabs and others) with the rules that govern their use: SAG-AFTRA and WGA terms, copyright and training-data litigation, right-of-publicity laws, and content-provenance and labelling duties.
courses.description:
Generative video, image, voice and music models are now usable in real productions, but every use raises a question someone has to answer: Is it allowed under the talent agreement? Can the output be copyrighted? Was the model trained on licensed material? Must it be labelled? This course takes producers and rights teams through those questions in the order a production meets them. It covers concept art and previsualisation, generative VFX and clean-up in post, AI dubbing and voice localisation, trailer and marketing variants, and newsroom and publishing uses.

Alongside the workflows, it explains the governing framework as of October 2026: the AI and digital-replica provisions of the SAG-AFTRA TV/Theatrical Agreement ratified in June 2026, the WGA's rules on AI-generated material, the US Copyright Office's guidance on copyrightability of AI-assisted works and its pre-publication report on generative AI training, the major training-data lawsuits and licensing deals, state digital-replica and voice laws such as Tennessee's ELVIS Act, the proposed federal NO FAKES Act, EU AI Act Article 50 transparency duties for deepfakes, and C2PA Content Credentials. It ends with vendor due diligence and a studio AI policy. This course is educational and is not legal advice.

Post-production, VFX and localisation leads
Business affairs, legal and rights-clearance teams
Newsroom, publishing, music and games leaders
outcomes: Map generative AI tools to stages of the production pipeline and judge where they save time without degrading quality
Apply SAG-AFTRA and WGA AI provisions to decide when consent, notice and compensation are required for digital replicas and AI-generated material
Assess the copyright position of AI-assisted work, including human-authorship requirements and chain-of-title documentation
Evaluate a generative AI vendor's training-data provenance, indemnities and output terms before production use

courses.title: AI Hardware Fundamentals: GPUs, CPUs, Memory, Networking and Storage
courses.subtitle: For IT staff, buyers, managers and newcomers who need to understand the physical layer of AI well enough to read a spec sheet, size a simple system and ask vendors the right questions.
courses.summary: A plain-language tour of the hardware that runs AI: why AI is limited by compute, memory bandwidth and data movement; what GPUs, HBM and precision formats are; how servers, networks, storage, power and cooling fit together; and how to size a simple inference or training system and weigh cloud against buying.
courses.description:
AI projects succeed or stall on hardware decisions that are often made by people who were never shown how the physical layer works. This course explains it from the ground up without assuming an engineering background. You will learn why modern AI is as much a memory and data-movement problem as a compute problem, how CPUs, GPUs and other accelerators differ, what is inside a GPU (cores, tensor units, high-bandwidth memory) and why precision formats such as BF16, FP8 and FP4 change what fits and how fast it runs. You will get an overview of the current accelerator lineup from NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and the cloud providers, reviewed as of October 2026.

The second half follows the system outward: PCIe cards versus SXM and OAM modules, 8-GPU servers and rack-scale systems, Ethernet versus InfiniBand, NVMe and parallel filesystems, and the power and liquid cooling that dense GPU racks demand. The course closes with practical skills: reading a spec sheet critically, sizing an inference server and a small training system with worked arithmetic, and structuring a cloud-versus-buy decision. It ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment.

courses.summary: An engineer's tour of the modern data center GPU: how SMs and CUs, warps and wavefronts, tensor and matrix cores and the on-chip memory hierarchy work; what FP64 through FP4 and sparsity really buy you; how HBM, PCIe, NVLink, Infinity Fabric, UALink and CXL move data; and how power, cooling and reliability features shape real deployments. courses.description:
Spec sheets for AI accelerators are dense with numbers that are easy to quote and easy to misread. This course gives hardware and infrastructure engineers the architectural model needed to read them correctly. It starts inside the chip: streaming multiprocessors and compute units, the SIMT execution model of warps and wavefronts, tensor and matrix cores, register files, shared memory and caches. It then covers number formats from FP64 down to block-scaled FP4 (MXFP4 and NVFP4), structured sparsity, and why the headline throughput figure on a datasheet is rarely the one your workload will see.

The second half follows data outward: HBM generations from HBM2e to HBM4 and the capacity-versus-bandwidth trade-off, roofline analysis with worked arithmetic, and the accelerator generations that matter in 2026 (NVIDIA Hopper, Blackwell and Vera Rubin; AMD CDNA 3, CDNA 4 and the MI400 series; Intel Gaudi 3 and Intel's roadmap). It covers PCIe Gen5 and Gen6, NVLink and NVSwitch generations, Infinity Fabric, UALink and CXL, and rack-scale designs such as NVL72 and Helios. It closes with power and thermal design, liquid cooling, ECC, row remapping and error telemetry, and a worked datasheet comparison. Product figures are stated as of October 2026 and labeled where vendors still mark them preliminary. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification.

courses.title: CPUs for AI: x86, Arm, AVX-512/AMX and Grace/Graviton
