courses.summary: How server CPUs are built and where they matter in AI systems: cores, chiplets, caches, memory channels and PCIe lanes; vector and matrix extensions from AVX-512 and AMX to SVE2 and SME; the 2026 Xeon 6, EPYC 9005 and 9006, Grace and Vera, and cloud Arm lineups; and how to pick and tune a host CPU so GPUs are never starved. Reviewed against vendor sources as of October 2026.
courses.description:
In an AI server the CPU rarely gets the headlines, yet it decides how many GPUs and NICs a node can feed, how fast data is decoded and tokenized, how much memory bandwidth is available to offload and preprocessing, and whether small-model or batch inference can run without a GPU at all. This course gives engineers a working model of the modern server CPU: core microarchitecture, chiplet and tile packaging, cache hierarchy, NUMA, memory channels and PCIe and CXL lanes, and how each of those shows up in AI workloads.

The middle of the course covers the instruction-set features that matter for AI on CPUs, including AVX-512, AVX10, AMX with BF16 and FP16 tiles, and Arm SVE2 and SME, and how libraries such as oneDNN, ZenDNN, Arm Compute Library and llama.cpp use them. It then surveys the platforms current in October 2026: Intel Xeon 6 P-core and E-core and Xeon 6+ (Clearwater Forest), AMD EPYC 9005 (Turin) and the Zen 6 EPYC 9006 (Venice), NVIDIA Grace and the Vera CPU in Vera Rubin systems, and cloud Arm CPUs such as AWS Graviton4 and Graviton5, Google Axion and Microsoft Cobalt. It closes with selection and tuning: lanes-per-GPU arithmetic, NUMA pinning, BIOS and power settings, and a worked host-CPU sizing exercise. Vendor figures are stated as of October 2026 and marked as vendor claims where independent results are not yet available. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification.

courses.summary: The physical layer of AI networking: SerDes and lane rates, NICs and SuperNICs, DPUs, InfiniBand and Ethernet switch silicon, rail-optimized topologies, and the transceivers, cables and co-packaged optics that connect them. Covers ConnectX-8 and ConnectX-9, BlueField-3 and BlueField-4, Quantum-X800, Spectrum-X, Tomahawk 6, Pollara and Thor Ultra, and Ultra Ethernet, reviewed against vendor sources as of October 2026.
courses.description:
Collective communication across thousands of GPUs turns the network into part of the computer, and most of what goes wrong in an AI fabric is physical: the wrong optic, a marginal link, a mis-split cage, an oversubscribed rail or a NIC on the wrong PCIe root. This course teaches the hardware of AI networks from the SerDes up. It starts with lane rates and encodings (PAM4 at 100G and 200G per lane), the difference between scale-up, scale-out and front-end networks, and how NICs connect to GPUs over PCIe and through PCIe switches.

You then work through the device classes current in October 2026: NVIDIA ConnectX-8 and ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, BlueField-3 and BlueField-4 DPUs, AMD Pensando Pollara 400 and Vulcano, and Broadcom Thor Ultra; InfiniBand (Quantum-X800) and Ethernet switch silicon (Spectrum-X, Broadcom Tomahawk 5 and 6 and Jericho, Cisco Silicon One) in the systems sold by NVIDIA, Arista, Cisco and others; and the Ultra Ethernet 1.0 specification. The optics module covers OSFP and QSFP-DD form factors, DR, FR and SR optics, DACs, ACCs and AECs, linear-drive optics and co-packaged optics such as Spectrum-X Photonics and Quantum-X Photonics. The course closes with topology and radix arithmetic, cabling and breakout planning, and link bring-up and validation with real tools. Shipping status is stated as of October 2026 and announced-but-not-shipping products are labeled. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification.

courses.title: Storage Hardware for AI: NVMe, SSD Endurance, Arrays and GPUDirect Storage
courses.subtitle: For storage and infrastructure engineers who must choose drives, servers and storage systems that keep GPUs fed, survive checkpoint traffic and hold data at petabyte scale.
courses.summary: The hardware view of AI storage: NAND types and SSD internals, endurance and DWPD, NVMe and EDSFF form factors, PCIe Gen5 and Gen6 drives, high-capacity QLC, storage servers and arrays, NVMe over Fabrics, GPUDirect Storage and KV-cache storage tiers, and how to size bandwidth and capacity for training, checkpoints and inference. courses.description:
GPUs that wait on storage burn money, and SSDs that wear out early or stall under mixed writes cause outages that look like software bugs. This course gives engineers the hardware model needed to specify storage for AI. It begins inside the SSD: NAND cell types from TLC to QLC, the flash translation layer, over-provisioning, write amplification, and how endurance ratings (DWPD and TBW) translate into service life under real AI write patterns such as checkpointing. It covers the NVMe protocol, queues and namespaces, EDSFF E1.S, E3.S and E3.L and U.2 form factors, and the drives current in October 2026, from PCIe Gen5 performance drives to the first PCIe Gen6 drives and 122 TB and 245 TB class QLC.

The second half moves out to systems: storage servers and the PCIe and network bandwidth budgets that bound them, parallel filesystems and AI storage platforms (IBM Storage Scale, Lustre-based DDN EXAScaler, VAST, WEKA, Pure Storage, NetApp and others), NVMe over Fabrics, and NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage with cuFile. It explains the emerging context-memory tier for inference KV cache, including NVIDIA's BlueField-4-based Inference Context Memory Storage platform, and labels vendor claims as such. It closes with sizing worked examples for data ingest, checkpoint bursts and inference, and with benchmarking traps that make storage look faster than it is. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification.

courses.description:
Most AI workloads are bounded by memory capacity or memory bandwidth long before they run out of arithmetic. This course explains the memory technologies in AI systems from the DRAM cell up, so engineers can predict what fits, how fast it moves and what it costs. It starts with DRAM organization (banks, ranks, channels, refresh and timing) and why bandwidth, latency and capacity trade against one another.

It then covers each tier in turn. HBM: stacks, TSVs, base dies, 2.5D packaging, the HBM3E and HBM4 generations (JEDEC JESD270-4) and what HBM4E and custom base dies change. Host memory: DDR5 RDIMM speeds and channel counts, MRDIMM, and the bandwidth per core of current Xeon and EPYC platforms. LPDDR5X and SOCAMM modules in Grace and Vera systems, and the coherent CPU-GPU memory they enable. CXL: Type 3 memory expansion, CXL 2.0, 3.x and the CXL 4.0 specification released in November 2025, pooling, switching and the latency cost. Reliability: ECC, on-die ECC, chipkill-class protection, row remapping and error telemetry. The course closes with capacity planning arithmetic for training and inference, including KV cache growth, offload tiers and a worked memory plan. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification.

courses.title: Edge and Embedded AI Hardware: Jetson, NPUs and Mobile SoCs
courses.subtitle: For embedded, robotics and device engineers who must choose and deploy AI silicon under tight power, thermal, cost and latency budgets, from Jetson modules to laptop and phone NPUs and discrete edge accelerators.
courses.summary: The silicon behind on-device AI: NPU, GPU and DSP architectures, what TOPS ratings do and do not mean, the NVIDIA Jetson Orin and Thor families, PC and mobile SoC NPUs from Qualcomm, Apple, Intel, AMD and MediaTek, discrete edge accelerators, and the quantization, toolchain, power and thermal work needed to ship a model on a device. courses.description:
Edge AI is constrained by watts, heat, memory bandwidth and bill-of-materials cost, and the datasheet number that marketing leads with (TOPS) is rarely what limits a deployed model. This course teaches engineers to read edge AI silicon critically and to carry a model from a training framework onto real hardware. It starts with the architectures: NPUs as fixed-function or programmable matrix engines, integrated GPUs, DSPs and CPU vector units, and how memory bandwidth and on-chip SRAM bound performance for vision and language models.

It then surveys the hardware current in October 2026: NVIDIA Jetson Orin modules and the Blackwell-based Jetson Thor family; PC NPUs in Qualcomm Snapdragon X2, Intel Core Ultra and AMD Ryzen AI processors, and the Copilot+ PC NPU requirement; Apple M-series and A-series Neural Engines and GPU neural accelerators; mobile SoCs from Qualcomm and MediaTek; and discrete and microcontroller-class accelerators such as Hailo and Google's Edge TPU. The second half is practical: INT8 and INT4 quantization and its accuracy cost, toolchains (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime execution providers, Qualcomm AI Runtime, OpenVINO, Core ML, LiteRT), power modes and thermal design, carrier boards and camera and sensor I/O, fleet updates and security, and a worked selection for a robotics vision system and an on-device assistant. TOPS figures are vendor peak ratings and are labeled with precision and sparsity where the vendor states them. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification.
audience: Embedded and robotics engineers selecting compute modules for vision, speech and language at the edge
Device and product engineers deploying on-device AI in laptops, phones and appliances
IoT and industrial engineers evaluating NPUs and discrete edge accelerators
Solutions architects deciding what runs on the device versus in the cloud
outcomes: Explain how NPUs, integrated GPUs, DSPs and CPU vector units differ in architecture, programmability and efficiency for edge AI
Interpret TOPS ratings by precision, sparsity and sustained power, and estimate real throughput from memory bandwidth and model size
Compare NVIDIA Jetson Orin and Thor modules, PC and mobile SoC NPUs, and discrete edge accelerators for a stated workload and power budget

courses.title: AI Accelerators Beyond GPUs: TPU, Trainium, Gaudi and Wafer-Scale
courses.subtitle: For senior hardware and infrastructure engineers who must evaluate non-GPU AI accelerators on architecture, system design, software maturity and total cost, and decide when one beats a GPU for a given workload.
courses.summary: An architect's comparison of AI accelerators that are not general-purpose GPUs: systolic-array TPUs, AWS Trainium and Inferentia, Intel Gaudi and its successors, Cerebras wafer-scale engines, SRAM-centric dataflow and LPU designs from Groq and SambaNova, and hyperscaler in-house chips such as Maia and MTIA. Covers microarchitecture, memory and interconnect, compilers and software stacks, and a structured method for evaluating them against GPUs. Reviewed against vendor sources as of October 2026.
courses.description:
GPUs dominate AI compute, but a growing share of training and inference runs on accelerators built around different bets: large systolic arrays with compiler-scheduled dataflow, on-chip SRAM instead of HBM, whole-wafer silicon, or chips co-designed with a single company's models. This course teaches the architecture behind those bets well enough to predict where each wins and where it struggles. It opens with the design space (spatial versus temporal architectures, systolic arrays, dataflow, SRAM-versus-HBM memory strategies and deterministic scheduling) and the roofline and memory-capacity reasoning that separates them.

It then examines the platforms current in October 2026: Google TPUs through Trillium and Ironwood (TPU v7) with optical circuit-switched pods and the JAX and XLA stack; AWS Trainium2 and Trainium3 UltraServers, Inferentia2 and the Neuron SDK; Intel Gaudi 3 and Intel's announced Crescent Island inference GPU; Cerebras WSE-3 and CS-3 systems; Groq LPUs, including NVIDIA's Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator for Vera Rubin following NVIDIA's December 2025 licensing agreement with Groq; SambaNova reconfigurable dataflow units; Tenstorrent; Qualcomm AI200 and AI250; and in-house chips such as Microsoft Maia 200 and Meta MTIA. Each is treated through the same lens: compute and number formats, memory hierarchy, scale-up and scale-out interconnect, compiler and framework support, availability model (cloud-only or purchasable), and operational maturity. The course closes with a rigorous evaluation method: workload characterization, porting cost, benchmark design that avoids vendor-favorable traps, and total-cost modeling. Vendor performance figures are presented as vendor claims; announced-but-not-shipping products are labeled. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification.

courses.subtitle: For senior infrastructure, hardware and data center engineers who design, procure and deploy AI servers and racks, from 8-GPU HGX nodes to liquid-cooled rack-scale systems and OCP open racks.
courses.summary: How AI servers and racks are built: the HGX baseboard and 8-GPU node, MGX modular servers, rack-scale systems such as GB300 NVL72, Vera Rubin NVL72 and AMD Helios, OCP Open Rack v3 and Open Rack Wide, power delivery from 48 V busbars to 800 VDC, direct liquid cooling and CDUs, management and serviceability, and how to plan, procure and commission them. courses.description:
AI compute is now bought and deployed as racks rather than servers, and the hard problems have moved from the motherboard to the rack and the facility: 100 to 200 kW per rack and rising, liquid cooling loops, busbars and power shelves, cable cartridges and spine trays, floor loading and the commissioning sequence that brings it all up. This course gives senior engineers an end-to-end architectural model of AI servers and racks. It starts with the node: HGX baseboards, SXM and OAM modules, PCIe switch and NIC topologies, host CPU and memory, boot and management controllers, and the MGX modular reference architecture used by OEMs.

It then moves to rack-scale systems current in October 2026: NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 NVL72 and the Vera Rubin NVL72 that began shipping in 2026, the announced Kyber rack for Rubin Ultra, and AMD's Helios rack built on the OCP Open Rack Wide specification. It covers the OCP standards that shape the rack (Open Rack v3, Open Rack Wide, DC-MHS, OAM and the power and cooling workstreams), power delivery from AC and 48 V busbars to the 800 VDC architectures NVIDIA and partners are introducing, and direct liquid cooling with cold plates, manifolds, in-rack and in-row CDUs and facility water. Management with Redfish and OpenBMC, serviceability and spares, and a full planning and commissioning sequence close the course. Shipping status and specifications are stated as of October 2026, and announced or roadmap products are labeled. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification.

courses.title: Hardware Validation, Burn-In and Failure Analysis
courses.subtitle: For senior hardware, HPC and AI infrastructure engineers who must accept new GPU systems, prove them healthy under load, catch weak components before production, and find root causes when hardware fails.
courses.summary: A practitioner's method for proving AI hardware healthy and finding out why it is not: acceptance criteria, layered burn-in from component to fabric, GPU diagnostics with DCGM and the ROCm Validation Suite, CPU, memory, storage and network stress, silent data corruption screening, telemetry and error codes, failure analysis and RMA practice. Reviewed against vendor documentation as of October 2026.
courses.description:
Large AI clusters fail constantly at the component level, and the cost of a weak GPU, a marginal optic or a corrupting CPU core is paid in stalled training runs, wrong answers and lost engineer time. This course teaches a disciplined approach to hardware validation and failure analysis that works across vendors. It starts with the reliability basics engineers need (infant mortality and the bathtub curve, MTBF arithmetic at fleet scale, and why the job failure rate of a synchronous training run grows with GPU count) and with writing acceptance criteria that can be enforced in a contract.

The core of the course is a layered burn-in and validation plan: component and node tests for GPUs (NVIDIA DCGM diagnostics at increasing levels, NVIDIA field diagnostics, AMD ROCm Validation Suite and AMD GPU field health tools), CPUs and memory (stress-ng, memory testers, OpenDCDiag), storage (fio) and NICs (perftest); then multi-node tests (NCCL and RCCL collectives, HPL, nvbandwidth and representative training jobs) and thermal and power soak. It covers silent data corruption and how hyperscalers screen for it, drawing on published industry work and the OCP Server Component Resilience workstream. The final modules teach telemetry and error interpretation (NVIDIA XID and SXid events, ECC and row remapping, PCIe AER, BMC SEL and Redfish logs), structured failure analysis from symptom to field-replaceable unit, and RMA, spares and fleet-health practice. The course ends with an automated exam and a Wirewalk Institute certificate of completion and assessment; it is not a vendor certification.

courses.title: Robotics and Physical AI Hardware
courses.subtitle: For engineers and technical buyers who need to specify the compute, sensors, actuators, power and safety hardware for robots that run AI models, from mobile manipulators to humanoids.
courses.summary: The physical stack under embodied AI: robot architectures and form factors, onboard compute such as Jetson AGX Thor, cameras, depth sensors, LiDAR, IMUs and tactile sensing, motors, gearboxes and grippers, real-time buses like EtherCAT and CAN, batteries and power, and the functional-safety standards that govern robots working near people.
courses.description:
Physical AI moves models off the data-center floor and into machines that see, move and touch. The hardware choices decide what the AI can do: a policy cannot outperform its cameras, its actuators' torque and backdrivability, its compute's latency, or its battery. This course gives engineers a working map of that hardware, organized around the questions a robot program has to answer.

You start with robot architectures, from arms and mobile manipulators to legged and humanoid platforms, and how degrees of freedom, payload and reach translate into a hardware bill of materials. You then compare onboard compute (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and Orin, Qualcomm Dragonwing robotics processors, and offload to edge servers), focusing on what perception and vision-language-action workloads need rather than restating the Jetson internals covered in hw-206. The sensing module covers RGB, stereo and time-of-flight depth, LiDAR, IMUs, force-torque and tactile sensors, and synchronization; the actuation module covers motors, harmonic and planetary gearing, quasi-direct-drive and series-elastic actuators, and end effectors. The last modules cover real-time communication (EtherCAT, CAN FD, Time-Sensitive Networking, ROS 2 middleware), battery and thermal design, and functional safety under the 2025 editions of ISO 10218 and related standards. Product facts are current as of October 2026.

courses.title: Python AI Integration: SDKs, Async, Pydantic, Packaging and Testing
courses.subtitle: For Python developers who need to put LLM calls into real codebases: typed, concurrent, testable, observable and deployable.
courses.summary: A code-first course on integrating LLMs into Python the way production code needs it: uv projects and secrets, the OpenAI, Anthropic and Google GenAI SDKs side by side, async concurrency and streaming, Pydantic structured outputs and tools, retries, local models, embeddings and RAG, FastAPI and pandas integration, testing and evals with pytest, observability, cost tracking and deployment.
courses.description:
Most Python LLM code starts as a notebook cell and ends up in production without changing shape: a global client, a hard-coded key, a for-loop over ten thousand rows, JSON parsed with a regex, and no tests because "the model is non-deterministic". This course teaches the engineering habits that turn that cell into a component you can trust. You set up a uv project with locked dependencies and typed settings, then call the official OpenAI (Responses API), Anthropic (Messages API) and Google GenAI (Interactions API) Python SDKs side by side, using the SDK versions current in October 2026.

From there you learn async clients, bounded concurrency with semaphores and rate-limit awareness, streaming, Pydantic models as the contract for structured outputs and tool calls, and timeouts and retries that do not multiply into outages. You run models locally with Ollama, llama-cpp-python, Hugging Face Transformers and ONNX Runtime, build a small embeddings-based RAG, and wire everything into a FastAPI service and a pandas batch pipeline. The final module covers testing without burning tokens (seams, transport mocks, recorded fixtures), eval tests in pytest, OpenTelemetry tracing and cost accounting, and packaging and shipping with uv and Docker.
audience: Python backend developers adding LLM features to services and APIs
Data engineers running LLM steps inside batch and pandas pipelines
ML engineers moving from notebooks to packaged, tested Python code
Tech leads setting Python standards for AI integration across a team

courses.title: Perl and AI: Modernizing Scripts and Text Pipelines with LLM APIs
courses.subtitle: For engineers who own production Perl and need to call LLM APIs from it safely, add AI steps to text pipelines, and use AI assistants to modernize legacy code without breaking it.
courses.summary: Call OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and local Ollama models from Perl with real CPAN modules, add streaming, concurrency and validated JSON output to text pipelines, and use AI coding assistants to modernize legacy Perl behind characterization tests.
courses.description:
A great deal of production text processing still runs on Perl: log parsers, ETL jobs, report generators, bioinformatics pipelines and glue scripts nobody wants to touch. Most LLM tutorials assume Python, but Perl talks HTTP and JSON perfectly well, and the CPAN ecosystem now has working options for every major provider.

This course shows how to integrate LLMs into real Perl code. You will compare the HTTP layers (HTTP::Tiny, LWP::UserAgent, Mojo::UserAgent, Furl), call providers directly over their REST APIs or through CPAN clients such as OpenAPI::Client::OpenAI, Langertha and WebService::Ollama, stream responses with Mojo::UserAgent and Mojo::Promise or IO::Async and Future::AsyncAwait, and enforce structured JSON output with Cpanel::JSON::XS and Type::Tiny. You will then add LLM steps to line-oriented pipelines with batching, caching and cost control, and test everything offline with Test2::V0 and mocked HTTP. The second half is about modernization: using AI assistants (GitHub Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT and similar) to explain unfamiliar code, write characterization tests before any change, and refactor incrementally toward strict/warnings, signatures, Moo or Object::Pad, Perl::Critic and Perl::Tidy, with an honest decision framework for when to port instead. Module versions and Perl releases are stated as of October 2026; the stable Perl at that date is 5.44.
audience: Engineers and sysadmins maintaining production Perl scripts, cron jobs and CGI/PSGI apps
Bioinformatics and research staff with Perl text-processing pipelines
Platform teams deciding whether to wrap, modernize or replace legacy Perl

Stream model output in Perl using Mojo::UserAgent or IO::Async with Future::AsyncAwait, and run bounded concurrent requests without exceeding rate limits

courses.title: TypeScript and Node.js AI Integration

courses.description:
TypeScript is now one of the main languages for shipping AI features, because the same code can run on a Node.js server, in a serverless function, on an edge runtime and in the browser. That flexibility comes with choices: official provider SDKs or a provider-neutral layer, server or edge, a hosted API or a model running in-process.

This course works through those choices with current tools. You will use the official SDKs (openai, @anthropic-ai/sdk and @google/genai), then the Vercel AI SDK (the ai package with @ai-sdk providers) for streaming text, typed objects and tool calls across vendors. You will define schemas once with Zod and get typed, validated outputs, stream tokens to React and other UIs, and control concurrency, cancellation and retries with AbortController and p-limit. You will compare agent layers (LangChain.js, Mastra, the OpenAI Agents SDK and the Claude Agent SDK) and expose or consume tools over the Model Context Protocol. For local and private work you will run models in-process with Transformers.js and node-llama-cpp or call Ollama. Finally you will test with Vitest and MSW, and package and deploy to Node.js LTS, Bun, Deno and Cloudflare Workers. Package versions are stated as of October 2026 (for example ai v7, zod v4, Node.js 24 as Active LTS).

Platform engineers deploying AI features to Node.js, serverless and edge runtimes

Most enterprise backends run on the JVM, and the JVM AI ecosystem has matured fast. Spring AI reached 2.0 on Spring Boot 4 with ChatClient, advisors, structured output and MCP support; LangChain4j offers declarative AI Services across Spring, Quarkus and Micronaut; OpenAI, Anthropic and Google all publish official Java SDKs; and Kotlin developers have JetBrains Koog and Embabel for agent workflows.

This course teaches how to choose and use these tools in real services. You will call providers through the official SDKs and through the frameworks, map model output to Java records and Kotlin data classes, expose methods as tools, and connect to Model Context Protocol servers with the MCP Java SDK. You will build retrieval with vector stores, stream responses with Reactor Flux or Kotlin Flow, and use virtual threads for high-concurrency blocking calls while keeping within provider rate limits. For private or offline workloads you will call Ollama or run ONNX Runtime and DJL models inside the JVM. You will test with mocks, WireMock and Testcontainers' Ollama module, evaluate output quality, and package and deploy with observability through Micrometer and OpenTelemetry. The .NET AI stack consolidated considerably during 2025 and 2026. Microsoft.Extensions.AI now provides a common IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator abstraction with middleware for caching, telemetry and function invocation; the official OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.GenAI SDKs all plug into it; Microsoft Agent Framework (GA since April 2026) has replaced Semantic Kernel as the recommended agent layer, with Semantic Kernel in maintenance mode; and local inference is available through ONNX Runtime GenAI, Foundry Local, LLamaSharp and Ollama.

This course teaches that stack the way production .NET code uses it. You will register chat clients through dependency injection, compose middleware pipelines, get strongly typed structured output into C# records, stream tokens with IAsyncEnumerable to ASP.NET Core endpoints and Blazor or SignalR clients, and handle concurrency with System.Threading.Channels and resilience with Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience. courses.title: SQL and Databases with AI: pgvector, In-Database AI and Text-to-SQL
courses.subtitle: For database developers and data engineers who need to store and search embeddings in SQL, call models from inside the database, and build text-to-SQL that is safe to point at real data.
courses.summary: Work with AI where the data already lives: vector types and indexes with pgvector and SQL Server 2025, hybrid search, in-database model calls in AlloyDB, Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks, embedding pipelines that stay in sync, and text-to-SQL with schema grounding, read-only guardrails and evaluation.
courses.description:
Most enterprise data that AI features need sits in relational databases and warehouses, and the databases have moved to meet that need. PostgreSQL has pgvector (with HNSW and IVFFlat indexes, halfvec and sparsevec types, and iterative index scans) plus pgvectorscale; SQL Server 2025 has a native VECTOR type and AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS; Oracle AI Database 26ai has AI Vector Search; and the cloud warehouses expose model calls as SQL functions, such as Snowflake Cortex AI Functions, BigQuery AI.GENERATE and Databricks ai_query.

This course teaches you to use these capabilities soundly. You will design vector columns and indexes, tune recall against latency, and combine vector similarity with full-text search and ordinary SQL filters. You will build embedding pipelines that keep vectors consistent with changing rows (triggers, queues or change data capture) now that one-step tools such as the Timescale pgai extension are no longer maintained. You will call models from SQL for classification, extraction and summarization at warehouse scale and control their cost. Then you will build text-to-SQL properly: schema and semantic-layer grounding, few-shot examples, read-only roles, query validation, row limits, and evaluation against your own question set, informed by public benchmarks such as Spider 2.0 and BIRD. Feature availability differs by product and some features (for example SQL Server 2025 vector indexes) are still in preview; all such facts are stated as of October 2026.

courses.subtitle: For statisticians, data scientists and analysts who work in R and need to call LLMs reproducibly, extract structured data from text at scale, and keep AI-assisted analysis statistically sound.
courses.summary: Use LLMs from R with ellmer and httr2: structured extraction into data frames, parallel and batch calls, local models through Ollama, retrieval with ragnar, evaluation with vitals, Shiny chat apps, and reproducible, tested workflows with renv, testthat and recorded HTTP.
courses.description:
R users now have a mature, tidy toolkit for working with language models. The ellmer package provides one interface to OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama and other providers, with tool calling, typed structured output via type_object and friends, and parallel_chat and batch_chat for running thousands of prompts. Around it sit ragnar for retrieval, vitals for evaluation, shinychat and querychat for applications, mall for row-wise LLM operations on data frames, and btw and mcptools for connecting R sessions to AI assistants.

This course teaches you to use that toolkit as a statistician would. You will extract structured variables from free text into tidy data, measure how reliable that extraction is against hand-coded samples, and treat model output as a measurement with error rather than ground truth. You will run large jobs with parallel and batch APIs and asynchronous code with mirai and promises, use local models for sensitive data, build retrieval over your documents, and ship Shiny apps with chat interfaces. You will keep everything reproducible with renv, pinned model versions, cached responses and testthat tests that replay recorded HTTP with vcr or httptest2. The course also covers AI coding assistance in RStudio and Positron and how to check generated analysis code. Package versions are as of October 2026 (R 4.6, ellmer 0.5).

courses.title: Julia for Scientific Machine Learning
courses.subtitle: For scientists and engineers who use Julia, or are evaluating it, to combine differential-equation models with neural networks, train them on CPUs and GPUs, and call LLMs from scientific code.
courses.summary: Scientific machine learning in Julia: universal differential equations, neural ODEs and physics-informed networks with SciML, Lux and ModelingToolkit; automatic differentiation with Enzyme, Zygote and Mooncake; GPU and multithreaded training; surrogates and symbolic regression; LLM calls with PromptingTools.jl; and testing and packaging research code.
courses.description:
Scientific machine learning combines mechanistic models, usually differential equations, with machine-learned components. The result can be more data-efficient, more extrapolable and more interpretable than either alone. Julia's SciML ecosystem is one of the most complete platforms for this work, because its solvers, symbolic modeling tools and automatic differentiation systems are designed to compose.

This course teaches that ecosystem in practice. You will model systems with OrdinaryDiffEq and ModelingToolkit, add neural components with Lux to build universal differential equations and neural ODEs, compute gradients through solvers with SciMLSensitivity using Enzyme, Zygote or Mooncake, and fit them with Optimization.jl. You will try physics-informed neural networks with NeuralPDE, learn interpretable equations back from trained models with DataDrivenDiffEq and SymbolicRegression, and build fast surrogates for expensive simulations. You will use threads, distributed processes and GPUs (CUDA.jl, AMDGPU.jl, KernelAbstractions.jl and Reactant.jl) efficiently, and call LLMs from Julia with PromptingTools.jl and local models through Ollama or LlamaCpp.jl. Finally you will make research code reliable with ReTestItems, Aqua and JET, and package it with Pkg and PackageCompiler or JuliaC. Versions are as of October 2026 (Julia 1.13, ModelingToolkit v11).
audience: Computational scientists and engineers in physics, chemistry, biology, climate and engineering
Research software engineers maintaining simulation codes
ML practitioners who need physics-informed or data-efficient models

Train and run models efficiently on multithreaded CPUs and NVIDIA or AMD GPUs, avoiding type instability and excess allocation

courses.description:
Most operational automation still lives in shell scripts, PowerShell modules and pipeline YAML. This course shows how to bring language models into that world without making it less safe or less predictable.

You start with the mechanics: calling vendor APIs from Bash with curl and jq and from PowerShell 7 with Invoke-RestMethod, requesting structured output and validating it before any script acts on it, and handling rate limits, timeouts and API keys correctly. You then work with terminal-native coding agents (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, Kiro CLI) in interactive and non-interactive modes, including permission and allowlist settings. The second half moves into pipelines: AI-assisted log triage and change review in GitHub Actions and GitLab CI, generating and refactoring scripts with lint and test gates (ShellCheck, PSScriptAnalyzer, bats-core, Pester), and a guardrail model for any automation that turns model output into commands. courses.description:
Phones now ship with system language models and capable neural engines, which changes what a mobile team can build without a server round trip. It also adds new failure modes: features that only work on some devices, models that are still downloading, tight context windows, battery and thermal limits, and app-size budgets.

This course covers both platforms in parallel. On iOS you use the Foundation Models framework (guided generation with @Generable types, tool calling, availability checks) and Core ML for your own models, with Core ML Tools for conversion and MLX Swift for experimentation. On Android you use the ML Kit GenAI APIs on top of AICore and Gemini Nano, and LiteRT and LiteRT-LM for custom models. You compare cross-platform options (ExecuTorch, ONNX Runtime Mobile), learn how to quantize and profile models on real devices, design hybrid flows that fall back to a cloud model through Firebase AI Logic or your own backend, and handle privacy, consent and store review. Platform features are stated as of October 2026; capability checks are taught as a habit precisely because availability keeps changing.

courses.description:
Infrastructure code is a strong fit for AI assistance because it is declarative, repetitive and well documented. It is also a risky one: a plausible-looking resource argument from an old provider version, a destroy hidden in a long plan, or a playbook that is not idempotent can cause outages that ordinary application bugs do not.

This course teaches a verify-everything workflow. For Terraform and OpenTofu you generate and refactor modules with an assistant grounded in current provider documentation (including through HashiCorp's Terraform MCP server), import existing resources, write terraform test suites, and use the model to explain plans rather than approve them. For Ansible you generate roles and playbooks, use Red Hat Ansible Lightspeed and the Ansible development tools, and prove idempotency with ansible-lint and Molecule. You then wire policy as code (Sentinel, OPA/Conftest, Checkov, Trivy) into CI so that every AI-assisted change faces the same gates, and finish with an operating model for agents that touch state, credentials and drift. Product capabilities are stated as of October 2026.

Many organizations will meet generative AI first through the platforms they already run their business on. Each vendor now offers an agent builder, a prompt or skill layer, a trust or governance layer, and ways to call external models and tools. Each also has its own data model, permission system and release cadence, and the details change several times a year.

This course gives developers a comparative, hands-on view. On Salesforce you build Agentforce agents with topics, actions and Agent Script, write prompt templates grounded in CRM and Data 360 data, and call models from Apex, with the Einstein Trust Layer as the control point. On ServiceNow you build custom skills with Now Assist Skill Kit and agents in AI Agent Studio, and govern them with AI Control Tower. On SAP you build Joule agents in Joule Studio, use the generative AI hub in SAP AI Core through the SAP Cloud SDK for AI from CAP applications, and see how ABAP code reaches the same services. The final modules cover cross-platform integration through MCP, A2A and APIs, testing and release management, and licensing and consumption models. Product names and features are as of October 2026; the course emphasizes the architectural patterns common to all three.

courses.title: Rust for AI: Candle, Burn, ONNX Runtime and High-Performance Services
courses.subtitle: For experienced Rust and systems engineers who want to run models in-process, bind to native inference libraries safely, and build memory-safe, high-throughput AI services.
courses.summary: Expert-level Rust for AI: in-process inference with Candle, Burn and ONNX Runtime (ort), bindings to llama.cpp through FFI, GPU integration with CUDA, PyO3 bridges to Python, and high-performance async services with batching, backpressure and observability. Emphasizes unsafe-code discipline, zero-copy data paths and measured performance.
courses.description:
Rust has become a serious option for the parts of an AI system where Python is too slow, too memory-hungry or too hard to deploy: tokenizers, pre- and post-processing, embedding and reranking services, edge inference and the serving layer itself. Doing this well requires more than calling a crate. You need to understand how tensors are laid out and moved, where the FFI boundary sits and what invariants it must uphold, how GPU memory and streams interact with async runtimes, and how to measure rather than guess.

The course starts with the ecosystem map and the decision between pure-Rust frameworks (Candle, Burn) and bindings to native runtimes (ONNX Runtime via ort, llama.cpp via bindgen-generated or community bindings). You load safetensors and GGUF weights, run transformer inference with Candle, build and export models with Burn and its CubeCL backends, and run ONNX models with execution providers. You then go below the safe APIs: writing sound FFI wrappers with bindgen and cxx, ownership and lifetimes across the boundary, Send/Sync for native handles, and CUDA integration through cudarc. The final modules build production services with Tokio and Axum (dynamic batching, backpressure, cancellation, streaming), expose Rust to Python with PyO3 and maturin, and cover profiling, allocation control, SIMD and release engineering. Crate versions move quickly; versions and API details are stated as of October 2026, and several key crates (including ort 2.x) were still on release candidates at that date.

courses.title: C and AI: Embedding Inference with llama.cpp and the ONNX Runtime C API
courses.subtitle: For C and embedded systems engineers who need to run models inside native programs, firmware-adjacent services and constrained hosts, with predictable memory and no Python at runtime.
courses.summary: Embed LLM and classic model inference directly in C programs: the llama.cpp/ggml C API and GGUF models, the ONNX Runtime C API, CUDA from C, memory and threading discipline, and the testing and fuzzing needed to make native inference code safe to ship.
courses.description:
C remains the lingua franca of native integration. Daemons, appliances, plugins and embedded Linux products often cannot take a Python runtime, a container or a network dependency, yet they increasingly need speech, vision or language features. The two most practical routes are llama.cpp (and its ggml tensor library) for LLM and speech workloads and ONNX Runtime's C API for everything that can be exported to ONNX.

This course works at the API level. You build llama.cpp as a library with the right backends, then drive the libllama C API directly: loading GGUF models, creating contexts, tokenizing, batching with llama_batch, managing the KV cache and sampling with sampler chains, plus whisper.cpp for speech. You run ONNX models through the OrtApi function table: environments, sessions, tensors, allocators, execution providers and error-status handling. You then go into memory and performance: memory-mapping weights, arena and custom allocators, threading models, NUMA and cache effects, quantization formats, and calling CUDA from C. The final module covers what makes native AI code shippable: an ABI-stable wrapper library, sanitizers, fuzzing GGUF and ONNX parsers, defending against malicious model files, and build and packaging practice. The llama.cpp C API evolves frequently; function names are taught as of October 2026 together with a method for tracking header changes.
audience: Senior C developers on Linux, embedded Linux or real-time-adjacent systems
Engineers maintaining native daemons, plugins or appliances that need AI features
Performance engineers who own memory and latency budgets
Engineers writing language bindings over C inference libraries
outcomes: Build llama.cpp and ONNX Runtime as libraries with the correct CPU and GPU backends and link them into a C program with a reproducible build
Implement a complete text-generation loop on the libllama C API, including batching, KV-cache management, sampler chains and correct resource teardown
Run ONNX models through the ONNX Runtime C API with explicit allocators, execution providers and status-checked error handling
Control memory and threading for native inference: mmap'd weights, arenas, thread pools and NUMA placement, with measured footprints
Call CUDA from C to manage device memory and streams around an inference library without leaks or implicit synchronizations
Harden native inference code with sanitizers, fuzzing of model-file parsers and treatment of model files as untrusted input
Design an ABI-stable C wrapper that other languages can bind to safely
prerequisites: Professional C experience: pointers, manual memory management, build systems (CMake or Make) and a debugger
Basic understanding of neural network inference (tensors, layers, quantization)

courses.title: C++ for AI: LibTorch, ONNX Runtime, TensorRT and CUDA Integration
courses.subtitle: For senior C++ engineers who must run models in-process at production latency on CPUs and NVIDIA GPUs, and build safe, high-throughput inference services around them.
courses.summary: Expert C++ for AI inference: exporting PyTorch models for C++ with torch.export and AOTInductor, LibTorch, the ONNX Runtime C++ API, building and running TensorRT engines, writing CUDA kernels and custom plugins, and designing concurrent, memory-safe inference services with measured performance.
courses.description:
When a model has to run inside a C++ product (a robot, an imaging pipeline, a trading system, a game engine or a high-throughput service), the hard problems are rarely the model itself. They are the export path from Python, the choice of runtime, memory ownership across CPU and GPU, concurrency, and keeping latency predictable under load.

This course covers the main production routes side by side. You export models with torch.export and package them with AOTInductor for C++ loading, and use LibTorch where its full API is needed (noting TorchScript's legacy status). You run ONNX models through the ONNX Runtime C++ API with execution providers and I/O binding. You build TensorRT engines from ONNX, manage precision (FP16, BF16, FP8, INT8 and FP4 where hardware supports it) through strongly typed networks and explicit quantization, dynamic shapes and optimization profiles, and run them with the TensorRT runtime API, including TensorRT for RTX on client GPUs. You then write CUDA code where libraries stop: custom kernels, TensorRT plugins, CUDA graphs, streams and pinned memory, with CUTLASS as a reference point. The final modules build concurrent inference services (thread pools, request batching, lifetime management with RAII, lock-free queues) and cover profiling with Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute, numerical validation against the Python reference, and build, packaging and ABI concerns. Version-specific facts are as of October 2026 (PyTorch 2.14, ONNX Runtime 1.31, TensorRT 11.4 with migration notes for teams still on 10.x, TensorRT for RTX 1.7, CUDA 13.4); TensorRT 11 made strongly typed networks mandatory, so reduced precision is expressed in the model graph rather than through builder flags.
audience: Senior C++ engineers in performance-critical products
Inference and serving engineers working below the Python layer
Robotics, imaging, trading and simulation teams adding learned models
Engineers maintaining C++ plugins for inference servers

courses.title: Fortran and HPC Codes: AI Surrogates in Scientific Simulation
courses.subtitle: For computational scientists and HPC developers who want to replace or accelerate expensive parts of Fortran and C++ simulation codes with machine-learned surrogates, without compromising correctness, scaling or reproducibility.
courses.summary: Couple trained neural-network surrogates to Fortran and C++ HPC simulations: choosing what to replace, generating training data from the simulation, coupling in-process with FTorch, TorchFort, Fiats, LibTorch or ONNX Runtime via iso_c_binding, running inference on GPUs alongside MPI ranks, online training, and validating stability, conservation and scaling.
courses.description:
Many scientific codes spend most of their time in a few expensive components: a radiation or microphysics parameterization, a chemistry solver, a closure model, a constitutive law. A trained surrogate can make those components orders of magnitude cheaper, but only if it is coupled efficiently, stays stable over long integrations, respects physical constraints and can be validated to the standard a scientific result requires.

This course takes the HPC developer's view. You start by identifying surrogate candidates with profiling and by designing training data generation from the simulation itself. You then couple models to Fortran in-process: FTorch (LibTorch-backed, no Python at runtime), NVIDIA's TorchFort (inference and online training driven from Fortran or C/C++), Berkeley Lab's Fiats (native Fortran 2023 inference), and ONNX Runtime through iso_c_binding, and compare these with remote or file-based coupling. For C++ codes you use LibTorch and ONNX Runtime directly, including from Kokkos-based applications. You place inference on GPUs alongside MPI ranks, batch across grid points, manage device memory shared with the solver, and train online while the simulation runs. The final modules cover what makes results trustworthy: a priori and a posteriori testing, long-run stability, conservation and constraint enforcement, fallbacks to the physics routine, uncertainty, reproducibility and scaling studies. Library facts are as of October 2026; several of these libraries are research software with evolving APIs, and the course teaches how to isolate them behind a stable interface.
audience: Computational scientists maintaining Fortran or C++ simulation codes
HPC software engineers and research software engineers
Climate, weather, CFD, materials and energy modelers exploring hybrid ML-physics models
HPC center staff supporting AI-coupled workflows

Design training data generation from a running simulation, including sampling of rare regimes and versioned, reproducible datasets
Couple a PyTorch model to a Fortran code with FTorch or TorchFort, and explain when Fiats or ONNX Runtime via iso_c_binding is the better fit
Integrate surrogate inference into a C++ or Kokkos-based code with LibTorch or ONNX Runtime, sharing device memory with the solver where possible
Place and batch inference on GPUs within an MPI-decomposed simulation and measure its effect on strong and weak scaling
Validate a hybrid model with a priori and a posteriori tests, long-run stability checks, conservation constraints and a physics fallback
Set up online training coupled to a running simulation and describe its numerical, reproducibility and resource risks
prerequisites: Professional experience with modern Fortran (2008 or later) or C++ in a scientific code
Working knowledge of MPI and of running jobs on an HPC cluster

courses.title: Event-Driven AI Integration: Kafka, Queues and Streaming
courses.subtitle: For backend and data engineers who put LLMs and ML models into event-driven systems and need them to be reliable, idempotent, cost-controlled and observable at stream scale.
courses.summary: Design event-driven architectures that call LLMs and ML models: Kafka topics, consumer groups and share groups, queues and DLQs, Flink SQL model inference, CDC-driven enrichment and embedding pipelines, durable agent workflows, and the idempotency, rate-limit, ordering and cost controls that make AI calls safe inside streams.
courses.description:
Model calls are slow, expensive, rate-limited and non-deterministic compared with the rest of a stream-processing pipeline. Putting them into event-driven systems naively produces duplicate charges, poison messages, consumer-lag spirals and results nobody can reproduce. Done well, events are the most natural way to run AI at scale: enrichment, classification, embedding refresh, document processing and agent workflows all become asynchronous, replayable and observable.

This course starts from messaging fundamentals as they apply to AI: delivery semantics, partitioning and ordering, consumer groups versus Kafka share groups (Queues for Kafka, production-ready in Kafka 4.2), and when a classic queue such as RabbitMQ, SQS, Pub/Sub, Service Bus or NATS JetStream fits better. You then build AI consumers with idempotency keys, retries, dead-letter topics, backpressure and provider rate-limit handling, and use batch APIs where latency allows. You run model inference inside stream processors with Flink SQL ML_PREDICT and managed Flink AI functions, keep vector indexes fresh with Debezium CDC, and design schemas and contracts with Schema Registry, CloudEvents and AsyncAPI. The final modules cover agentic and long-running work (durable workflows with Temporal, event-driven agents, human-in-the-loop steps), replay and reprocessing when models change, observability and cost control, and data protection in streams. Product capabilities are stated as of October 2026.

Data streaming engineers running Kafka or Flink
Architects designing event-driven and agentic systems

It teaches how to review AI output, protect PHI under HIPAA, and recognise where FDA and transparency rules draw the line.
courses.description:
AI arrived in clinical work through documentation first. Ambient scribes such as Microsoft Dragon Copilot and Abridge draft notes from the visit conversation, EHRs draft replies to patient portal messages, and evidence tools such as OpenEvidence and the clinician and healthcare editions of ChatGPT and Claude answer clinical questions with citations. This course teaches you to use these tools as a clinician who signs the note: how to consent patients to ambient recording, how to review a draft note for omissions and invented findings, and how to check a cited answer before it changes care.

The course also covers the guardrails. You will learn what makes a tool HIPAA-appropriate (a business associate agreement, not a marketing claim), why consumer chatbots are the wrong place for PHI, how FDA's clinical decision support guidance separates regulated devices from tools you can independently review, and what transparency information to ask for about predictive models in your EHR while federal certification requirements for that information are being revised. It closes with bias, automation complacency, patient communication and how to report an AI-related safety event. Product names and regulatory status are current as of October 2026; this course is educational and is not legal or medical-practice advice.
audience: Physicians and residents
Nurses and nurse practitioners
Physician assistants and allied health professionals
Clinical informatics champions and department leads
outcomes: Explain how ambient AI scribes, EHR-embedded drafting and clinical AI search tools work and where each fails
Obtain patient consent for ambient documentation and review an AI-drafted note for omissions, errors and fabricated findings
Verify an AI-generated clinical answer against its cited sources before acting on it
Determine whether a given AI tool and workflow is appropriate for PHI under HIPAA and your organisation's policy
Distinguish non-device clinical decision support from FDA-regulated AI-enabled device software at a practical level
Recognise automation bias and dataset bias in clinical AI and report AI-related safety events through the right channel
prerequisites: Active clinical role or clinical training

courses.title: AI for Operations and Supply Chain Teams
courses.subtitle: For planners, buyers, logistics coordinators and ops managers who want to use AI to forecast, handle exceptions and talk to suppliers faster, without losing control of the plan.
courses.summary: A hands-on course on everyday AI for operations work: reading forecasts and their error, investigating exceptions in natural language, drafting supplier and carrier communications, and summarising S&OP inputs. It covers both general assistants and the copilots and agents built into ERP and planning suites.
courses.description:
Operations teams live in exceptions: a late container, a forecast that missed, a supplier that changed a confirmation date. This course shows how AI helps with that work today. You will learn what machine-learning forecasts in planning systems actually do and how to read forecast error, how to use general assistants and Excel with Copilot to investigate a shortage or a cost variance, and how the copilots and agents in Microsoft Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Management, SAP (Joule in S/4HANA and IBP), Oracle Fusion SCM, Kinaxis Maestro and Blue Yonder are designed to surface risks and draft actions.

It then turns to communication and control. You will draft supplier, carrier and customer messages with AI, summarise contracts and specs for the key terms that matter, and build a short S&OP pre-read. Throughout, the course stresses the line between an AI recommendation and an executed transaction: who approves, what gets logged, and which data (pricing, supplier terms, customer orders) must stay inside approved tools. Product capabilities are described as of October 2026 and vary by licence and release; check your own system before relying on a specific feature.

courses.title: Leading Engineering Teams with AI Coding Agents
courses.subtitle: For engineering managers, tech leads and staff engineers who must roll out autonomous coding agents, keep quality and security intact, and measure whether it is working.
courses.summary: A leadership course on moving from autocomplete to agents that open pull requests. It covers choosing and configuring Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot's coding agent and Cursor; preparing repositories with AGENTS.md and good tests; reviewing agent-authored code; securing agents and MCP integrations; and measuring impact with DORA-style metrics instead of anecdotes.
courses.description:
Coding assistants have become coding agents: tools such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot's coding agent (and GitHub Agent HQ, which runs several of them side by side) and Cursor's cloud agents can take an issue, change many files, run tests and open a pull request. That changes the job of an engineering leader. This course is about the decisions that follow: which work to delegate to agents, how to make a codebase agent-ready with AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md instructions, fast tests and clear conventions, and how to change code review when a large share of diffs were not written by a person.

You will also work through the risks that matter at team level: secrets and production credentials in agent sandboxes, prompt injection through issues and dependencies, permissions for MCP servers and tools, licence and provenance questions, and the quiet erosion of junior engineers' skills. The course closes with measurement, using the DORA AI Capabilities Model and delivery metrics to separate real throughput gains from rising instability, and with a phased rollout plan. Tool capabilities and plan availability are described as of October 2026 and change frequently.
audience: Engineering managers and directors
Tech leads and staff or principal engineers
Platform and developer-experience teams
Heads of engineering evaluating agent tooling

Prepare a repository for agent work with instruction files, reliable tests, CI gates and scoped permissions
Decide which tasks to delegate to agents and write issue specifications agents can complete reliably
Adapt code review, ownership and merge policies for agent-authored pull requests
Identify and mitigate security risks from coding agents, including secret exposure, prompt injection and over-privileged MCP tools

courses.title: AI Product Management: From Use Case to Launch
courses.subtitle: For product managers taking an AI feature from idea to launch: choose problems AI actually solves, write specs that include evals and failure behavior, decide build versus buy, and ship with the right gates.
courses.summary: The product manager's playbook for AI features. You learn to screen use cases for AI fit, run discovery with real model output, write a spec that defines quality with an eval set, choose between APIs, open-weight models and fine-tuning, and plan a staged launch with risk, compliance and support ready on day one.
courses.description:
AI features fail differently from conventional software: the output is probabilistic, quality is hard to define, costs scale with use, and vendors change models underneath you. This course adapts the product manager's job to those facts. It starts with use-case selection, asking where the cost of an error is tolerable and a human can check the result, then moves to discovery techniques that use real model output, such as Wizard-of-Oz tests and prompt prototypes in tools like Google AI Studio, the OpenAI and Anthropic consoles or a no-code assistant builder.

You then write the AI product requirements document: target behavior, an eval set as the acceptance criteria, failure and fallback behavior, latency and cost budgets. You decide among hosted APIs (direct or through Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry), open-weight models and fine-tuning, and plan the launch: risk review, EU AI Act transparency duties, staged rollout behind feature flags, and the support and feedback loops that keep a feature improving after launch. Metrics and experiments are covered in depth in prd-203, UX patterns in prd-202 and pricing in prd-301. Facts are stated as of October 2026. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Product managers responsible for a first or second AI feature
Founders and product leads deciding where AI belongs in a roadmap
Engineering and design leads who co-own AI product decisions

Run discovery with prompt prototypes and Wizard-of-Oz tests before committing engineering effort
Write an AI product requirements document with an eval set as acceptance criteria and explicit fallback behavior

courses.subtitle: For designers and product teams building AI features: design interfaces that set accurate expectations, show their work, recover from errors and keep people in control, from chat to agents.
courses.summary: A practical course on AI interaction design. You apply Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction and Google's People + AI Guidebook to real patterns: onboarding and expectation setting, chat versus embedded AI, streaming and latency, citations and uncertainty, error recovery, agent approvals, transparency labels and accessibility.
courses.description:
Generative AI breaks familiar interface assumptions: the same input gives different outputs, answers can be fluent and wrong, and agents take actions on a user's behalf. Good AI UX makes these properties visible and manageable instead of hiding them. This course builds on published research-based guidance, including Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (HAX), Google's People + AI Guidebook and Apple's Human Interface Guidelines for generative AI, and turns it into patterns you can use in design reviews.

Modules cover choosing the right surface (chat, inline assistance, a command bar or a background agent), designing input with prompt scaffolds and examples, presenting output with streaming, citations and appropriate confidence cues, recovering gracefully from errors and refusals, and designing approvals and activity logs for agents. You also learn the transparency requirements that now shape interfaces, including EU AI Act Article 50 disclosure and labeling duties and C2PA Content Credentials, plus accessibility under WCAG 2.2 and how to usability-test non-deterministic features. Facts are stated as of October 2026. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Product and UX designers working on generative AI features
Product managers who review AI interaction designs
Front-end engineers implementing streaming, citations and agent interfaces

Choose between chat, inline, command and background-agent surfaces for a given task
Design onboarding and empty states that set accurate expectations of capability and limits

courses.subtitle: For product managers, analysts and data scientists: define what success means for an AI feature, connect offline evals to product metrics, and run online experiments that hold up to scrutiny.
courses.summary: How to measure AI features end to end. You build a metric tree from business outcome to model quality, instrument implicit and explicit feedback, link offline eval scores to online behavior, and design A/B tests for non-deterministic features with guardrail metrics, variance reduction and sequential testing.
courses.description:
AI features are easy to demo and hard to measure. Usage can rise while value falls, thumbs-up rates mislead, and offline eval scores do not always predict what users do. This course gives product teams a measurement system. You start with a metric tree linking a business outcome to task success, quality and cost, adapt frameworks such as HEART and north-star metrics to AI, and decide what to log, including acceptance, edit distance, retries, escalations and abandonment.

You then connect evaluation to product decisions: how offline eval sets (covered technically in bld-230) become ship criteria, and how to check that eval gains move product metrics. The experimentation modules cover A/B test design for features whose output varies, randomization units, novelty effects, guardrail and cost metrics, CUPED variance reduction and sequential testing, using platforms such as Statsig, Optimizely, GrowthBook, LaunchDarkly and Datadog Experiments, which Datadog built on its 2025 acquisition of Eppo. The course closes with dashboards, readouts and decisions when results conflict. Facts are stated as of October 2026. It ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.

courses.title: Pricing and Unit Economics of AI Products
courses.subtitle: For product, finance and pricing leads: model the true cost to serve an AI product, choose between seat, usage, credit and outcome-based pricing, protect gross margin, and run billing that customers trust.
courses.summary: An expert course on the economics of AI products. You build a cost-to-serve model from tokens, caching, retrieval, tools and infrastructure, compare seat, usage, credit, hybrid and outcome-based pricing using public examples, design packaging and limits that protect margin, and implement metering and billing with tools such as Stripe Billing, Metronome and Orb.
courses.description:
AI breaks the near-zero marginal cost assumption behind classic SaaS pricing. Every request carries model, retrieval and tool costs; heavy users can cost many times more than light ones; and vendor price cuts and new models shift the cost base every quarter. This course teaches the economics end to end. You build a cost-to-serve model per task, per user and per account, including prompt caching and batch discounts, reasoning-token variance, retrieval and vector storage, agent tool calls, and the break-even between API usage and self-hosted inference.

You then study pricing models through public, documented examples: per-seat AI add-ons, usage and credit systems such as Salesforce Agentforce Flex Credits, outcome-based pricing such as the per-resolution model of the Fin AI agent (sold by the company formerly named Intercom, which renamed itself Fin in May 2026), and GitHub Copilot's June 2026 move from premium-request allowances to usage-based billing with monthly AI credits. You learn to package tiers, set fair-use limits and overage, forecast gross margin under different usage distributions, and run metering and billing on Stripe Billing (including Metronome, which Stripe acquired in January 2026), Orb or an in-house ledger. Price points are stated as of October 2026 and treated as examples to analyze, not benchmarks. The course ends in an automated exam; passing earns a Wirewalk Institute of AI certificate of completion and assessment.
audience: Product and pricing leads at software companies adding AI to their products
Finance and FP&A staff modeling AI gross margin
Founders setting pricing for an AI-native product
